takaichi-rejects-weak-yen-bond-yield-cri:
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has rejected criticism that she was on one hand responsible for a weak yen and on the other for pushing up interest rates in the country.

Speaking in parliament, Takaichi said; "I have been repeatedly criticized for 'Takaichi's weak yen' and 'Takaichi's high interest rates,' but I clearly deny that," according to a Reuters translation of her remarks in Japanese.

She was responding to a question from an opposition party lawmaker Yoshifumi Hamano, who asked about the compilation of a second supplementary budget for the country.

Takaichi also said that her administration will increase confidence in the yen by building a strong economy.

Under her administration, yields on Japanese government bonds have risen to multi-decade highs, while the yen weakened to its lowest since 1986, prompting Tokyo and even Washington to step into the forex market to support the currency.

In January, Takaichi had reportedly said that a weak yen presented an opportunity for export industries and acted as a buffer against U.S. tariffs, though she quickly clarified that she held no specific preference for the currency's direction.

Japan's exports have been partly boosted by yen's depreciation, as a weak currency makes exports more competitive.

For bond markets, Takaichi said that "We intend to appropriately control the amount of government bond issuance," at a time when yields have been rising as Japan's central bank raises its policy rate and continues to normalize its monetary policy.

Earlier this year, Takaichi had announced a plan to cut the country's food tax and unveiled a supplementary budget earlier this year, raising the possibility that Japan might need to issue more bonds to sustain its government spending.

Takaichi has said that the total bond issuance for calendar year 2026 would remain unchanged from the original budget plan, according to Bloomberg, although experts were skeptical.

Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group told CNBC back in April — when the supplementary budget was announced — that "Bond markets are a lot of things, but they're not stupid. You cannot increase spending without increasing debt."

An NYC school bus driver failed to deliver six nonverbal special education students to school for nearly four and a half hours last December — leaving one child lying soaking wet in her own urine in a bus seat, investigators said Friday.

Driver Eric Chery bounced between the wrong schools and completely missed his morning drop-off window at PS 289 in Crown Heights on Dec. 16, 2025, according to the Special Commissioner of Investigation for the New York City School District, Anastasia Coleman.

“It is highly disturbing that six nonverbal children were left on a school bus for hours while their whereabouts remained unknown to school officials,” Coleman said in a statement.

“These particularly vulnerable students rely on the adults entrusted with their care to ensure their safety.”

Instead of pulling up between 8:20 a.m. and 9:00 a.m., Chery didn’t show up until 1:25 p.m. — nearly five hours late.

School staff then contacted Consolidated Bus Transit — the contractor who employed Chery — around 10 a.m. but received no response.

Official Department of Education GPS data later revealed that Chery was outside one student’s home as late as 10:59 a.m., despite the fact that Chery claimed all students were picked up by 10 a.m.

A mother of two of the students used tracking devices tucked inside their backpacks to determine that her children were traveling all across Brooklyn as well.

At 11:45 a.m., a bus dispatcher told school staff the driver was lost but said he would arrive in 15 minutes.

He never showed — forcing school officials to report the missing children to the NYPD.

When the bus finally arrived at P.S. 289, also known as “The Brower School,” in Crown Heights around 1:25 p.m., school staff inspected the bus and found that one child had urinated on herself, removed her own diaper and leggings and was laying down flat on the bus floor soaking wet, investigators said.

Germina Thomas, a bus matron of nearly 20 years, admitted to investigators that she didn’t speak with the driver during his morning trip, and she did not attempt to contact the school, bus depot or anyone else for help.

It is not immediately clear if Chery was arrested.

Councilmember Gale Brewer said that school bus delays are not uncommon.

“As the former Chair of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, I held hearings on this issue in November 2022, issued reports, and requested audits,” said Brewer in a statement.

“At the time, 350 school buses experienced delays daily, and the problem continues,” she said.

“SCI has highlighted one important case affecting several students, their families, and their schools, but this is not an isolated situation.”

Consolidated Bus Transit, the special commissioner of investigation and the NYC Department of Education did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

NYPD is looking into the incident and could not immediately provide The Post with additional information.

Local prosecutors said that at least 15 people have been arrested in connection with the riots that broke out in Limoges and the arson which destroyed the city’s historic City Hall.

The supposed demonstration against the cost of living and education spending on Saturday evening saw the destruction of Limoges City Hall, an 1883 Neo-Renaissance building designed to pay homage to Paris’s Hôtel de Ville.

Designated as a historic monument in 1975, the 143-year-old building was largely destroyed in a fire allegedly set by rioters who entered the building. Dramatic images shared on social media show the building’s tower collapsing amid the conflagration.

According to Limoges prosecutor Emilie Abrantes, police have made “more than 15 arrests” in connection with the fire and the riots, which also saw six police cars burned and multiple businesses in the city centre looted.

The Limoges-based Le Populaire du Centre newspaper reported that, according to a City Hall source, “the rioters entered through a cellar door beneath the council chamber. They reportedly threatened to kill those inside.

During the demonstration on 17 October in Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France on 17 October 2026. (Photo by Elise Cabane / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)

Abrantes said that her entire office has been mobilised to deal with the riots, vowing to “provide a very firm response regarding these criminal acts. The law must prevail.”

Responding to the attack, Mayor of Limoges Guillaume Guérin said while holding a charred French flag rescued from the burnt building: “What happened is unacceptable, shameful; there are no words to condemn it, it’s so despicable.”

“Tonight, I feel pain for my country. Especially in Limoges with the destruction of our City Hall, our common home. It’s hard for me, for the people of Limoges, for those who believe in the values ​​of the Republic. I am very sad for the users, for the people of Limoges. Tonight, they destroyed a magnificent historical building, one that the people of Limoges love, but the Republic will endure.”

Like the federal government, Mayor Guérin also placed blame for the riots on the far-left, whom he accused of “inciting violence”.

“I’ve heard elected officials say that violence is legitimate, and well, this is what happens! It’s hatred of institutions, of high school principals, of the police, of elected officials. These weren’t petty criminals who did this; these were very methodical, organised people. I have no doubt that once the truth comes out, one thing is certain: the perpetrators will be brought to justice,” he said.

Guérin singled out the “behaviour of La France Insoumise”, the far-left party of French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélencon, noting the “presence of two LFI parliamentarians at the start of the demonstration” on Saturday.

This photograph shows a fire burning and destroying the city hall after a group of individuals forced entry into the building during ongoing protest action against the “high cost of living”, in Limoges, central France on October 17, 2026. (Photo by PASCAL LACHENAUD / AFP via Getty Images)

Others expressed similar sentiments, with French MEP Marion Maréchal saying that the burning of the Limoges Town Hall was a “terrible allegory of 10 years of Macronism that have prepared the chaos carried by Mélenchon’s New France.”

Maréchal said earlier this week that the youth protests and riots were a result of mass migration and the failure to integrate people who have a “hatred of France“.

Limoges residents also expressed their dismay over the destruction of the local monument. A high school student said: “My grandmother’s house is 100 meters away. I saw my grandmother cry. My parents got married in that town hall. It’s an attack on the Republic. I’m scared. How far will this go? It’s frightening. I’m so angry about these unacceptable extremist political opportunisms. I’m speechless… It’s the beginning of a civil war.

As more companies insist their employees return to the office, they know they need to offer something in return to attract and retain good people. That's why finding a place where people will want to live is an increasingly important factor as companies decide where to set up shop.

"Quality of place, especially investing in quality of place, is the top thing you can do for talent attraction and retention," said site selection consultant Larry Gigerich, managing executive director of Ginovus in Indianapolis, and chairman of the Site Selectors Guild.

CNBC is placing increasing emphasis on Quality of Life, one of the 10 categories of competitiveness in our annual America's Top States for Business study. It is our annual ranking of every state's business climate, now in its 20th year. Under this year's methodology, the category makes up 11.6% of a state's overall score, up from about ten percent last year.

To score the states for quality of life, we use hard data on factors like crime rates, air quality and healthcare. We also consider the cost and availability of childcare, inclusiveness of state laws, and reproductive rights. Some states offer exemplary quality of life. But these ten states do not make the grade.

Arkansas is a most-improved state overall this year in our annual rankings, but nearly 19% of its households lack the resources to put adequate food on the table, placing the Natural State dead last for food insecurity, according to the United Health Foundation. Last year, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed legislation guaranteeing free breakfast in public schools, but there is clearly more work to do. Arkansas also has one of the highest violent crime rates in the nation, according to FBI statistics, and among the weakest protections against discrimination, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

2026 Quality of Life score: 103 out of 290 points (Top States grade: D–)

Strengths: Childcare, Air Quality

Weaknesses: Crime, Health, Inclusiveness

Oklahoma imposes one of America's strictest bans on abortion, even though studies, including one by the National Bureau of Economic Research last year, found abortion bans increase net migration outflows, particularly among single adults. The Sooner State ranked 40th for worker protections last year, according to Oxfam America, which said that the state's $7.25 minimum wage covers only about 19% of the cost of living for a family of four, and noted that state law prohibits municipalities from setting their minimum wages any higher. A ballot measure last month to have voters approve a minimum wage increase failed.

2026 Quality of Life score: 103 out of 290 points (Top States grade: D–)

Strengths: Childcare, Air Quality

Weaknesses: Reproductive Rights, Worker Protections

Alabama ranks dead last for mental health providers per capita, even though nearly a quarter of residents have been told by a health professional that they have a depressive disorder. Alabama also ranks at the bottom for its worker protections, which include only two of the 16 measures that Oxfam America considers critical (mandating equal pay by gender and race, and restricting access to salary history). Workers lack other basic protections including mandatory paid sick leave and protections against sexual harassment. Alabama is one of five states with no public accommodation law protecting non-disabled people against discrimination, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

2026 Quality of Life score: 99 out of 290 points (Top States grade: D–)

Strengths: Childcare, Air Quality

Weaknesses: Worker Protections, Health, Inclusiveness

With 462 violent offenses per 100,000 residents in 2024, according to FBI crime statistics, Missouri is among America's most violent states. The Show-Me State also ranked in the top 10 for firearm deaths last year. In June, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed a sweeping crime bill aimed at helping to get the situation under control. It includes tougher sentences, a greater ability to charge juveniles as adults, and several new offenses involving cyberstalking and the use of drones.

For all its natural beauty, Utah is not the healthiest place to live, ranking No. 47 for primary care providers. Air quality leaves something to be desired, with high ozone levels, according to the American Lung Association. The Beehive State gets its nickname from the industriousness of its workers. And Utah has just 513 licensed childcare centers in a state with 3.5 million people, according to Child Care Aware of America.

"Georgia still remains a state where there is no place for hate, and I can assure all Georgians of that today," Republican Gov. Brian Kemp said in April, when he signed a bill aimed at protecting religious freedom.

sozialdemokratie_oesterreich_babler_2026:
Nr. 42 – 15. Oktober 2026

Woran linke Hoffnungsträger:innen scheitern können, wenn sie einmal an die Macht gewählt sind. Andreas Babler liefert ein Lehrstück.

Florian Bayer, Wien

Politik mit «Herz und Hirn» wollte er machen. «Ordnen statt spalten» war seine Devise. Ein «Comeback der Sozialdemokratie» rief er aus. Gekommen ist es anders. Andreas Babler, der linke Hoffnungsträger aus Österreich, hat seinen schrittweisen Rückzug als Vizekanzler und Parteichef angekündigt. Nur Minister will er bleiben. Unter ihm erreichte die SPÖ 2024 ihr bisher schlechtestes Wahlergebnis – und verlor seither weiter.

Damit hat die Linke, die andernorts mit dem Demokraten Zohran Mamdani in New York oder Elif Eralp von Die Linke in Berlin auf der Erfolgswelle surft, einen Hoffnungsträger verloren. Dabei war Babler einst selbst ein Vorbild. Das US-Magazin «Jacobin» feierte ihn nach seiner Wahl zum Parteichef im Juni 2023 als «Österreichs Bernie Sanders», Tausende Linke traten seinetwegen in die SPÖ ein. Gerade Österreich hatte einen wie ihn bitter nötig. Linke Politik fristet ein Nischendasein, stärkste Kraft ist mit Abstand die rechtsextreme FPÖ. Warum also ist Babler gescheitert? Und ist er das überhaupt?

Die SPÖ steckt seit Jahren in der Krise. Der Bundeskanzler ging ihr schon Ende 2017 verloren, was mit eigenen Fehlern, aber auch dem Aufkommen eines gewissen Sebastian Kurz zu tun hatte. Der Rechtspopulist führte die konservative Volkspartei (ÖVP) zurück an die Spitze, die SPÖ landete in der Opposition. Die folgenden Jahre waren von interner Zerstrittenheit geprägt – und einer fehlenden Linie bei Kernthemen wie Migration und Klimaschutz. Offen blieb auch, wofür eine moderne Sozialdemokratie heute stehen soll.

Anfang 2023 fiel die SPÖ in Umfragen hinter die FPÖ zurück, dazu kamen Verluste bei den Landtagswahlen in Niederösterreich und Kärnten. Parteichefin Pamela Rendi-Wagner geriet stark unter Druck, eine Mitgliederbefragung sollte über den Vorsitz entscheiden. Rendi-Wagner landete dabei knapp auf Platz drei und trat ab. Übrig blieb ein Duell zwischen dem burgenländischen Landeshauptmann Hans Peter Doskozil, einem Vertreter des rechten Flügels – und dem dezidiert linken Babler, der zuvor jahrelang Bürgermeister der Kleinstadt Traiskirchen südlich von Wien gewesen war, die vor allem für das grösste Flüchtlingslager Österreichs bekannt ist. Als einer, der sich beständig für eine humane Flüchtlingspolitik einsetzte, wurde er in den Jahren der sogenannten Migrationskrise überregional bekannt (siehe WOZ Nr. 10/24).

Im parteiinternen Wahlkampf versprach Babler vieles: Eine Vermögens- und Erbschaftssteuer. Eine Fachärzt:in-Termingarantie binnen vierzehn Tagen. Eine sechste Ferienwoche. Eine Reduktion der Wochenarbeitszeit auf 32 Stunden. Ein Ende von Postenschacher und Politikfilz. Und das scheinbar Unmögliche gelang: Babler setzte sich bei der Kampfabstimmung im Juni 2023 durch. Mit 53 Prozent zwar knapp, aber doch.

Dass die Partei geeint hinter ihm stand, kann man nicht behaupten. Seinen parteiinternen Gegner:innen galt Babler als zu «klassenkämpferisch», zumal er sich im Vorsitzwahlkampf als Marxist bezeichnet hatte. Belastend wirkte zudem ein Satz aus dem Jahr 2020. Damals hatte Babler die EU als «aggressivstes aussenpolitisches militärisches Bündnis» bezeichnet, «schlimmer als die Nato». Später spielte er das als «semantische Spitzfindigkeiten» herunter.

Bei seiner ersten Nationalratswahl im Herbst 2024 holte Bablers SPÖ nur 21 Prozent, ein historischer Tiefstwert für die einst staatstragende Partei. Erst verhandelten die konservative ÖVP, die SPÖ und die liberale Neos, doch die Gespräche platzten. Dann verhandelte die ÖVP mit der FPÖ, und es drohte ein Kanzler Herbert Kickl (FPÖ). Anfang März 2025 trat schliesslich doch die ursprünglich geplante Dreierkoalition an. Unter ÖVP-Chef Christian Stocker wurde Babler Vizekanzler sowie Minister für Medien, Kultur, Sport und Wohnen.

Und es gab durchaus Erfolge. Die Abgabe für Banken, die Bremse bei den Mieten, der halbierte Steuersatz auf Lebensmittel – all das wäre ohne die SPÖ kaum gekommen. Der Mietpreisdeckel entlastet 2,7 Millionen Menschen, Bezüger:innen der Mindestsicherung zahlen inzwischen einen vergünstigten Energietarif. Gegen interne Widerstände holte Babler zudem Markus Marterbauer vom linken Parteiflügel ins Kabinett, den ersten SPÖ-Finanzminister seit 25 Jahren.

Als Teil eines ideologisch bunt gemischten Bündnisses hatte es die SPÖ aber von vornherein schwer. Grosse Reformen gelangen bisher nicht, die meisten Babler-Versprechen erwiesen sich als nicht haltbar – zumal gegen Österreich ein EU-Defizitverfahren läuft und gespart werden muss.

Über allem lag die Teuerung. 2025 betrug die Inflation im Schnitt 3,6 Prozent. Im Januar 2026 sank sie kurz auf 2 Prozent, seither ist sie wieder gestiegen. Dazu kamen Wirtschaftsflaute und Kündigungswellen; gerade da blieb die SPÖ sozialpolitisch hinter den Erwartungen zurück. Dringend nötige Strukturreformen bei Rente, Gesundheit, Schulen oder Sozialhilfe blieben aus, wofür freilich auch die Koalitionspartner Verantwortung tragen.

Hinzu kam der Konflikt mit dem Boulevard: Als Medienminister drehte Babler den Geldhahn für Regierungsinserate weitgehend zu. Bund, Länder und Kammern gaben im ersten Halbjahr 2025 nur mehr 3,2 statt 18,7 Millionen Euro für Werbung in den Medien aus. Babler blieb bei diesem Kurs. Das «ungeordnete Rausschiessen von Inseraten» müsse beendet werden, sagte er. Ein überfälliger Schritt in einem Land, in dem die Abhängigkeit der Presse von Regierungsgeld unter den Kanzlern Werner Faymann und Sebastian Kurz ihr grösstes Ausmass erreicht hatte. Die üppigen Inserate hatten die Branche bequem gemacht, Innovation blieb aus.

Das Zurückfahren der Werbegelder hatte aber seinen Preis. Seither arbeiten sich die drei grossen Boulevardzeitungen an Babler ab. Auch die geplante Neuordnung der Medienförderung, die stärker Qualität statt Auflage belohnen soll, ist ihnen ein Dorn im Auge. Es geht um Millionen. Wohl ein Grund, warum «Kronen Zeitung», «Österreich» und «Heute» gerade wieder so heftig gegen Babler Stimmung machen; im Übrigen auch gegen die gesamte Bundesregierung, deren «letzte Chance» ein sofortiger Abgang Bablers auch als Medienminister sei.

Den grössten Schaden richtete aber, wie so oft, die eigene Partei an. In der SPÖ ist die Macht auf viele Zentren verteilt, von den Gewerkschaften bis zu den Landesparteien. Gerade die drei sozialdemokratischen Landeshauptleute verfolgen gerne eigene Interessen. Gewicht hat insbesondere die Wiener Landespartei, ohne die lange Zeit gar nichts ging.

Im Februar dieses Jahres lotete Exkanzler Christian Kern eine Rückkehr an die Parteispitze aus. Er sagte aber ab, als sich wichtige Teile der Partei nicht hinter ihn stellten, allen voran die Wiener Genoss:innen. Beim Parteitag im März kam Babler ohne Gegenkandidat:innen auf 81,5 Prozent – nur ein SPÖ-Chef vor ihm schnitt je schlechter ab. Babler sprach dennoch von einem «starken Zeichen». Die Umfragen sahen die SPÖ da bei achtzehn Prozent.

Zuletzt war die Partei auf nur mehr fünfzehn Prozent gefallen. Dann brachte sich Ende September der 71-jährige Medienmanager und frühere ORF-Chef Gerhard Zeiler ins Spiel, per Interview in der «Kronen Zeitung». Manche trauten dem langjährigen Sozialdemokraten durchaus zu, die Partei aus der Krise zu führen. Doch der Alleingang verärgerte viele Funktionär:innen, und was er inhaltlich anders machen wollte, blieb vage.

Zeilers Vorstoss entfachte die Debatte über Babler aber endgültig neu, und die Landesparteichefs drängten ihn nun offen zum Rückzug. Anfang Oktober einigte sich die Parteispitze nun nach langen Beratungen auf folgende Lösung: Anfang 2027 übernimmt Finanzminister Marterbauer das Amt des Vizekanzlers. Die Partei führt Babler bis Jahresende gemeinsam mit Frauenministerin Eva-Maria Holzleitner und Fraktionschef Philip Kucher, danach übernehmen die beiden allein. Wer die SPÖ darüber hinaus leitet, soll im Frühjahr feststehen. Babler wird weiterhin Minister für Medien, Sport und Wohnen bleiben, die Medienreform kann er so selbst zu Ende bringen. An der Koalition soll sich nichts ändern: ÖVP, SPÖ und Neos wollen weiterregieren, allen Buhrufen von FPÖ und Boulevard zum Trotz.

Marterbauer geniesst in der Regierung den Ruf grosser Sachkenntnis, und kein anderes Kabinettsmitglied schneidet in Beliebtheitsumfragen besser ab. Der 61-jährige Keynesianer leitete einst die Ökonomieabteilung der Arbeiterkammer Wien und wirbt wie Babler für Vermögens- und Erbschaftssteuern. Doch auch er hat Kratzer – etwa durch die neue «Paketsteuer», mit der er das Versprechen brach, keine neuen Steuern einzuführen. Offen ist allerdings, wie belastbar Marterbauer in seiner neuen Rolle sein wird. Mit Verweis auf seine Krebserkrankung hatte er eine Kandidatur bis vor kurzem noch abgelehnt. Jetzt muss er rasch genesen.

Viel Zeit bleibt nicht. Die nächste Nationalratswahl ist zwar planmässig erst 2029, doch schon in rund einem Jahr muss sich die SPÖ in Oberösterreich und Tirol schwierigen Landtagswahlen stellen. Dass mit der Rochade nun Ruhe einkehrt, darf bezweifelt werden.

Dreieinhalb Jahre stand der linke Hoffnungsträger an der Spitze der SPÖ, anderthalb davon in der Regierung. Ist Babler also gescheitert? Bei seinen eigenen Versprechen gewiss. Aber er hat die SPÖ zurück in die Regierung geführt, einiges durchgesetzt und sich mit mächtigen Medienhäusern angelegt. Vor allem ist er an einer Partei gescheitert, die ihre Vorsitzenden verschleisst und bis heute nicht geklärt hat, wofür sie letztlich steht.

Lehrreich ist das auch für die Linke anderswo. Babler hat gezeigt, dass einer, der authentisch auftritt und offen für Umverteilung eintritt, Menschen begeistern kann. Er hat aber zu viel auf einmal versprochen, wohingegen sich Mamdani und Eralp auf ein Thema konzentrierten – das leistbare Leben in der Stadt – und damit gewannen.

Schwieriger wird es nach der Wahl. Babler musste als Juniorpartner unter Sparzwang regieren, mit einer Partei, die ihm nie geschlossen folgte. Das hat seine Glaubwürdigkeit aufgezehrt. Eralp steht nun vor einer ähnlichen Herausforderung: Regieren kann sie nur mit SPD und Grünen. Dass linke Versprechen dem Regierungsalltag langfristig standhalten, müssen auch die Hoffnungsträger:innen in New York und Berlin erst unter Beweis stellen. ●

OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.

See All by Emma Roth

Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?

In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.

Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”

Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems

This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.

“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”

Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.

The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”

The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.

While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

New Jersey officials are warning commuters to be wary of an increased number of horny deer — as mating season kicks into full swing.

Motorists should expect an increase in white-tailed deer activity in the morning and evenings on roadways “as bucks attempt to court does” during prime season, the state’s Department of Environmental Protection warned Friday.

Known as the “fall rut,” peak mating times for deer in the Garden State continues from mid-to-late October through the middle of December, the agency said.

“Collisions with deer pose a very serious safety threat and can cause significant damage to vehicles and possible loss of life,” Dave Golden, assistant commissioner for NJDEP Fish & Wildlife cautioned.

“It’s especially important that drivers be extra vigilant to this threat and take time to know steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of collision.”

Officials said that visibility issues spying the four-legged bucks on roadways will become more hazardous when daylight savings time ends on Nov. 1.

The time change will see more commuters on the road during peak periods of bucks engaging in raunchy activity — which can significantly increase the risk of car collisions, the department warned.

An estimated 25,000 car accidents involving deer occur every year in New Jersey, according to the New Jersey Conservation Foundation.

Similarly, an estimated 60,000 to 70,000 accidents are caused by deer each year in the New York, according to the New York State Department of Transportation, which recently launched a new ad campaign to spread awareness.

To stay protected against the sex-charged bucks, officials urge drivers to drive slower, watch for “Deer Crossing” signs and use high beams during dark hours.

The population of white-tailed deer in New Jersey has reached problematic numbers in many suburban areas — with an estimated 100,000 deer roaming throughout the state, Gothamist reported.
the_national_arabic_word_finjan:
Culture

October 16, 2026

Some of the most meaningful gestures in Arab culture come in small packages. A finjan, the little cup traditionally used to serve Arabic coffee, is one such example. Though modest in size, it represents hospitality, generosity and the bonds formed through shared experiences.

Our Arabic word of the week, finjan, translates to cup, particularly a small vessel used for coffee or tea. Its plural is fanajeen, while in Gulf dialects, including Emirati Arabic, it is commonly pronounced finyan or finyal. The word is generally traced to the Persian pingan, meaning a bowl or drinking vessel, which was adapted into Arabic through centuries of cultural exchange.

The word has also travelled beyond Arabic. Turkish uses fincan for a cup, reflecting the shared vocabulary that developed across neighbouring regions.

Arabic word of the week'Qadar' is the destiny we cannot control

While finjan can refer to an ordinary drinking cup, its strongest cultural associations are with gahwa, the traditional Arabic coffee served throughout the Arabian Gulf.

The finjan is usually small, handleless and made from porcelain or ceramic. Some are plain white, while others feature intricate geometric patterns, floral motifs, Arabic calligraphy or gold detailing. These decorations can draw on regional artistic traditions, transforming an everyday drinking vessel into a miniature canvas.

Its size is deliberate, allowing coffee to be served in modest quantities and refilled throughout a gathering.

In the UAE and much of the Arabian Peninsula, offering a finjan is an established expression of welcome. Coffee is poured from a dallah, the distinctive long-spouted pot, and traditionally presented first to the eldest or most honoured guest.

The cup is received with the right hand, and the coffee is generally poured only a quarter or a third of the way up. A gentle shake of the empty finjan signals that the guest has had enough.

These gestures form a language of their own, allowing hosts and guests to communicate respect and appreciation without exchanging a word.

The tradition also extends into Bedouin customs, in which successive cups have acquired symbolic meanings. Finjan al dhaif represents hospitality, finjan al kaif is associated with enjoyment, while finjan al saif evokes loyalty and a willingness to defend one's companions.

In 2015, Arabic coffee was inscribed on Unesco's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising its cultural importance.

The finjan also occupies a place in Arabic poetry. Syrian poet Nizar Qabbani famously used the cup as a symbol of fate and romantic longing in Qari'at Al Finjan, a poem later immortalised in song by Egyptian singer Abdel Halim Hafez.

The poem centres on a fortune-teller who examines an overturned coffee cup and predicts a man's troubled romantic future. Through the familiar practice of reading coffee grounds, Qabbani transforms the finjan into a vessel of destiny, longing and heartbreak.

Whether used for conversation, ceremony or fortune-telling, the finjan is rarely just a drinking vessel. Its significance comes from what happens around it: an invitation to sit, an opportunity to talk and an expression of welcome repeated with every refill.

Alaska Democratic Senate hopeful Mary Peltola faced ridicule Thursday night after her use of notecards during a debate with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan drew mocking responses from GOP critics — including a pointed jab from her incumbent opponent.

Sullivan is in an unusually close race with Peltola, a former congresswoman, that is further complicated by another candidate with his same name but a different middle initial, as Republicans fight to hold their narrow Senate majority.

“Really, Mary? Reading off a script? You can’t cue-card your way through the Senate,” Sullivan wrote on X after Peltola appeared to have a notecard-sized paper with bullet points that she looked down at for several seconds while responding to earlier questions.

The criticism quickly became a flashpoint in the candidates’ debate-night exchanges, with Republican commentators seizing on Peltola’s apparent use of prepared notes.

“Mary, blink twice if you are okay. It seems you can’t string a sentence together without reading from the talking points your Lower 48 handlers wrote you,” NRSC official Joanna Rodriguez posted on X.

Another social media user took aim at Peltola’s apparent reliance on notes even while discussing personal details.

“Mary Peltola can’t read her name or that she’s a grandmother without needing a cue card,” the user wrote, adding a laughing emoji.

After Peltola appeared to read from her card another time, Sullivan cut in that he had a question for the moderators.

“We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?” he asked the debate moderators.

“No sir,” Alaska’s News Source reporter Wil Courtney replied. “Absolutely not,” added Alaska Public Media chief editor Lori Townsend.

“OK,” Sullivan said. “I’m just watching my opponent.”

Peltola defended herself, interjecting that she was better “prepared.”

The Republican Party’s research arm hit back on X, highlighting a clip of Peltola appearing to read from her card:

“Mary Peltola — who did not introduce a single bill to help Alaska fisherman during her first term in Congress — has to read off of a script when talking about Alaska’s fishing industry,” the party tweeted.

The debate also turned personal when Sullivan confronted Peltola over allegations that she mistreated former staffers, citing reporting by The New York Times and claiming that 25 employees had quit while working for her.

Peltola rejected the allegations as “outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” arguing that the election should not be about her “worst day.”

The heated exchange prompted moderators to call for decorum and warn that microphones could be shut off if the candidates continued interrupting one another.

Sullivan maintained that the allegations reflected a pattern of behavior, while Peltola accused her opponent of exploiting the controversy for political gain.

The candidates also faced questions over Alaska’s long-discussed liquefied natural gas pipeline after moderators reported South Korea had not committed to investing in the project despite President Trump’s public promotion of a potential deal.

Sullivan defended the administration’s efforts, arguing Seoul had committed funding through a broader trade agreement while acknowledging that the specific investment amount remained under negotiation.

Peltola also expressed support for the pipeline but cautioned against raising expectations without firm commitments, saying Alaska should not be “promoting falsehoods that just have no substance.”

Both candidates emphasized the project’s economic potential, although the exchange exposed uncertainty over whether promised foreign investment would materialize.

Peltola previously became the first Democrat in decades to represent Alaska in the House after the death of Republican Rep. Don Young, and her Senate candidacy again carries potentially sweeping statewide and national repercussions.

The showdown comes as Republicans fight to defend their narrow Senate majority, with Sullivan’s seat emerging as a major Democratic pickup opportunity in a state President Trump carried in 2024.

The Cook Political Report rates the contest a toss-up, making Alaska one of several battlegrounds that could determine which party controls the chamber in January.

Retired Yuma Arizona Sector Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem recalls agents being overwhelmed during the Biden-era migrant surge, explains what changed under President Donald Trump, and warns political shifts could jeopardize progress.

President Donald Trump’s border crackdown has sharply reduced the illegal crossings that overwhelmed agents under former President Joe Biden, with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reporting Thursday historic lows in apprehensions and a full fiscal year without Border Patrol releasing migrants into the country.

For retired Yuma Arizona Sector U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem, the turnaround stands in sharp contrast to days when his agents could not pick up migrants fast enough and the consequences spilled into neighborhoods, farms and local businesses.

"They just started walking through the agriculture fields. They started running through town," Clem told Fox News Digital, recalling the surge in December 2021. "They started going to the food bank. They started knocking on people’s doors at all hours of the nights."

TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94%

Migrants attempt to cross into the U.S. from Mexico are detained by U.S. Customs and Border Protection at the southern border, Aug. 15, 2021, in San Luis, Ariz. (Nick Ut/Getty Images, File)

But while Clem said he credits stronger enforcement and the prospect of deportation with helping drive the decline, he warned that the gains could face another threat — a political shift in Washington.

"There are a lot of policy decisions that can be really jammed up by a Congress that’s gung-ho to overturn what this president has done," said Clem, who warned that changes in congressional control could complicate enforcement through funding decisions and policy restrictions, while a future presidential administration could pursue broader reversals.

Preliminary DHS figures released Thursday show Border Patrol recorded 98,708 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026, roughly 95% below the annual average of more than 1.8 million during the Biden administration.

That translates to about 270 apprehensions a day across the southwest border, compared with roughly 5,000 using the department’s Biden-era annual average.

In Yuma alone, Clem recalled daily arrivals climbing from roughly 25 in December 2020, to more than 1,000 by December 2021. During a particularly difficult three-day stretch that month, he said, daily arrivals approached 1,500.

TRUMP HITS DRAMATIC MILESTONE IN MASSIVE DEPARTURE FROM BIDEN BORDER PLAN: 'WHAT A DIFFERENCE'

A stretch of the U.S.-Mexico border wall in Yuma, Ariz., May 21, 2025. (Danielle Wallace/Fox News Digital, File)

Weather problems and a shortage of resources compounded the strain, leaving agents struggling to transport people from the border, he said.

"That was really when it, you know, was the most critical for me because we had the true community impact of a failed border security policy out of Washington, D.C.," Clem said.

His agents remained committed to the mission, he said, but the volume was overwhelming.

"The agents, their heads were in the right place. They knew they had to do the job," Clem said. "But when you’re outnumbered, literally 100 to one, it’s very difficult."

The new DHS figures put an entire fiscal year of southwest border apprehensions below half the 249,740 recorded during the Biden administration’s single busiest month.

DHS also said September marked the 17th consecutive month without Border Patrol releasing migrants into the country, completing what it described as the agency’s first full fiscal year with zero releases.

DHS TOUTS MILLIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DEPARTURES AS BORDER CROSSINGS DROP 94% UNDER TRUMP

Migrants line up at a U.S. Border Patrol processing center after crossing the U.S.-Mexico border on Dec. 7, 2023, in Lukeville, Ariz. (John Moore/Getty Images, File)

Clem said the prospect of being released had given smugglers a powerful selling point during the previous administration.

"If you get to the border, you’re gonna be processed, and you’ll be let go," he said, describing the pitch.

He argued that changing that expectation is central to discouraging illegal crossings.

"They know that they’re not gonna be processed and released, which was the status quo under the Biden-Harris administration," Clem said.

the-weekly-cybers-138:
16 October 2026

There’s a lot to get through this week, so let’s just get on with it.

Following a brief period for public comment on the exposure draft, the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 was introduced to parliament on Thursday. Professor Kimberlee Weatherall explains what’s in it, but the tl;dr is:

It is not, as some Opposition politicians have claimed, a way for the government to block political opinions. It’s about “harmful” content, and the so-called sock puppet accounts permitted to be sued by the eSafety Commissioner and authorised researchers are to be used for verification, not to spread political content or disinformation.

“They give the eSafety Commissioner the ability to go undercover to make sure big tech is complying with the law,” communications minister Anika Wells said in her speech to the National Press Club on Thursday.

“How does Grok prevent an account from generating child sexual abuse material? Does Roblox allow an adult profile to talk to kids? Can a 14-year-old girl create a profile on Instagram without being asked once to prove they are over the age of 16? In many cases, the only way eSafety or researchers can examine those questions is to create a test account as a 14-year-old for the purpose of investigation,“ she said.

“These provisions simply make that lawful, and the evidence they collect usable.”

Wells also pushed back on the claim that the law amounted to censorship.

“If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake — they can continue to do so without restriction,” she said.

There are concerns that the law could undermine sex and drug education, however.

The bill has been spun out to a Senate inquiry. No deadline for submissions has been set yet, but the committee has to report back by 20 November.

Death to the algorithms! Oh wait...

Part of the Duty of Care Bill would give people the option of turning off algorithmic feeds and other personalised content recommendations. A piece in The Conversation describes what that might look like, because this is how some Chinese social media works.

“Unlike its American or Chinese counterparts, which used algorithmic recommendations to keep users on the platform, WeChat is designed for users to open the app, do what they need, close the app and put their phone away,” they write.

But creators are still competing for attention, which is on the most recent posts. This translates into increased publication speed — increased even further by generative AI.

“Outlets, restricted by their own budgets, produce low-quality, clickbait content, often compiled from multiple fragmented and unverified sources, to attract subscribers and maximise user engagement.”

How many eSafety Commissioners does one country need?

Meanwhile with this and other new online safety laws coming, the eSafety Commissioner seems to have an ever-increasing workload. Communications minister Anika Wells is now considering appointing multiple commissioners.

The current commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, reaches the end of her term in January 2027.

Donald Trump has cancelled the livestream of the execution by firing square of Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan. In Australia, we learned that there’s little we could have done to prevent it being seen here.

While the Greens demanded it be blocked, as we all know by now that isn’t technically feasible because any number of new livestreams could pop up.

The eSafety Commissioner can order content to be taken down, but only after it’s been up. There’s no legal power to “proactively prevent a livestream from occurring online”, as the commissioner’s office put it.

In any event, there’s an exemption for news reporting if violent content is used in a reasonable way. That raises the usual ethical and commercial questions for TV and online newsrooms regarding how much should have been shown — although perhaps that’s outside the scope of this newsletter.

On Thursday the Australian Signals Directorate released ASD Essentials, which replaces their award-winning Essential Eight cybersecurity framework.

The Essential Eight advised organisations focus first on eight specific cybersecurity controls, those controls which mitigated the most common attacks, based on the ASD’s own data and experience. The E8 was developed further into a maturity model for measuring an organisation's progress in implementing each of the controls.

The ASD acknowledges that the world has changed. In the ASD Essentials it provides a new structure for thinking about cyber defence, one that “provides organisations with a consistent approach to cyber security across different technology environments”.

The change has been welcomed by the Australian Information Security Association (AISA). I imagine that CISOs will be digging into this, if they haven’t already started.

Much has been written about Ukraine smashing Russian data centres belonging to Yandex, that nation’s rough equivalent to Google, and how Russian bot traffic was nearly eliminated — but that part of the story has been debunked.

According to analyst Joohn Choe, the claim that went viral was based on a misleading, misread chart.

“No reputable source supports the reading that Russian social media bot activity is down 50%, or by any other amount,” he wrote.

“The Cloudflare chart going around measures something unrelated: automated web-page requests from Yandex’s own network, mostly its search crawlers. Even that number had partly recovered, to about 20% of its earlier level, by the evening of Oct 11, the same day as the latest strike (t3n).”

Indeed, much of the commentary has confused the term “bot”, in this context a generic term for anything accessing a website that isn’t human, with the Yandex search engine’s indexing bots, or with automated or semi-automated posting on social media.

What was blown away, however, was Russian citizens’ ability to conduct their lives. They variously lost banking and payments, ride-hailing, maps, shopping, email, and perhaps most disturbingly, vodka shipments.

Cloudflare’s own analysis indicated that instead of going dark, malicious bots just went elsewhere.

Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.

Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.

Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.

That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.

The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.

In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".

"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.

"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"

Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.

"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.

"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.

"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."

The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.

"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.

An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.

cornell-jane-doe-lawsuit-fallout:
Two developments in recent days show just how bad things are getting for young adults following Jane Doe’s exceedingly thin claim that she was gang-raped by frat men at Cornell University.

The first one comes in a New York Times article from Saturday featuring some incredible quotes that should offend any self-respecting woman. The story covered the Delta Delta Delta sorority of which Doe was a member and which is named as a defendant in her lawsuit related to her rape claim. “What do we expect to happen?” said a Tri Delta alumna of Texas A&M University identified as JoDee Neil. “We’re not giving them (sorority members) any tools. And we’re sending them off, basically, into a lion’s den.”

This is the type of therapy-speak too many women are growing familiar with in order to deflect and absolve themselves of accountability. What “tools” should a Greek life organization at a university be “giving” to adults that would possibly prevent what allegedly happened at the Chi Phi fraternity house back in 2024? Jane was 20 at the time she says she got drunk, did drugs, and then opted to have a threesome with two frat men. Even her lawsuit filed last month doesn’t claim she was forced, only that she wasn’t capable of taking responsibility for her actions because she got drunk. This was, by her own contemporaneous account, a “gangbang,” not a gang rape.

Another quote comes from Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, who I’m half-convinced actually hates his client, given how absurd his arguments made on her behalf are. He told the Times that it was incumbent upon literally anyone but Doe to have ensured she never left the Tri Delta sorority house that night. “Somebody should have said: ‘Hey, no, you’re intoxicated. You’re not, you shouldn’t be going outside. It’s not safe,’” he said. “And that failed.” Doe reportedly said in investigation proceedings after the incident that she hid her intoxication from an authority figure at the sorority house that night. “I didn’t want to tell her I was drunk because she’s a mandated reporter,” she said, according to the Times.

So if she was hiding it, how is anyone supposed to stop her? And if they had tried and she insisted that she be let go to leave the house, then what? A sorority house isn’t a prison. (Though maybe it should be.) The only logical conclusion is that women, at least young ones, can’t be trusted to take care of themselves and therefore shouldn’t be permitted to attend college without a chaperone.

Around the same time that article cursed our nation’s history, a high school football team captain in Santa Rosa, California, was punished for expressing his First Amendment-protected opinion on the Cornell issue. He reportedly posted on social media, “Free the Cornell Seven,” a reference to the seven men Doe has accused of raping her. After some students protested, school officials announced it had taken action against him, though it’s unclear what form of discipline he received. The student was also reportedly excluded from a team dinner.

In other words, for stating his view on a public controversy — a view widely shared by others — a young man was censored and effectively told his opinion doesn’t count. It’s an outrage, and if anyone thinks there’s a crisis in relations between the sexes now, this is the exact type of thing to fuel it.

What should be a cautionary tale about drugs and high-risk behavior in college is instead being used to infantilize young women and villainize young men: Women can’t be expected to take responsibility for themselves and men can’t do anything right.

That destructive message has been pushed for far too long, and when there’s a backlash, everyone will remember the Cornell Seven.

how-i-cured-my-panic-attacks:
By INDIA STURGIS

Updated:  10:35 AEDT, 16 October 2026

It started in the middle of the night, always with a racing chest. My heart would pound like a steam train, despite the fact I was tucked up safely in bed.

My palms would sweat and I’d fidget under the covers, unable to lie still. I’d go to the bathroom constantly, my bladder having developed a mind of its own.

At some point, concerned that I’d wake my husband Guy or our ten-month-old daughter, I’d head to our attic bedroom.

And there I’d stew.

If you’re not part of the 10 per cent of the population who has experienced a panic attack in their lifetime, let me tell you, there’s nothing like it.

They feel different for everyone, but mine were like sinking deep under water, unable to breathe, my heart hurting, as the surface grew further out of reach. Sheer, bright white terror. Every nerve strained. You feel out of control; stuck, but on fire. I’d scream into a pillow or punch my legs to try to jolt myself out of it. Afterwards came feelings of pathetic exhaustion, futility and self-loathing.

India Sturgis is part of the 10 per cent of the population who has experienced a panic attack and says hers were like sinking deep under water

Alison Hammond experienced a panic attack live on ITV’s This Morning earlier this month and posted a video on Instagram saying it was the scariest thing she’d ever been through

Chest tightness and hyperventilation are common, which explains the feelings of dizziness. Some assume they’re dying. Others shake or feel sick.

A few hallucinate.

When Alison Hammond experienced a panic attack while presenting ITV’s This Morning earlier this month, she thought it was a heart attack and was rushed to hospital. The next day she posted a video on Instagram saying it was the scariest thing she’d ever been through.

I had panic attacks for a few months at the zenith of suffering a potent mix of generalised anxiety disorder, chronic insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder in 2019. Each lasted perhaps five to ten minutes but felt much longer.

Now, aged 39, I no longer have anxiety and the panic attacks at first loosened, then disappeared, as I treated the anxiety and insomnia in tandem. For while they may seem insurmountable, I’ve learned there are many things that can help beat them.

For me, panic was a lot to do with insomnia, the fear of not sleeping (again), anxiety about feeling anxious, and the belief that I was slowly wrecking my life, mind and body with my seeming inability to shut off my brain.

Prince Harry spoke to neuroscientist Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor last week about the panic attacks he used to have while performing royal duties

This had been going on and off for years. I didn’t want to take medication because I thought it would prevent me waking up for our daughter, I might get hooked on it and, if I’m honest, I didn’t want to believe I needed it.

I got help only after a doctor admitted me to a psychiatric hospital, The Priory in Roehampton, because I was deemed a threat to myself in terms of self-harm and suicidal thoughts – the insomnia had driven me to a cliff edge. But there I began the slow journey back to myself.

My experiences meant I identified with Prince Harry, who last week spoke about the panic attacks he used to have while performing royal duties. Talking to neuroscientist Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor, the Duke of Sussex described how putting on a dress shirt triggered panic. ‘The tightening of the collar literally felt like I was suffocating, and I would be experiencing panic attacks just in the car on the way to work,’ he said. ‘And that’s when I realised, OK, there’s something bigger, there’s something else that you need to look into here.’

It’s ‘looking into it’ that helped me get my panic attacks under control. Learning the physiology of panic – that it’s just adrenaline and cortisol surging, and that it will pass – was life-changing.

Panic attacks are caused by our fight-or-flight response triggering an almighty surge of fear and stress hormones that can last from five to 20 minutes. Factors such as a build-up of stress, hormone fluctuations, genetics, hypersensitivity and exposure to trauma can make you more susceptible.

Cruelly, the fear of experiencing one can encourage it to happen, leading sufferers to self-isolate or barely dare to leave their house for fear of having an attack in public.

Many things can help, including grounding exercises, distraction, slow breathing or other forms of cognitive training, and exposure therapy – facing things that trigger panic. James Nestor, author of Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art, says the number one thing you can do to inhibit panic attacks is to control your breathing.

‘It’s in the scientific literature,’ he says, citing a 2010 study by Dr Alicia Meuret, at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, that showed slow, shallow breathing reversed hyperventilation and panic attacks in those with panic disorder.

You are in control of your breathing,’ he says, ‘and your breathing is controlling your panic. Once you master control of your breathing, you are driving the car – you are no longer a passenger.’

I’ve met those who have used music, feeling grass under their bare feet, singing or taking a shower to navigate away from panic.

Now I know a panic attack is not dangerous, despite how unpleasant it is. I haven’t experienced another one since about a month after coming out of hospital in 2019, largely thanks to my sleep improving with medication and cognitive behavioural therapy (among other things). But, crucially, if a panic attack does occur, I now know I will not fear it. That, perhaps, is the greatest deterrent of all.

By NOOR QURASHI, NEWS REPORTER

Published:  11:17 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  11:17 AEDT, 16 October 2026

Stunning photos captured a red squirrel's journey across a Yorkshire pond to reach an acorn for its supper.

The small animal dipped its nose into the water to reach the acorn as it bobbed above the surface.

But after realising the food was too far it decided to take the plunge – entering the pond and swimming towards it with its tail acting as a rudder.

Finally, the squirrel reached the nut, clasping it in its claws and bringing it safely back to land to devour.

The scene was captured by wildlife enthusiast Alan Benson who watched on from a hide in Hawes, North Yorkshire.

He said: 'I was sat in a hide all day watching and waiting for the reds to come in close to a pool. To see it so close as it retrieved a nut was fantastic.'

Red squirrels were once common in the UK, but the introduction of the grey squirrel from North America almost wiped out the native species.

Grey squirrels carry a pox virus which they are immune to but which is deadly to red squirrels.

The total UK population is now thought to be as low as 120,000.

aboard-an-icebreaker-a-writer:
By

Dave Davies

Rana Foroohar reports from the USS Healy (pictured above) in Sea Change.
                
                    
                    Crown
                    
                
                hide caption

As polar ice melts in the Arctic, shipping lanes are opening up, making the region a new zone of superpower competition. Writer Rana Foroohar got an up-close look aboard the USS Healy, a Coast Guard icebreaker. She says that traversing the North Pole by ship — once a "largely conceptual" route — is now becoming a "real possibility" for two or three weeks a year.

"If you are taking one of these Arctic routes, you can save as much as 40% of the time it would take you to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and depending on the price of oil, that's a heck of a lot of money," she says. "China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest."

In her new book, Sea Change: America's New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Foroohar makes the case that the "High North" may become as critical to world shipping as the Suez or Panama canals. But she also notes that beneath the Arctic waters are large deposits of oil, natural gas and rare earth minerals, as well as underwater cables, which carry a large part of the world's intercontinental information flow.

"Undersea cables have become a real touchstone in wars and conflicts around the world," she says. "So you are seeing a race to lay down new cable, and who can get there fastest, and then who can potentially commercialize and even militarize areas where those cables have been laid."

Foroohar describes the Arctic Circle as one of the few areas of the globe where countries and companies can still "hunt" for territory and "duke it out potentially with rivals." And she predicts more conflict in the coming decades as the region continues to warm.

"There is going to be more commerce done through this area. There is gonna be greater military interest in the area, and all of that matters because it really is in America's backyard," she says. "I just think that everything in the High North is going to be higher priority for America in the future."

On increased international interest in the Arctic

China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest. And that's very interesting because it starts to dovetail with something that's happening in U.S. policy, which is more of a sense of we need to protect what's close to home. And so if you look at things that way, then you have the U.S. and China coming into much closer geographic conflict. Whether or not it would ever be a hot conflict, I hope not, but certainly competition in that area.

On the debate over rights to resources in international waters

There's some debate over that. There is something called the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which governs maritime activities, including those in the Arctic. It has ... rules about where you can mine, how you can mine, who gets what. But the U.S. never signed on to that convention. Various presidents from Clinton to Bush [to] Obama did support it, but key Republican senators opposed it, basically on ideological grounds, the notion that no international body should have sovereign right over what the U.S. does. ... And so it makes it much more of a free-for-all as to who gets what in the Arctic. And then you throw in the fact that Russians and Chinese don't always play by the U.N. rules either.

On how Arctic power struggles are part of a larger global trend

It's kind of part and parcel of a bigger collapse of international rule and a pendulum shift from globalization to something that is much more about regionalization and spheres of power ... and influence, which is exactly what's happening in the Arctic, which to me is so interesting, not only just for itself, but because it's a mirror into what's happening in other parts of the world. Some of the same conflicts over territory and mineral rights and ports that you see in the Arctic now are also happening in Latin America or West Africa or parts of the South China Sea. So it's a bit of a bellwether for geostrategy more broadly. …

And then there's this — kind of largely theoretical up until now, but becoming more realistic — trans-polar route where right now it might be a couple of weeks that you could consider going right across the pole, but if global warming continues the way it seems to be going in the next decade or two, that could turn into a month, two months, three months. And so who's going to control that area? This is what's up for stake now.

On what it's like to be onboard an Arctic icebreaker

You begin to feel and hear the ice as it is being broken by the ship. And I remember being down on the mess hall, which is a couple floors down from the waterline, and I was sitting eating my lunch and you begin to hear this shhhhhh kind of sound, like something traveling through sound, and then it becomes squeaky, like fingers on chalkboard, and you can kind of feel vibration and it gets louder and louder and you're like, "Wow, there are only 12 inches of reinforced steel between me and death." That's very sobering.

On the region's changing climate

I actually touched base with some of those scientists several months after we had come off of the Healy, and they were starting to go through that data and look at it. And there is some real scientific data showing that these areas are changing. They are warming. They are becoming different than they have been in the past. And that affects all kinds of things. It affects the kind of fish that could live there. It affects wind and wave patterns that you might get, which could in turn affect things like the Canadian boreal forest fires that I experience in my home in Brooklyn, New York. You would think that has nothing to do with the Arctic, but it actually has everything to do with what's happening in the High North.
