idaho-faith-healing-deaths:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
            corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms. Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Co-published with The Oregonian/OregonLive

This story contains detailed descriptions of children and babies dying.

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches, a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

A sheriff’s deputy opens the door of an Idaho farmhouse where a newborn baby has just died. It’s almost 10 p.m., but the house is filled with adults and children seated anywhere they can find a spot: in reclining chairs, on the wood-stove hearth, on a chest of drawers. Some of the women hold babies in their laps.

“Sorry,” the deputy whispers as the door creaks.

No one greets the officer. No one speaks or even looks at anyone else, casting their eyes instead at the floor or around the room.

The deputy’s video camera records as he walks through the front room and past a bedroom door adorned with children’s artwork. Inside the bedroom, newborn Malachi’s mother sits in a recliner. His body lies in her lap, covered by a blue blanket.

As people in uniform ask Malachi’s parents about his birth, death and the two days in between, members of the family’s church — one of at least four Followers of Christ churches in Idaho — watch from folding chairs. People come and go from the bedroom; one woman cradles a sleeping toddler.

Malachi died from pneumonia and bleeding lungs, according to an autopsy.

It would have been treatable with antibiotics and newborn care in a hospital, said doctors who reviewed his death records for ProPublica.

But Malachi’s parents belong to a faith-healing sect that doesn’t believe in medical care, based on a literal interpretation of several Bible verses. The Followers of Christ sect believes that God heals the faithful and that life and death must be left to God’s divine will.

When the coroner’s deputy lifted Malachi’s body to take it away that night in October 2023, there was no wailing or sobbing from his parents. Malachi’s father stood quietly as his mother hung her head and rested it in her hand.

A pediatrician who reviewed Malachi’s death records said a baby in his condition would have been gasping for air, turning blue from lack of oxygen and breathing so hard that the outline of his rib cage was visible.

It was the first time the coroner and sheriff sent their deputies out to that house, to interview those parents and document the slow suffocation of a newborn boy.

The next time was 13 months later, when their next newborn, Liam, died from the same treatable condition that killed his brother Malachi.

In any Idaho household not steeped in faith-healing, those two deaths would be investigated as crimes. Idaho law says parents can’t endanger, injure or neglect their children or let them suffer. To do so is a crime, and if the child dies as a result, the parent could be charged with manslaughter.

But those laws do not apply to children like Malachi and Liam. Since the 1970s, Idaho’s criminal and civil laws have allowed parents who belong to Followers of Christ and the state’s other faith-healing sects to pray rather than seek medical care as their children die.

Lawmakers in Oregon, where the same religious groups exist, removed the state’s faith-healing exception to child abuse laws nearly 30 years ago, countering the overwhelming pressure former Followers say parents face from their congregations. More parents chose to get medical care for their children after the change, Oregon prosecutors and detectives said.

Idaho lawmakers have chosen a different path.

Since 2014, they have rejected repeated efforts to dial back Idaho’s faith-healing exemption, instead crafting legislation to further limit the role of anyone but a parent when it comes to children’s health and safety. The state has codified “parental rights,” banned vaccine requirements in schools and childcare centers, and made parental consent a prerequisite for medical care of minors. Legislators also have tried to narrow the definition of “medical neglect” for all families to only the most life-threatening situations, but those attempts have failed.

Local and national media outlets have reported on deaths among Followers of Christ families in Idaho. ProPublica went further, enlisting the help of experts to determine which of those deaths could have been prevented.

ProPublica gathered death records from coroners and police in five Idaho counties and shared them with more than a dozen pediatricians and birthing specialists.

At least 15 babies and children from the faith-healing sect died between 2015 and 2025 from illnesses that doctors could have successfully treated, the experts concluded.

The estimate of preventable deaths is almost certainly an undercount. The experts could not evaluate six more deaths because coroner records were incomplete or unavailable. In another four cases, they couldn’t say with confidence whether medical care would have changed the outcome.

Separately, the experts identified numerous preventable losses of babies who died during birth or in utero very close to their due dates, cases that coroners labeled as stillbirths.

For some families like Liam and Malachi’s, the death of a child wasn’t a one-time tragedy: Records show at least five sets of parents have lost multiple children, a phenomenon that has not previously been reported.

None of the parents responded to letters or text messages from ProPublica, and one declined to comment during a brief phone call. (ProPublica is choosing not to identify them or use the children’s full names out of respect for their privacy.)

But Nathan Kangas, a patriarch in the sect’s Caldwell, Idaho, church, defended faith healing and its legal protection during an interview with ProPublica.

Children and babies can’t make their own decision to rely on faith healing. Kangas said their parents must keep them away from the doctor to set an example, so the young ones won’t be cursed later in life by turning to medicine.

Kangas lost his own wife and their last child during labor 23 years ago. Three of his 65 grandchildren also have died.

Asked why God would not want children to live full and healthy lives, Kangas said he had no answer but quoted a verse from the Book of Psalms: “Precious in the eyes of the Lord are the death of His saints.” The Followers believe that life on Earth is “a preparing ground,” Kangas said. He pointed to the Book of James, which tells people to “be afflicted and mourn and weep” and “let your laughter be turned to mourning.”

“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here,” Kangas said. “It’s actually quite the opposite.”

Some outsiders take a very different view.

Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue, one of the most vocal opponents of Idaho’s faith-healing laws, has sent deputies to follow up on the deaths of at least 10 Followers’ children and infants since he took office in 2013.

“This is needless,” Donahue said. “This shouldn’t be happening.”

David Peterman, a retired Idaho pediatrician, reviewed the deaths of 18 infants and children at ProPublica’s request.

Peterman saw patients for 40 years and did his residency at a center that offered special training in child abuse and neglect. He said the vast majority of the deaths he reviewed for ProPublica “are the result of neglect and unequivocally preventable.” (He couldn’t tell whether a few deaths were preventable, and he surmised that one infant had a fatal, untreatable chromosomal defect.) He said it is “beyond comprehension” that the Idaho Legislature has refused to change the law.

“How is this tolerable?” he said. “I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Maicy was 16 years old but the size of a third grader: 62 pounds and just shy of 4 feet tall. She had suffered from a constellation of ailments: stomach irritation, severe anemia, erratic menstrual periods, a blocked artery, thickened aorta and thinning hair. An autopsy after she died on New Year’s Day 2019 traced it all back to a benign, treatable pituitary tumor.

Doctors who reviewed her death records said her stunted growth would have been obvious earlier in childhood, when her tumor could have been diagnosed and treated. Instead, it sent her body into a hormonal tailspin that destroyed her organs. She died in bed, lying on a towel and absorbent pad, wearing a diaper under her sweatpants and a T-shirt that read “LOVE.”

“I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Some of the children who died preventable deaths over a decade were sick for hours or days; others endured months or — in Maicy’s case — years of disease. Most died in their parents’ arms. Many would have experienced pain and distress from their untreated conditions, the healthcare professionals consulted by ProPublica said.

“I don’t know how to come to terms with that,” said Beth Hartman, an Idaho midwife and former chair of the state’s midwifery licensing board. “Because when you see respiratory distress, and when you have seen a person pass, it’s not pretty. They don’t just close their eyes.”

In America at large, the risk that a child will die is highest during the first year of life. The vast majority of Followers’ children who died were infants. But nationally, fatalities in this age group tend to follow premature birth or profound congenital disorders. The deaths among Followers’ infants came from ailments that rarely take children’s lives.

At least three children died from sepsis caused by common infections that antibiotics can easily stop. Camden died in 2024. Weston died in 2025. They were brothers. Stanley, a newborn whose parents said he was “alert and happy” for his first 36 hours, spent the next 29 getting darker in color, coughing up phlegm and clenching his limbs in convulsions. He died in 2017.

The deaths almost never came without warning.

In the case of Malachi, the police and coroner reports don’t say how long before his death his parents first noticed him breathing fast, making a gurgling noise “like stuff was in his throat or chest.” Nor do the documents say what the parents did in the interim other than that they “chose not to perform life saving measures.”

But when they noticed their next newborn, Liam, was struggling to breathe and his “color was not good,” they again did not call for help, and he died over the course of at least 12 hours. While he was dying, members of their church came to see the baby and pray for him. Ten people were in the room when the boy died, and more had gathered outside the room, Liam’s father told police.

It’s rare in developed countries for children to die from pneumonia as Liam and Malachi did, wrote Barton Adrian, a retired Idaho pediatrician who reviewed the death records for ProPublica. The annual pneumonia-related death rate in the U.S. for infants is 1 in every 30,000 to 40,000, according to federal data. Adrian wrote that with a total of 12 children in Malachi and Liam’s family, the death rate was 1 in 6, “equivalent to third-world countries.”

Several healthcare professionals who reviewed the death records for Malachi and Liam suspected their problems originated from a birth-related strep infection so dangerous that expectant mothers in the U.S. are routinely screened for it. Women who test positive get antibiotics to keep the baby safe. In cases where a full-term newborn does become infected, almost all who receive treatment survive.

Dallas, a 2-year-old, was sick for six weeks with an untreated bacterial infection that settled into a valve in his heart and slowly destroyed it. He had fevers, abdominal pain, vomiting and swelling that started in his feet, then spread to his hands and finally to his face. He died in his father’s arms in 2020. Although an autopsy found Dallas was born with a heart condition that made him susceptible to infections, doctors who reviewed the document for ProPublica said the condition was treatable and antibiotics would have halted the infection.

Had his parents taken him to a doctor at any point during the six weeks they knew he was sick, Dallas could have been saved, the doctors said.

Whenever a child dies in the Followers of Christ, the scene is unlike anything police see in deaths outside the sect.

Police describe what seems to be a phone tree the church members use to call on the congregation to pray and go to the family’s home — sometimes before the death, sometimes after. A church elder or family member calls the coroner directly, instead of calling 911.

The sheriff’s deputies and local police who accompany the coroner’s team to the death scene have learned what to expect. There won’t be an ambulance parked outside. There won’t be a frantic, inconsolable parent. There won’t be children’s ibuprofen in the medicine cabinet or a pediatrician’s phone number to call for medical records. All the police will find is a crowd sitting in silent vigil and a bottle of olive oil for anointing the ill.

There is little for police to do besides offer condolences, ask questions and carry out their legal duty to confirm the parents did nothing that constitutes a crime in Idaho.

Yet some of these cases are etched into officers’ memories.

For Chuck Gentry, a captain in the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, it was a baby girl named Jolene who died at 3 months old from a congenital heart defect. Some doctors told ProPublica that a cardiologist’s care could have saved her, although some suspected she also had a chromosomal defect that only 10% of babies survive past their first year.

What haunts Gentry was the lack of medical attention for the baby’s cleft palate, which he recalls was severe.

She died at an address that’s become familiar to local police because children from four Followers families have died there since 2017.

(Jolene’s father, reached by phone, declined to talk with ProPublica.)

Gentry echoed what other investigators told ProPublica: By the time detectives arrive, the congregation has already assembled. Dozens of people, Gentry said. So many vehicles that he’d sometimes struggle to find a place to park his patrol car.

“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here. It’s actually quite the opposite.”

Once he’d get inside, he said, the grandparents of a dead child would make it hard for him to get the child’s parents alone to ask them questions. “They’re very hover-y. They don’t want you to separate them off,” he said. “They kind of seem overprotective of what they might say.”

(Kangas, the Caldwell church elder, said the congregation’s presence at a dead child’s home isn’t meant as intimidation. “They’re not there to keep from saying anything. That’s absolutely false,” he said. “We, as a people, when somebody suffers, we go there to suffer with them.”)

Gentry said it wasn’t until he got the parents alone in another room that their grief would spill out. “You see the mom crying. You see the dad kind of pacing,” he said. “It’s normal behavior for someone who has lost a child,” but the death itself and the scene that follows it are “so bizarre that normal still isn’t normal.”

Jolene was her parents’ first child to die, they told police. Other investigators arrived at the scene for the next, the couple’s toddler son, Malone, in 2021.

Written reports from a pathologist and death investigators describe the body that detectives saw: arms and legs skinny from malnourishment, a belly swollen to the size of a basketball.

Malone never had normal bowel movements in his 16 months of life, his parents would later tell investigators. His belly would swell, then he’d have an enormous poop, and the cycle would repeat. As his condition worsened, his mother brought him to his grandparents’ house on a busy country road. She held him while he died.

An autopsy determined that the boy’s bowels had compressed his lungs and heart, which stopped beating. His rib cage had grown outward to accommodate his backed-up intestines, and his lungs were so cramped they’d stayed the size of a newborn’s.

One detective wrote that Malone’s abdomen was “distorted to the extent of nothing like I’ve ever seen before.”

The underlying problem was an intestinal condition that doctors can fix with a routine, minimally invasive surgery, experts who reviewed Malone’s death records said.

The day Malone died, investigators arrived to find dozens of family and friends at the house. Malone’s mother sat in the front room, in a chair holding the child’s covered body in her lap. Malone’s father knelt beside them.

A detective asked the parents questions in a quiet voice, according to audio recordings from the scene. Did Malone have trouble going to the bathroom? Had he been to a doctor? Did they have any other children? Where was Malone when he died? They gave brief answers, volunteering few details. The entire interaction took about 10 minutes.

The paperwork wrapped up, and the case was closed.

The Followers of Christ sparked curiosity in Idaho from the time they arrived in 1899. Two “wayfarers from Oklahoma” appeared in a mining town near what is now Sun Valley, calling themselves “the disciples of a new religion.” They said God sent them to spread their gospel, according to reporting from the time in the Idaho Statesman.

“One was tall and dark, about 30 years of age, and wore a pair of greasy overalls, black, baggy sweater and flaring yellow mackinaw coat,” a reporter wrote. That man went by “Brother Charley.” He was “decidedly illiterate” and preached that education wasn’t necessary but had an impressive knowledge of Scripture, able to recite entire books of the Bible by memory, the reporter wrote.

They held their first worship service a week later in a schoolhouse.

Over time, Followers of Christ formed congregations across southern Idaho. It went on to become the state’s largest faith-healing religion and later spread into Oregon.

The first few generations of holy men who led Idaho’s congregations died, and no one took their place. Each church was left with, at most, a loose hierarchy and leadership structure. Each operates independently, with subtle differences in how it interprets doctrine. Although congregations have elders, families are the main conduit for ritual and belief.

The religion also breaks with most Christian denominations in that it does not recruit or proselytize. Other than on the rare occasion an outsider marries in, the sect grows only through existing families. This insularity causes the same surnames to show up over and over in public records from Followers communities in Idaho, and, just as happened in the faith’s earlier generations, the sprawling Followers families tend to intermarry.

Linda Martin, a former Follower who traced her genealogy, calls her family tree “a trunk.”

When the Followers began, healthcare on the Western frontier was primitive, unsanitary and riddled with con artists peddling fake cures. Hospitals and medical practitioners could treat many ailments and save lives, but medications like insulin for diabetes and antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia didn’t exist.

Like other faith-healing sects, the Followers sought answers elsewhere. They looked to Bible verses such as in the Book of James: “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.”

Kangas said “the whole Scripture” informs faith-healing doctrine and that no one went to the doctor in Christ’s time.

“It was a matter of trusting in God to heal them,” he said.

When someone dies despite fervent prayers, the Followers believe it is God’s will. When someone sees a doctor, the Followers see it as a sin. When someone recovers without medication or surgery or a 911 call, it seems to validate the sect’s doctrine.

No mainstream Christian denomination today accepts this interpretation of the Bible.

“I think over time, it’s kind of morphed into, ‘This is one of the things that separates us from all other faiths or religions, is that we don’t go to the doctor,’”  said Laren Eells, who left one of Idaho’s Followers of Christ churches about a decade ago. He now believes that because of cherry-picked passages of biblical Scripture, “my eyes were completely clouded with presupposition.”

As a child, Eells watched his father endure what Eells believes was a burst appendix. The man was bedridden for over a month and had foul waste coming out of his mouth, but he emerged alive.

As an adult, though, Eells watched his younger brother die of an ear infection that spread to his blood. He sat by his brother’s side around the clock, “praying and wringing my hands,” he said. “An infection that some antibiotics could have probably taken care of, relatively simple, but we just say, ‘Well, we trust God with our life.’”

By the time Followers are grown, the idea that they could lose their own children isn’t foreign. They may have been present for their own siblings’ or cousins’ deaths. Their parents have likely taken them for vigils at other congregants’ houses.

The possibility of being isolated from their congregation can be a concern for Followers because of how much their lives revolve around extended family and church.

Former members say that someone who visits a doctor might be shunned, reprimanded or simply left out of social events — although Kangas said only “a few people here and there” in his church would go that far.

Kangas believes some ex-Followers perceive condemnation where none exists because of a guilty conscience. A single doctor’s visit can be chalked up to fear or weakness that “people can be forgiven of,” Kangas said.

What matters, he said, is that the person repents and never goes again.

ProPublica reporter Audrey Dutton obtained coroner and law enforcement records for deaths of children whose parents self-identified as refusing medical care for religious reasons. She redacted and shared these records with healthcare professionals from Idaho and elsewhere: eight pediatricians, a midwife, two pediatric cardiologists, two epilepsy specialists and a labor and delivery nurse. They each answered the question, “Could this death have been prevented with medical care?” At least three professionals reviewed each case; if they didn’t reach the same conclusion, ProPublica sought opinions from more professionals until a near-consensus was clear. The count of preventable deaths includes one case where some doctors theorized the child might have died later in infancy even with treatment: Jolene, the 3-month-old girl in this story. In cases where experts didn’t have enough information to reach a strong conclusion, ProPublica did not categorize those deaths as preventable.

A sheriff’s deputy opens the door of an Idaho farmhouse where a newborn baby has just died. It’s almost 10 p.m., but the house is filled with adults and children seated anywhere they can find a spot: in reclining chairs, on the wood-stove hearth, on a chest of drawers. Some of the women hold babies in their laps.

“Sorry,” the deputy whispers as the door creaks.

No one greets the officer. No one speaks or even looks at anyone else, casting their eyes instead at the floor or around the room.

The deputy’s video camera records as he walks through the front room and past a bedroom door adorned with children’s artwork. Inside the bedroom, newborn Malachi’s mother sits in a recliner. His body lies in her lap, covered by a blue blanket.

As people in uniform ask Malachi’s parents about his birth, death and the two days in between, members of the family’s church — one of at least four Followers of Christ churches in Idaho — watch from folding chairs. People come and go from the bedroom; one woman cradles a sleeping toddler.

Malachi died from pneumonia and bleeding lungs, according to an autopsy.

It would have been treatable with antibiotics and newborn care in a hospital, said doctors who reviewed his death records for ProPublica.

But Malachi’s parents belong to a faith-healing sect that doesn’t believe in medical care, based on a literal interpretation of several Bible verses. The Followers of Christ sect believes that God heals the faithful and that life and death must be left to God’s divine will.

When the coroner’s deputy lifted Malachi’s body to take it away that night in October 2023, there was no wailing or sobbing from his parents. Malachi’s father stood quietly as his mother hung her head and rested it in her hand.

A pediatrician who reviewed Malachi’s death records said a baby in his condition would have been gasping for air, turning blue from lack of oxygen and breathing so hard that the outline of his rib cage was visible.

It was the first time the coroner and sheriff sent their deputies out to that house, to interview those parents and document the slow suffocation of a newborn boy.

The next time was 13 months later, when their next newborn, Liam, died from the same treatable condition that killed his brother Malachi.

In any Idaho household not steeped in faith-healing, those two deaths would be investigated as crimes. Idaho law says parents can’t endanger, injure or neglect their children or let them suffer. To do so is a crime, and if the child dies as a result, the parent could be charged with manslaughter.

But those laws do not apply to children like Malachi and Liam. Since the 1970s, Idaho’s criminal and civil laws have allowed parents who belong to Followers of Christ and the state’s other faith-healing sects to pray rather than seek medical care as their children die.

Lawmakers in Oregon, where the same religious groups exist, removed the state’s faith-healing exception to child abuse laws nearly 30 years ago, countering the overwhelming pressure former Followers say parents face from their congregations. More parents chose to get medical care for their children after the change, Oregon prosecutors and detectives said.

Idaho lawmakers have chosen a different path.

Since 2014, they have rejected repeated efforts to dial back Idaho’s faith-healing exemption, instead crafting legislation to further limit the role of anyone but a parent when it comes to children’s health and safety. The state has codified “parental rights,” banned vaccine requirements in schools and childcare centers, and made parental consent a prerequisite for medical care of minors. Legislators also have tried to narrow the definition of “medical neglect” for all families to only the most life-threatening situations, but those attempts have failed.

Local and national media outlets have reported on deaths among Followers of Christ families in Idaho. ProPublica went further, enlisting the help of experts to determine which of those deaths could have been prevented.

ProPublica gathered death records from coroners and police in five Idaho counties and shared them with more than a dozen pediatricians and birthing specialists.

At least 15 babies and children from the faith-healing sect died between 2015 and 2025 from illnesses that doctors could have successfully treated, the experts concluded.

The estimate of preventable deaths is almost certainly an undercount. The experts could not evaluate six more deaths because coroner records were incomplete or unavailable. In another four cases, they couldn’t say with confidence whether medical care would have changed the outcome.

Separately, the experts identified numerous preventable losses of babies who died during birth or in utero very close to their due dates, cases that coroners labeled as stillbirths.

For some families like Liam and Malachi’s, the death of a child wasn’t a one-time tragedy: Records show at least five sets of parents have lost multiple children, a phenomenon that has not previously been reported.

None of the parents responded to letters or text messages from ProPublica, and one declined to comment during a brief phone call. (ProPublica is choosing not to identify them or use the children’s full names out of respect for their privacy.)

But Nathan Kangas, a patriarch in the sect’s Caldwell, Idaho, church, defended faith healing and its legal protection during an interview with ProPublica.

Children and babies can’t make their own decision to rely on faith healing. Kangas said their parents must keep them away from the doctor to set an example, so the young ones won’t be cursed later in life by turning to medicine.

Kangas lost his own wife and their last child during labor 23 years ago. Three of his 65 grandchildren also have died.

Asked why God would not want children to live full and healthy lives, Kangas said he had no answer but quoted a verse from the Book of Psalms: “Precious in the eyes of the Lord are the death of His saints.” The Followers believe that life on Earth is “a preparing ground,” Kangas said. He pointed to the Book of James, which tells people to “be afflicted and mourn and weep” and “let your laughter be turned to mourning.”

“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here,” Kangas said. “It’s actually quite the opposite.”

Some outsiders take a very different view.

Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue, one of the most vocal opponents of Idaho’s faith-healing laws, has sent deputies to follow up on the deaths of at least 10 Followers’ children and infants since he took office in 2013.

“This is needless,” Donahue said. “This shouldn’t be happening.”

David Peterman, a retired Idaho pediatrician, reviewed the deaths of 18 infants and children at ProPublica’s request.

Peterman saw patients for 40 years and did his residency at a center that offered special training in child abuse and neglect. He said the vast majority of the deaths he reviewed for ProPublica “are the result of neglect and unequivocally preventable.” (He couldn’t tell whether a few deaths were preventable, and he surmised that one infant had a fatal, untreatable chromosomal defect.) He said it is “beyond comprehension” that the Idaho Legislature has refused to change the law.

“How is this tolerable?” he said. “I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Maicy was 16 years old but the size of a third grader: 62 pounds and just shy of 4 feet tall. She had suffered from a constellation of ailments: stomach irritation, severe anemia, erratic menstrual periods, a blocked artery, thickened aorta and thinning hair. An autopsy after she died on New Year’s Day 2019 traced it all back to a benign, treatable pituitary tumor.

Doctors who reviewed her death records said her stunted growth would have been obvious earlier in childhood, when her tumor could have been diagnosed and treated. Instead, it sent her body into a hormonal tailspin that destroyed her organs. She died in bed, lying on a towel and absorbent pad, wearing a diaper under her sweatpants and a T-shirt that read “LOVE.”

“I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Some of the children who died preventable deaths over a decade were sick for hours or days; others endured months or — in Maicy’s case — years of disease. Most died in their parents’ arms. Many would have experienced pain and distress from their untreated conditions, the healthcare professionals consulted by ProPublica said.

“I don’t know how to come to terms with that,” said Beth Hartman, an Idaho midwife and former chair of the state’s midwifery licensing board. “Because when you see respiratory distress, and when you have seen a person pass, it’s not pretty. They don’t just close their eyes.”

In America at large, the risk that a child will die is highest during the first year of life. The vast majority of Followers’ children who died were infants. But nationally, fatalities in this age group tend to follow premature birth or profound congenital disorders. The deaths among Followers’ infants came from ailments that rarely take children’s lives.

At least three children died from sepsis caused by common infections that antibiotics can easily stop. Camden died in 2024. Weston died in 2025. They were brothers. Stanley, a newborn whose parents said he was “alert and happy” for his first 36 hours, spent the next 29 getting darker in color, coughing up phlegm and clenching his limbs in convulsions. He died in 2017.

The deaths almost never came without warning.

In the case of Malachi, the police and coroner reports don’t say how long before his death his parents first noticed him breathing fast, making a gurgling noise “like stuff was in his throat or chest.” Nor do the documents say what the parents did in the interim other than that they “chose not to perform life saving measures.”

But when they noticed their next newborn, Liam, was struggling to breathe and his “color was not good,” they again did not call for help, and he died over the course of at least 12 hours. While he was dying, members of their church came to see the baby and pray for him. Ten people were in the room when the boy died, and more had gathered outside the room, Liam’s father told police.

It’s rare in developed countries for children to die from pneumonia as Liam and Malachi did, wrote Barton Adrian, a retired Idaho pediatrician who reviewed the death records for ProPublica. The annual pneumonia-related death rate in the U.S. for infants is 1 in every 30,000 to 40,000, according to federal data. Adrian wrote that with a total of 12 children in Malachi and Liam’s family, the death rate was 1 in 6, “equivalent to third-world countries.”

Several healthcare professionals who reviewed the death records for Malachi and Liam suspected their problems originated from a birth-related strep infection so dangerous that expectant mothers in the U.S. are routinely screened for it. Women who test positive get antibiotics to keep the baby safe. In cases where a full-term newborn does become infected, almost all who receive treatment survive.

Dallas, a 2-year-old, was sick for six weeks with an untreated bacterial infection that settled into a valve in his heart and slowly destroyed it. He had fevers, abdominal pain, vomiting and swelling that started in his feet, then spread to his hands and finally to his face. He died in his father’s arms in 2020. Although an autopsy found Dallas was born with a heart condition that made him susceptible to infections, doctors who reviewed the document for ProPublica said the condition was treatable and antibiotics would have halted the infection.

Had his parents taken him to a doctor at any point during the six weeks they knew he was sick, Dallas could have been saved, the doctors said.

Whenever a child dies in the Followers of Christ, the scene is unlike anything police see in deaths outside the sect.

Police describe what seems to be a phone tree the church members use to call on the congregation to pray and go to the family’s home — sometimes before the death, sometimes after. A church elder or family member calls the coroner directly, instead of calling 911.

The sheriff’s deputies and local police who accompany the coroner’s team to the death scene have learned what to expect. There won’t be an ambulance parked outside. There won’t be a frantic, inconsolable parent. There won’t be children’s ibuprofen in the medicine cabinet or a pediatrician’s phone number to call for medical records. All the police will find is a crowd sitting in silent vigil and a bottle of olive oil for anointing the ill.

There is little for police to do besides offer condolences, ask questions and carry out their legal duty to confirm the parents did nothing that constitutes a crime in Idaho.

Yet some of these cases are etched into officers’ memories.

For Chuck Gentry, a captain in the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, it was a baby girl named Jolene who died at 3 months old from a congenital heart defect. Some doctors told ProPublica that a cardiologist’s care could have saved her, although some suspected she also had a chromosomal defect that only 10% of babies survive past their first year.

What haunts Gentry was the lack of medical attention for the baby’s cleft palate, which he recalls was severe.

She died at an address that’s become familiar to local police because children from four Followers families have died there since 2017.

(Jolene’s father, reached by phone, declined to talk with ProPublica.)

Gentry echoed what other investigators told ProPublica: By the time detectives arrive, the congregation has already assembled. Dozens of people, Gentry said. So many vehicles that he’d sometimes struggle to find a place to park his patrol car.

“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here. It’s actually quite the opposite.”

Once he’d get inside, he said, the grandparents of a dead child would make it hard for him to get the child’s parents alone to ask them questions. “They’re very hover-y. They don’t want you to separate them off,” he said. “They kind of seem overprotective of what they might say.”

(Kangas, the Caldwell church elder, said the congregation’s presence at a dead child’s home isn’t meant as intimidation. “They’re not there to keep from saying anything. That’s absolutely false,” he said. “We, as a people, when somebody suffers, we go there to suffer with them.”)

Gentry said it wasn’t until he got the parents alone in another room that their grief would spill out. “You see the mom crying. You see the dad kind of pacing,” he said. “It’s normal behavior for someone who has lost a child,” but the death itself and the scene that follows it are “so bizarre that normal still isn’t normal.”

Jolene was her parents’ first child to die, they told police. Other investigators arrived at the scene for the next, the couple’s toddler son, Malone, in 2021.

Written reports from a pathologist and death investigators describe the body that detectives saw: arms and legs skinny from malnourishment, a belly swollen to the size of a basketball.

Malone never had normal bowel movements in his 16 months of life, his parents would later tell investigators. His belly would swell, then he’d have an enormous poop, and the cycle would repeat. As his condition worsened, his mother brought him to his grandparents’ house on a busy country road. She held him while he died.

An autopsy determined that the boy’s bowels had compressed his lungs and heart, which stopped beating. His rib cage had grown outward to accommodate his backed-up intestines, and his lungs were so cramped they’d stayed the size of a newborn’s.

One detective wrote that Malone’s abdomen was “distorted to the extent of nothing like I’ve ever seen before.”

The underlying problem was an intestinal condition that doctors can fix with a routine, minimally invasive surgery, experts who reviewed Malone’s death records said.

The day Malone died, investigators arrived to find dozens of family and friends at the house. Malone’s mother sat in the front room, in a chair holding the child’s covered body in her lap. Malone’s father knelt beside them.

A detective asked the parents questions in a quiet voice, according to audio recordings from the scene. Did Malone have trouble going to the bathroom? Had he been to a doctor? Did they have any other children? Where was Malone when he died? They gave brief answers, volunteering few details. The entire interaction took about 10 minutes.

The paperwork wrapped up, and the case was closed.

A maniac who allegedly barged into a Midtown synagogue yelling, “Allahu Akbar” last year wasbusted for the brazen act Wednesday morning when police found him trying to evade a subway fare, law enforcement sources said.

Shear Nobles, 48, of Philadelphia, allegedly stormed into Shuva Israel on East 58th Street during an evening service on July 21, 2025, started recording without authorization and made the disturbing declaration, police said.

Nobles – who had no connection to the synagogue – stood in the main service room during the anti-Semitic spectacle, authorities said.

He fled on foot and had not been caught for more than a year – until keen-eyed cops spotted him trying to catch a free subway ride at Fulton Street in Lower Manhattan, the sources said.

Nobles was ducking under a turnstile when police stopped him, according to the sources.

He was charged with aggravated harassment and disruption of a religious service, cops said.

Nobles has no previous arrests in the Big Apple, but has been arrested for robbery, burglary and retail crime-related offenses dating back about two decades in Philadelphia, the sources said.
mamdani-team-pissed-over-chevalier-tisch:

A sickle to the back!

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s allies are publicly breaking with him over his handpicked police commissioner — and Hizzoner is livid that the socialist House candidate he went out on a limb to endorse is leading the charge.

City Hall staffers have been openly whining about alleged ally Darializa Avila Chevalier — whom Mamdani endorsed just a few months ago during the primaries — after she led a crusade to slam NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch after ICE agents shot an illegal migrant in the Bronx.

“They were pissed about what she did on social media and her public rhetoric on NYPD,” one source with knowledge said. “City Hall was like, ‘what the f–k are you doing!’”

The ICE shooting may mark the end of the socialist honeymoon for some Mamdani supporters, as some lefty pols and the national branch of his comrades in the Democratic Socialists of America push for Tisch’s ouster despite Hizzoner standing by his commissioner.

Another source said that folks in the admin griped that, “this was a direct undermining of Mamdani.”

The DSA dysfunction unfolded publicly last Friday when Chevalier rage-tweeted about immigration officials shooting a suspected gang memberas he fled arrest in a car. The supposed Mamdani ally accused Tisch and the NYPD of violating the Big Apple’s sanctuary city laws that bar cops from assisting ICE.

“Last night, the NYPD and Commissioner Tisch violated the spirit, if not the letter, of our sanctuary city policies and fueled the Trump Administration’s attempt to demonize our communities,” she wrote in her nearly 400-word tirade.

“The NYPD’s Strategic Response Group must be disbanded as quickly as possible, and Commissioner Tisch must step down,” she continued.

The NYPD did not assist ICE in the immigration arrest, nor did the SRG respond to the protest.

City Hall was also annoyed about Chevalier encouraging the anti-ICE protests, worried that any signs of disorder could give the Trump administration reason to flood the streets, sources said.

The congressional candidate had also ranted in her screed about being pushed during an aggressive protest in Marble Hill Thursday night after video captured her getting in a calm police supervisor’s face, accusing him of escalating the situation.

“She is throwing her own fireball rhetoric to rally the folks,” one source said, adding, “But instigating doesn’t help.”

But the calls from the far-left fellow democratic socialist set off a media firestorm for Mamdani, who appointed Tisch — a Zionist Jew, despite his and his party’s outspoken criticism of Israel — and vowed to disband the SRG during the campaign.

Hizzoner, who dodged the city’s press corps for days, was inundated with demands from his socialist comrades and the national DSA chapter to get rid of the police commissioner and honor his campaign pledge when it came to dissolving the specialized police unit.

DSA member and state Senate candidate Illapa Sairitupac, who was also endorsed by the mayor, joined the call after Chevalier.

“Abolish ICE, disband the SRG, fire Tisch,” he wrote.

The NYC DSA chapter, whose leaders are close friends of the mayor, took a softer tone, saying Tisch should be fired if she can’t confront ICE.

“Jessica Tisch must get ICE out of New York and end NYPD complicity with these terrorists,” the group wrote on social media. “If the Commissioner can’t put a stop to these injustices, she must be fired.”

Neither of the other two other House candidates that Mamdani endorsed, Brad Lander and Claire Valdez, issued similar calls.

But insiders told The Post that Chevalier doesn’t plan on letting up.

The bombastic soon-to-be member of the House of Representatives and her team are working on a speech — potentially on Election Night or sooner — to call on Tisch to be fired.

Sources said that the young mayor was talked into endorsing Chevalier by his adviser, Morris Katz, but isn’t a fan of her.

For her part, Chevalier is distancing herself from the mayor, despite most crediting the mayor’s backing and campaigning for helping her win New York’s 13th Congressional primary, taking down incumbent Democrat Adriano Espaillat in June.

The 13th CD is overwhelmingly blue, and winning the Democratic line all but guarantees Chevalier’s win the general election next month.

Campaign canvassers are now under strict instructions not to say anything about the mayor, according to the sources.

“I can’t speak about the mayor, but I can tell you what Darializa is prioritizing,” the volunteers are told to say, according to a person briefed.

Sources said the impulsive Chevalier has been on City Hall and Mamdani’s radar as a potential liability for some time, but they didn’t think she would be an issue so early on.

“They are not naive to who their problems are — [Council Speaker Julie] Menin, Republicans, etc., and she is on the dartboard,” the insider said.

“She’s a loose cannon,” they continued, “They are sick of her, and she’s not even started in Congress.”

Six Flags Great Adventure has temporarily shut down its Nitro rollercoaster after a teacher fell to his death from a similar ride in Georgia on Monday.

The theme park in Jackson Township, NJ, shut down Nitro out of “an abundance of caution,” Six Flags said, as investigators probe the tragic mishap in which beloved teacher Hassan Kariem, 42, slipped from his safety restraint on the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia — slamming into fellow riders before dropping to his death.

Great Adventure’s “hypercoaster” — which boasts a glimpse of Philadelphia from its 215-foot drop — is one of nine coasters at parks across North America that have shuttered since Kariem’s death.

“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks,” Six Flags said in a statement. “The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities.”

The amusement park company said investigators are hard at work finding out what went wrong in Georgia.

The tragedy and ensuing closures came in the middle of the theme park’s annual autumn rush.

The “Fright Fest” event at Six Flags Great Adventure runs through Halloween — but it’s unclear if Nitro will be back up and running before the annual festivity ends.

Nitro was designed by the same company as Goliath: Swiss manufacturer Bolliger & Mabillard, which built eight of the nine temporarily closed coasters.

Some of those rides have safety belts as a backup to the lap restraints that secure riders to their seats.

But Goliath doesn’t have those safety belts — and neither does Nitro, according to travel blogger Nathan Kerney.

It remains unclear if the lack of seatbelts had anything to do with the deadly mishap. Six Flags has not replied to The Post’s request for comment on the matter.

The ride closures come just weeks after Magic Mountain in California permanently retired its X2 roller coaster in late September following claims from more than 100 riders that the attraction caused horrible head injuries.

In September, a 25-year-old woman was on a ventilator two months after she allegedly suffered a catastrophic brain injury.

Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and Gov. Gavin Newsom patted themselves on the back Wednesday as they celebrated California’s controversial climate laws at an event in Long Beach.

The two politicians shared a chummy “fireside chat” at the 2026 California Economic Summit, held Oct. 13-15 at the Long Beach Convention Center, to mark the 20th anniversary of the California Global Warming Solutions Act, which Schwarzenegger signed into law in 2006.

The law required California to slash greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 — a 30% reduction that the state says it achieved ahead of schedule through mandatory emissions caps and reporting for major industrial sources, along with a statewide cap-and-trade program.

Schwarzenegger said he pushed the legislation through despite objections from the Bush administration, that he said tried to slow the creation of the new rules.

“I was going through the struggle,” said Schwarzenegger, a Republican. “I mean, we knew that they were full of s–t, right?”

“The federal government fought us, and every step of the way, and we went to court,” he added. “To me, it doesn’t matter if you’re Republican or Democrat. What is important is that you are representing the people, that you are working for the people and not for the party.”

Schwarzenegger rarely endorses candidates, criticizing both sides of the aisle when he does speak out on issues.

The former governor broke from that tradition by endorsing Kamala Harris in the 2024 election after refusing to support Donald Trump’s bid for the White House in 2016. He declined to make an endorsement in the 2020 race between Trump and Joe Biden.

Schwarzenegger has not made an endorsement in the California governor’s race. He has not endorsed a candidate in the LA mayoral race, either, but recently hosted a high-powered meet-and-greet for democratic socialist Nithya Raman.

Newsom even tipped his hat to Republican President Richard Nixon for his environmental record, crediting him with creating the Environmental Protection Agency and signing the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act into law.

“California recognizes its role and responsibility in the absence of federal responsibility,” said Newsom. “The headwinds are well established as it relates to the Trump administration and the vandalism in terms of our efforts is second to none.”

Newsom said he’s been working with local governments “around the globe,” and across the US, “to substitute for the lack of federal leadership,” on environmental issues.

“We have no peers,” said Newsom of California’s environmental protections. “We are dramatically changing the way we’re producing and consuming energy, and we’re creating jobs and innovation, and we are dominating in this space.”

President Trump has taken issue with the state’s rules, repealing the EPA’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding,” which recognized greenhouse gases as a threat to public health and welfare. California and a coalition of states filed multiple lawsuits to block the repeal.

Trump and Congress have also tried to block California’s environmental rules by attempting to revoke California’s Clean Air Act preemption waivers, which allow the state to set its own stricter vehicle emission standards rather than follow easier federal rules.

A federal judge this year stopped Trump’s attempt to squash the rules, but legal and legislative attacks on the regulations continue.

The Global Warming Solutions Act has faced legal and legislative challenges as well but remains state law. Critics say the Act grants too much power to state regulators and allows rich companies to pollute while harming poor ones, through the cap-and-trade system.

Residents of Pittsburgh with outstanding debt on their water utilities can see it forgiven over a 24-month period.

Instituted by Pittsburgh’s water authority, certain customers have already been enrolled as of September, and need only keep up with monthly payments to see pre-September outstanding debt gradually forgiven.

Called the Arrearage Forgiveness Program, Pittsburgh Water recently updated and improved the program, while some 4,300 city households living below 200% of the Federal Poverty Line were automatically enrolled.

If such a household had, by September 1st, outstanding debt—$1,000, for example—they can see that total entirely erased if they begin meeting payment obligations. For every month the obligation is met, one twenty-fourth ($41.60, using the example) of their outstanding debt will be forgiven.

In two years’ time, the balance in arrears will thus be zeroed out.

Pittsburgh Water director of customer service Julie Mechling told the CBS News affiliate in the city that over the 24-month period, customers can miss up to 2 monthly payments and still stay on track for debt forgiveness. More than 2, however, and they are removed from the program.

“There’s help out there for people who are struggling. There are multiple opportunities for you to come to us and see what protections are available to you,” Mechling said.

Pittsburgh Water said the program is possible because a reasonably low number of total customers have outstanding debt or miss payments. Greater than 95% in fact have neither, and Pittsburgh Water sees it as a kind of mutual aid opportunity for the fewer than 5% who are struggling.

Conservative values, National renewal

Maria Corina Machado wants a voting day. So does Diosdado Cabello. Their apparent agreement should worry anyone who thinks Venezuela’s next election will end Chavismo.

In an interview with the Financial Times published Oct. 9, Machado said there is “more than enough time” to prepare for a presidential election by July 2027. She called for transparency over oil proceeds overseen by Washington and said both countries share one goal: to “turn Venezuela into a stable democracy.” Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, the question is whether anyone will name the day.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

Here is the problem. Venezuela had a vote on July 28, 2024. It did not have a credible election.

The National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without publishing precinct results, while opposition tally sheets showed Edmundo Gonzalez winning decisively. The Supreme Tribunal of Justice endorsed the disputed result, having already upheld Machado’s exclusion from office. Millions of Venezuelans abroad faced voting obstacles. The date was real, but the machinery was rigged.

Now look at who controls that machinery.

Cabello remains minister of Internal Relations, Justice and Peace, overseeing the police and internal security apparatus. As secretary-general of the ruling PSUV, he also influences its nationwide organization. Washington offers a $25 million reward for information leading to his arrest or conviction on narcoterrorism charges. Yet he is not hiding. He has met with U.S. officials, and his profile is Gotti-like.

He is not hiding from an election either. He is asking for one.

“If they tell us the elections are tomorrow, let’s hold elections tomorrow,” he told party members in September, adding that Chavismo does not like the silver medal. His confidence does not rest on public opinion. It rests on who controls the institutions surrounding the vote.

The real test is not whether chavismo permits an election. It is whether chavismo can lose one and surrender power.

Cabello need not falsify another tally. A government controlling the police, courts, and electoral authorities can shape the contest before voting begins. It can intimidate opponents, restrict candidates, manipulate registration, and challenge unfavorable results afterward. Counting votes is only part of the machinery.

Acting President Delcy Rodriguez plays the same hand more quietly. At the United Nations on Sept. 23, she promised elections and a transition to “full democracy,” but declined to set a date. She said Venezuelans would determine the timing. Analyst Antonio De La Cruz asked the obvious question: When will Venezuelans actually vote?

So the question for Machado is not whether July provides enough time. Enough time for whom?

Reuters cited experts estimating that a credible election could require at least 12 months to appoint reliable electoral authorities and organize balloting. July is nine months away. Millions abroad were effectively excluded in 2024, and rebuilding registration procedures across numerous countries takes time. A rushed election rewards whoever already controls the infrastructure.

There is a second danger, and it sits in Washington.

After President Donald Trump met Rodriguez in New York, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that “for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election.” Reuters reported that Rodriguez returned home with photographs beside Trump but no concrete agreements. Critics worried that oil production and commercial arrangements had moved ahead of democratic reform.

Washington still promises elections. But a vote held on Chavista terms could satisfy that commitment politically without transferring power. The administration could declare success, Rodriguez could claim international recognition, and Cabello could retain the apparatus that enabled the previous fraud.

Machado would have demanded the very election that legitimized her opponents.

But the opposition has unfinished business. For two decades, it has struggled with factional disputes, competing leadership structures, and difficulty sustaining a unified political organization. Its coordination behind González in 2024 demonstrated what unity could accomplish, but subsequent divisions exposed its fragility. Winning an election and governing through a contested transition require different skills.

Even an honest victory would leave the opposition confronting a difficult question: Can it govern institutions still populated by Chavista loyalists? Democratic legitimacy alone cannot resolve that challenge.

None of this means Machado should stop pressing. Her Nobel Peace Prize recognized her struggle for democratic rights, and her demand for oil transparency matters. But she remains outside Venezuela, politically excluded while those who barred her control the institutions needed for a credible vote.

She should demand a sequence, not merely a deadline.

Cabello must relinquish control over internal security, with safeguards against continued influence through loyalists. The National Electoral Council must be rebuilt with independent oversight and international auditing. Opposition candidates must be allowed to compete, and the military and security institutions must accept the results and permit a transfer of power.

Washington should tie further recognition and economic concessions to measurable progress. Otherwise, it risks financing a transition whose outcome is determined by the institutions it leaves untouched.

In April 2002, I was serving as U.S. Army attaché in Caracas when Hugo Chavez was briefly removed from power and then returned to power. Those days demonstrated how quickly an apparent political victory could unravel when control of the institutions remained contested.

Chavismo has repeatedly retained institutional power even when its political legitimacy collapsed. An election staged on its terms could become its most consequential managed event yet, this time with an American seal of approval.

MACHADO POSITS VENEZUELA ELECTIONS COULD BE HELD IN LESS THAN A YEAR

Machado is asking the right question, but there is a harder one. Who will guarantee that the winner actually governs?

A voting day with Cabello still standing behind the ballot box is not necessarily the end of chavismo. It may be its renewal.

By Russell Jackson

Topic:Cricket

Josh Hazlewood (left) took six wickets in the second innings to seal Australian victory in the first Test. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

That Australia wrapped up the Durban Test in such a resounding fashion on day five was, on the one hand, a quite spectacular validation of the selection strategy that plunged an entire cricket nation into conspiracy theories and conniptions last week.

Viewed another way, it simply added weight to the confidence bordering on arrogance that Pat Cummins's world-beating bowling attack maintains that it can win any game, against any opposition, from any position, on every corner of the globe.

Though South Africa pushed the contest well into the second session, and ever-so-briefly prompted speculation of a draw, Josh Hazlewood performed a quite ruthless clean-up job with 6-49 from 16.5 overs — his 15th five-wicket haul in Tests and his career-best figures. It hastened a 214-run victory for the tourists in a game they began entirely on the back foot.

Hazlewood's bundle included an assortment of his specialities: he broke the crucial partnership of the day by removing Wiaan Mulder after 25 overs of patient accumulation in the morning session; his delivery to clean bowl Marco Jansen was almost unplayable; the snorter that soon after sent Simon Harmer packing had reared up nightmarishly from a decent length.

The savage beauty of Harmer's dismissal brought to mind a piece of sponsor content featuring Hazlewood that was floating around earlier in the week — one of those cutesy interviews where the star athlete is interviewed by a bright-eyed little kid. The interlocutor asked the burly quick for his favourite thing about being a paceman.

"Intimidating batsmen", Hazlewood replied without hesitation. Welcome into the mind of an Australian fast bowler, kid.

As far as Australia goes, quite against most predictions, almost everything went right. But it is strange to consider the way a team that continues to set the world standard was, in this instance, composed from so many moveable and removable parts: opening batsmen variously underprepared and out of position, a number three on a very unpopular final chance, a four on borrowed time, a five who normally opens, a six who should be at seven and a seven who had recently been, well, at sixes and sevens.

Matt Renshaw (left) was player of the match for his 272 runs and two wickets. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Outside the Durban formation, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis, Scott Boland, Cooper Connolly and Michael Neser would not feel presumptuous mentally slotting themselves into a plausible XI.

Nathan Lyon, meanwhile, was less threatening in the second innings than spin dabblers Matt Renshaw, Beau Webster and Nic Maddinson, although it was not in the end a memorable game for the slow bowlers.

These are good problems for Australia to have, of course, and to get through a heavy schedule of Tests in the next 12 months, it will need to draw upon its reserves and pay particular attention to the workloads of its quicks.

In the immediate term, at the very least Australia will probably look to tinker with its batting order and switch Travis Head and Matt Renshaw, the latter of whom was the most popular man of the match in recent memory after adding a two-wicket cameo of off-spin to his batting masterclass.

How does South Africa regroup from such a comprehensive loss?

Perversely, compared to Australia, a larger percentage of its line-up is set in stone: opener Aiden Markram and number three David Bedingham were the shining lights in both innings, while skipper Temba Bavuma and gun all-rounders Wiaan Mulder and Marco Jansen are undroppable.

Anrich Nortje, the man most would have earmarked to be replaced by Kagiso Rabada for the second Test, was far and away the Proteas best bowler.

Markram was the batting standard-bearer for the Proteas on day five with another innings of tremendous substance — a lone hand of 75, which made him the only half-centurion of the game other than Renshaw.

Statistically speaking, when playing Australia Markram is twice the batsman who otherwise averages 35 in Tests. He just needs a few more mates.

The most straightforward change for the Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth) Test starting on Sunday would be the demotion of wicketkeeper-batsman Kyle Verreynne, a walking wicket at present.

Given the premium on players who can shift the momentum of a game in a single session, South Africa could only gain by replacing him with 20-year-old Lhuan-dre Pretorius, a rising star of the T20 world whose five centuries in 15 first-class games include a century on Test debut last year. Stylistically, think Rishabh Pant. Physically, also think Rishabh Pant.

Most enticingly, there is also the fearsome spectre of Rabada, the only undisputed great South Africa currently possesses and a past tormentor of the Australians.

The sight of him limbering up in the nets throughout this game has been tantalising. South Africa would do well to take his lead and be more attacking with the ball from here onward.

Another unknown is whether South African fans will rally around the Proteas and make life less comfortable for the Aussies.

Australia was not met with any sort of hostile crowd in Durban. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

In Durban, spectators were a non-factor. By Cape Town, they will surely be out in greater numbers and taking up Proteas coach Conrad Shukri's pre-tour advice to "give [Australia's players] some stick, but respectfully so".

A few decades ago a South African newspaper offered a slightly less generous assessment of this dynamic, lamenting the experience of the touring Australian cricketer: "They must wonder if our game parks are fenced."

Pakistan on Monday declared a state of emergency in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the stronghold of former prime minister Imran Khan’s PTI party, and suspended the PTI-dominated government.

The central government claimed these drastic measures were necessary because provincial leaders were not doing enough to contain an Islamist insurgency leaking over the border from neighboring Afghanistan.

PTI officials dismissed the official government explanation as merely an excuse to arrest opposition leaders and prevent Khan supporters from marching on Islamabad.

Khan, 74, was ejected from the prime minister’s office in 2022 by a vote of no confidence and has been jailed since 2023 on numerous corruption charges – all of which his supporters denounce as political fabrications created by the administration of current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to prevent Khan from making a political comeback.

PTI members have been rallying in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for days to prepare for the march on Islamabad, while government forces in the Pakistani capital have been blocking off roads and bracing for a siege.

Sharif asked PTI to postpone the march, due to the ongoing terrorist threat from Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban – a violent insurgency that wants to overthrow Pakistan’s secular government and replace it with an Islamist caliphate modeled on the Afghan Taliban.

Just as the marchers were preparing to embark from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for their week-long journey to Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the province and suspended the government. Zardari’s office said he signed the orders after the “failure of negotiations” between provincial representatives and emissaries from Islamabad.

Police arrested several high-ranking PTI members, including the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a Khan ally named Sohail Afridi. The police said some would only be detained temporarily, while others could face serious criminal charges. India’s The Hindu quoted two anonymous Pakistani police officials who said a total of 278 PTI members were detained.

The Hindu also said schools in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were closed on Monday, and “major disruptions to Internet connectivity” were detected in the province.

Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said a provincial governor would be appointed for at least six months, or until the state of emergency is lifted.

PTI leaders and spokesmen sneered at Zardari’s order as an “ambush on democracy” and “a coup disguised as an emergency.”

The provincial governor, Faisal Karim Kundi, posted a video message saying that residents of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would welcome President Zardari’s order, because they want “peace, stability, development and prosperity rather than unrest and insecurity.”

Kundi urged the people of the province to “refrain from violating the law, inciting violence or engaging in rioting.”

like-caring-for-pet-tree-app:
An open-source app has thousands of Berliners adopting and watering city trees as if they were their pets, helping keep the city green amid repeated summer heatwaves.

Gieß den Kiez translates to “water your neighborhood,” and offers users a map of the city with each one of the roughly 900,000 street trees of Berlin accessible as GPS pins. Users can sign up to adopt one, and in doing so receive real-time watering instructions based on the species, age, weather data, and location.

Trees in need of watering appear as orange or red dots, and the app also has icons for all citizen-accessible streetside water taps or pumps.

In green-minded Europe, trees are increasingly being seen as vital urban infrastructure rather than simple tools for beautification. Berlin saw temperatures of over 103°F (39°C) this summer, and the cooling effect provided by a tree canopy is more than just a pleasant relief, but a potential lifesaver.

Developed by CityLAB Berlin, Water your Neighborhood has been running since 2020, and benefited from the cabin fever suffered by the population during the city’s COVID-19 lockdowns. The opportunity to get out of the house and connect with nature—however limited—was welcome, and often stuck.

“It feels very fun, almost like a video game,” Amanda Gläser-Bligh, a suburban Berliner who uses the app, told the Guardian. “I think many people may want to water the trees, but they might feel weird about doing it or they’re not sure if it’s their responsibility. But, if you have this app encouraging you, you know it’s the right thing to do.”

The app’s developers describe it as helping people to think of trees like their pets, and allows them to care for them as such.

Yet it’s proved to be far more than just a novel pastime. Already, Potsdam, Leipzig, Magdeburg, and the 17th arrondissement of Paris have used the open-source code to launch their own versions of the application.

GREEN URBAN SOLUTIONS: Vertical Greening Brings Nature to Urban ‘Heat Islands’ Quickly and Easily (LOOK)

Trees seem at present to be one of the best ways of offering relief to denizens of cities experiencing summers hotter than historical norms. Trees provide shade, improve air quality, and reduce city temperatures on hot days. One American study showed that US counties with improved tree cover spend less on healthcare costs, while an Australian study found that communities with a healthy amount of tree cover—not just grass and green space—were psychologically healthier than those that didn’t.

Other benefits are more subtle. Green, leafy trees can provide sensory relief in urban areas dominated by hard surfaces, right angles, glass and concrete, and intrusive, attention-seeking advertising.

Gläser-Bligh adopted a Linden she has since named “Linda,” a species which lends its name to a famous street in the German capital, and their pollen and nectar to the city’s bees.

EUobserver

Opinion

A lethal plume of toxic smoke was blowing towards us from a blaze at a battery manufacturing plant in Kaliningrad.

Troops in the Russian exclave had been ordered to help put the fire out: untrained and under-equipped, they mutinied. Terrified civilians were thronging the borders.

The Kremlin, oblivious to the unfolding humanitarian and environmental catastrophe, blamed the West for sabotage and incitement, and demanded a transit corridor across Lithuania.

However, none of this actually happened.

We (20 retired and serving officials, experts, and others) were in the safety and comfort of the Wargaming Lab at the ISM university in Vilnius, as guests of the Baltic International Security Centre (BISC).

The crisis scenarios were hypothetical; the aim was to explore the dilemmas and trade-offs they created. (You are the Lithuanian government. Do you let the mutineers in? Or leave them to be massacred?)

The games-master provided regular “injects” – new developments – such as ill-written social media posts from US president Donald Trump. He blamed the authorities in “Lithvastonia” for having started the fire in “Kaliningradia”.

An amusing parody, we thought. A few hours later, the real US president published news of his deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin on sanctions-busting diesel imports, then blamed Ukraine for being invaded.

Not so amusing, especially for our Ukrainian participant, a senior military commander there.

As we were leaving (us to safety, him to danger), news broke that Russia is stepping up its assassination attempts in Europe, targeting defence industry bosses (and perhaps Polish politicians). Our scenarios seemed tame in comparison.
