An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb.

The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy. Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes.

In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month, Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search.

After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!”

That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property.

Later in the video, the Raven user takes a photo of a bathroom from social media. They upload it to Raven, and the tool points to an area of Montecito, California. The top result says, “Montecito Miramar Beach House on the Sand.” 404 Media found that result directly quotes a listing on the short term rental site Vrbo.

In other words, from a single photo, Raven appears to be able to quickly find the specific home it was taken in, without using location data or other metadata attached to the image. In the demonstrations the videos were from social media, but in practice they could be from anywhere a law enforcement officer has obtained them.

This is also not a reverse image search: a reverse image search would take an image then find an identical one posted somewhere else on the internet. What Raven is doing, instead, is identifying unique characteristics in the photo, then finding what are likely other photos from the same property on sites like Airbnb, even if those photos are not exactly the same, or even if time has passed between them being taken.

In another post, Heinen wrote, “For investigators working trafficking and exploitation cases, that connection can turn an unidentified room into a location lead they can verify and pursue.”

Raven is not limited to short term rentals, according to other demo videos. In a third example posted last year, Raven traces a photo of an interior room to a specific address in San Francisco. The interface returns other interior photos of the property; 404 Media found these are exactly the same photos as those posted on Zillow, indicating that Raven is at least pulling data from Zillow in some form.

Another video posted last week shows Raven identifying a particular hotel, too.

In another video, a part of the interface says, “City-specific property AI to determine an address.” That phrase implies the property search isn’t necessarily worldwide, but dependent on an AI model built specifically for that city. When 404 Media reported earlier this year that at least two law enforcement agencies have bought access to Raven, emails showed the MDSO had access to a custom model specifically trained for Miami-Dade County.

“In 2026, we’re investing heavily in interior geolocation across U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments,” Heinen adds in the post.

Graylark trained Raven on millions of images from around the world. When the tool first launched, it was focused on identifying distinct geographical markers like architecture and soil. Now Raven extends that same idea into buildings.

In an interview with the tech publication Indicator last year, Heinen discussed some of how the building interior searching capability came to be. “I’ll be honest, we didn't train it to do that,” he said. “That was kind of an ‘Oh shit’ moment for us. GeoSpy 1.0 couldn't do that. As we trained GeoSpy 2.0, we were just kind of red teaming and testing it out and I think I had a picture of my girlfriend just taking a selfie in the bathroom. I was curious what it would say and I dropped it in there and it put a pin on San Francisco. I was like, ‘Well hold on, wait a minute. That doesn't make any sense. It’s just a picture in a bathroom.’ And then I went over to Zillow and I just started screenshotting images and nine out of 10 of them it would get the right city.”

“We have huge datasets that we train the models on and these are geotagged images from all over. Usually, we would assume that the images are all outdoor images. I'm assuming some of those images would probably have some indoors, whether it's people at a party or just taking pictures of food on their counter. The models must have learned some details that relate to different locations,” he continued.

Airbnb told 404 Media in email “Protecting our community's privacy is important to us — that’s why location metadata is excluded from listing photos, hosts are given the option to show only an approximate location of their listing, and a home’s address is shared with a guest only after a reservation is confirmed. We also have technical safeguards in place to try to limit automated data collection from our site.” Airbnb stressed it has no relationship with Graylark, that its terms of service prohibit scraping, and that the company is reviewing this case.

Zillow told 404 Media that scraping data is against its terms of use, and when necessary it pursues legal avenues.

Vrbo did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

It is unclear if the examples shown in the marketing videos are truly representative of Raven’s speed or capabilities. While law enforcement agencies have paid for access to Raven, it hasn’t always impressed. Joseph R. Peguero Rivera, from MDSO’s Public Affairs Office, previously told 404 Media “To date, use of GeoSpy has been limited and largely exploratory. While it has been reviewed in a small number of cases, it has not resulted in any significant investigative breakthroughs or arrests. No case outcomes were driven solely or primarily by information generated by the tool.”

404 Media first covered Raven in January 2025. At the time, the tool was available to essentially anyone, and some people in the company’s Discord server asked for help stalking women. A day after 404 Media contacted Graylark for comment, the company restricted access to the tool to only government agencies and enterprise users.

In a September X post, Heinen said Alexandr Wang, now head of AI at Meta, was an angel investor in Graylark. Wang did not respond to a request for comment.

In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, Heinen showed Raven being used against a video of people vandalizing a Flock camera.

It was his only relief.

A whizzing Minnesota college professor allegedly spilled his own urine on a student’s backpack in what authorities believe to be the latest in a disturbing series of the educator’s pee-soaked incidents, according to new court docs.

The alleged piss plot was uncovered after a Macalester College student said biology professor Paul Fischer, 55, had heeded nature’s call on Dec. 5, 2025, after she briefly stepped away while working at the school’s science center – only to return to find her backpack moist with a pungent yellow liquid, CBS Minnesota reported.

The unidentified student reported the incident and told authorities that she believed Fischer, who had been teaching at the Saint Paul university for more than 25 years, was responsible for the urination since he was the only person nearby at the time, records show.

The pissed-off pupil provided receipts estimating $2,000 in damages from Fischer’s misplaced bathroom break, according to documents.

When local cops in Saint Paul investigated the tinkling, they found that Macalester Public Safety had received six prior reports complaining about urine found in places other than the restroom at the school’s Olin-Rice Science Center, records show.

Odd places where pee was discovered included trash cans, water bottles and even inside other professors’ decorations, according to documents.

When questioned by authorities, Fischer told police he developed a strange habit over the past two years of peeing in a cup and dumping it in campus trash cans or science lab sinks, records show.

The toilet-challenged educator told cops he may have accidentally soiled the student’s backpack while trying to dispose of a cup full of his wee into a trash can near his office, the document states.

Macalester College told CBS Minnesota that Fischer’s employment at the school ended during the 2025-2026 academic year. A criminal complaint noted he resigned as the college investigated the rash of urination incidents.

The serial sprinkler was charged with first-degree property damage and faces five years in prison and a maximum fine of $10,000. He is expected in court in early November.

Attorney information for Fischer wasn’t readily available, and he could not be reached for comment.

Long Beach residents have been left devastated after powerful waves from Tropical Storm Rachel battered their multimillion-dollar beachfront homes, destroying properties, forcing families to evacuate and ripping apart a century-old boardwalk as yet another storm slammed Southern California.

The destruction unfolded along the city’s Alamitos Peninsula, where massive waves tore through wooden sections of the historic waterfront boardwalk, sending seawater rushing into homes and streets.

At least eight buildings representing 13 addresses were red-tagged as unsafe to enter, while another was yellow-tagged, allowing residents limited access to retrieve their belongings, according to Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson.

For some residents, the storm has meant watching their dream homes get swallowed by the ocean.

Natalie Cabrera, 59, who has lived on the peninsula for just a year and a half, and rents a beachfront bungalow said she was devastated after the storm caused water damage to her home’s foundation.

“I don’t want to leave. At all. Ever. This was my dream,” Cabrera said.

Cabrera described how the relentless waves battered her property, sending water underneath the building and damaging everything inside.

“The floor is squishy. Because the ocean just kept hitting and hitting my home, and the water went underneath,” she said.

“Water didn’t come through my front door. It came up from the ground.” Cabrera said neighbors who had lived in the area for decades had never witnessed anything like it.

“My other neighbor’s been here 30 years, and never, ever have they seen this. So I’m a newbie to the neighborhood. And I’m just devastated to have to leave,” she said.

Cabrera said she was going to move to Ontario, where her son and daughter-in-law have a home. “That’s where I grew up. So I guess I’m just going to have to go back,” she said.

Despite the devastation, Cabrera said she was grateful that her family and neighbors were safe and recalled how complete strangers rushed to help protect her property.

“Everybody just came together, total strangers. There was a young kid from USC, fishing. He saw the devastation of the waves just rushing through my front door, and he came.

“As fast as the water came, they’re shoveling the sand out.”

Robert Wells, 80, whose family has owned a summer home on the peninsula since 1962, said he had never witnessed such severe destruction.

“It’s never happened like this before,” Wells said. “Yesterday, and this morning, the water came right over here. And just took everything out.”

Wells blamed the city’s efforts to protect beachfront properties, arguing that a sand berm constructed to hold back the ocean actually made the damage worse.

“There are more greater chances than not that if they hadn’t put that berm there, that the damage would be minor. And now the damage is major,” he said.

“If they had done nothing, it would have been better. They wouldn’t have all this damage.” Wells also claimed that residents were preparing legal action against the city.

“There is a class action lawsuit forming against the city of Long Beach,” he said.

Meanwhile, John Fernando, who has lived on the peninsula for more than a decade, said he evacuated his property as the tide began rising.

“I left when the high tide started building up around 9am this morning,” Fernando said.

He described how the powerful ocean waves had stripped away layers of sand, exposing structures that had previously been buried beneath the beach.

“No one’s ever seen the rocks and the extra stakes in the sand until now when the ocean just ripped it out,” he said.

Fernando said residents had been working around the clock to protect their homes and help neighbors whose properties had suffered more extensive damage.

“We’re all in this together. We’ve all been protecting our own properties. And then when we could provide support, we’d help each other out at the same time. This is definitely like 100% a group effort,” he said.

But with another unusually high tide expected, Fernando feared the destruction was far from over. “There’s tomorrow, there’s the king tide, so this is just the beginning, it’s not over,” he said.

The storm’s destruction was particularly severe along Seaside Walk, where massive waves breached the protective bulkhead, damaged the historic boardwalk and left beachfront properties vulnerable to further erosion.

Video captured a large crack running from the foundation to the roof of one waterfront home, while other footage showed powerful waves crashing into structures along the shoreline.

By Saturday evening, parts of the damaged boardwalk had become inaccessible, with officials posting no-trespassing signs as emergency crews scrambled to reinforce the coastline.

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for residents along Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th places, with the order scheduled to remain in effect until noon Tuesday, subject to changing conditions.

The city also restricted vehicle access to the peninsula to residents only, allowing emergency crews to move equipment and supplies into the hardest-hit areas.

Long Beach officials distributed 7,600 sandbags to residents, bringing the total handed out during the three recent storms to approximately 15,000.

Crews also deployed heavy equipment and massive sandbags to reinforce damaged sections of the seawall and prevent additional properties from collapsing.

The latest storm comes after Southern California’s coastline was battered by Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend and Hurricane Polo in the following weeks.

In Newport Beach, officials declared a local emergency Friday after coastal flooding inundated streets along the Balboa Peninsula, prompting crews to construct protective sand berms and deploy pumps.

The city temporarily closed its beaches and shut down the Newport Pier, Balboa Pier and the Wedge as officials worked to prevent additional damage.

Orange County officials coordinated the distribution of tens of thousands of sandbags, while public works crews used bulldozers to reinforce vulnerable stretches of shoreline.

Meanwhile, powerful winds reached the Inland Empire, where footage showed a structure being ripped from the ground as two people desperately attempted to hold it down.

Post-tropical Storm Rachel made landfall in northern Baja California, north of Ensenada, before moving inland and bringing heavy rain and flash-flood concerns to parts of the Southwest.

Back in Long Beach, residents were left assessing the damage to their homes and wondering how long it would take to rebuild.

Dave Uff, who has lived in the neighborhood for 12 years, said his home on 63rd Place had been spared after he surrounded it with sandbags, but several of his neighbors had not been as fortunate.

“On Seaside Walk, some of the fronts of the homes have been destroyed. On 63rd Place, a lot of water and sand intrusion, that’s going to be hard to mitigate,” he said.

“This is the worst anybody’s ever seen it. The people that have been here for 60 years say this is the worst they’ve seen it.”

Despite the losses, Uff said residents were determined to help one another recover.

“We’re a very tight community here, and what affects one affects all. And some of our neighbors have lost their homes. We’re all hurting for them. We’re all helping out,” he said.

“We’re heartbroken, but we’re steadfast, and we’re doing what we can to keep things normal, as normal as possible, and waiting to rebuild.”

Secret Service Director Sean Curran spoke to "60 Minutes" host Norah O'Donnell about the "massive" increase in threats against the presidency recently.

Secret Service leadership detailed the "massive increase" in threats against the presidency and agents in the past year during a special joint interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" on Sunday.

"It's like we've never seen before," Secret Service Director Sean Curran told host Norah O'Donnell. "The threats on our full-time protectees are up just over 40% than they were last year. That's a massive increase."

Curran, along with Deputy Director Matt Quinn, were questioned as to what they believed caused the rise in threats. Curran suggested that the growth of the internet was a factor, but O'Donnell wondered if President Donald Trump also drove the threats.

TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS

Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Deputy Director Matt Quinn appeared for a joint interview on "60 Minutes." (AP)

"President Trump is one of the most polarizing political figures in American history. Is that in some way leading to the increase in these threats?" O'Donnell asked.

"We are an apolitical organization. We're here to protect who we're sworn to protect," Curran answered.

"Look, I would say there's people on both sides of the aisle that either love or hate any president. I think the biggest factor we're dealing with today is mental health issues for sure. And more people are being pushed over the edge in either direction," Quinn added.

"The world is different than what it was 20 years ago. You know, social media changes people," Curran said.

The men also did not clarify whether more threats came from left-wing or right-wing sources, explaining that they do not "weigh" threats in that way, citing concerns from both the Jan. 6 Capitol riots and the assassination attempts against Trump.

'DECOY' AIR FORCE ONE WAS PROTECTED BY US FIGHTER JETS, OFFICIAL SAYS

Curran revealed there has been a 40% increase in threats against the presidency. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Curran, who was the lead agent protecting Trump during the first assassination attempt against him in 2024, emphasized the importance of preparation.

O'Donnell later connected this idea to the reports of Trump's Air Force One plane switch in August.

"Look, that's not the first time we've done that. We wish that wasn't reported, 'cause that takes some of our tactics away from being able to do something similar again. Certainly wasn't the first time where we did something like that," Curran said, though he clarified that he did not say whether they had ever used a decoy plane prior to this incident.

Quinn also defended the procedure which left agents behind in a decoy plane.

"When you're operating in any protective detail with the president of the United States, for any president, the priority is the president. Everyone else, staff, agents, media, personnel involved are not the priority, including our own personnel. As hard as that may be for some to understand, the mission is to protect the president of the United States," Quinn said.

I SERVED AS TRUMP’S NSA. SCOTUS NEED TO STOP COURTS PUTTING THE PRESIDENT'S SECURITY AT RISK

Security around the president has received extra scrutiny since the assassination attempts against President Donald Trump. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

This interview came as the Secret Service faces ongoing scrutiny after three officials were placed on leave in August.

Protection for the president has also come under scrutiny as the FBI hesitates to release documents pertaining to the investigation of the assassination attempt on Trump at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.

A 21-year-old Manhattan native went to a hospital to be treated for a simple broken ankle — only to end up dead because she was given too many painkillers, according to a shocking lawsuit.

The heartbroken family of tragic Dale Alice Martin said in court documents that Waterbury Hospital in Connecticut disastrously botched the college student’s care April 10, 2025, when she arrived there to be treated for the ankle she fractured while doing farm work — and was given a lethal cocktail of drugs that left her brain-dead, the Hartford Courant reported.

“We didn’t know till after Dale’s death that she was admitted to a bankrupt hospital that was under investigation, where nurses allegedly were buying food for patients, where the level of funding was so constrained that the hospital may not have been able to function properly,” said the dead woman’s father, Westchester County resident Lindsay Martin, to the outlet.

“Dale did not have a choice of where to go,” he said of his daughter, a Bethlehem, Connecticut, resident who attended middle and high school in Pelham in Westechester and was an English and history student at Trinity University in San Antonio, Texas, according to the Pelham Examiner.

“She was brought to the nearest hospital,” the dad noted.

An autopsy determined that Dale died from cardiac arrest after being given multiple painkillers, according to the suit filed by family lawyer Christopher Mattei.

“Within 14 hours of admission, providers at the hospital had administered so much pain medication that Dale stopped breathing and later died,” the lawsuit said. “No one checked on Dale during this time.

“The same medications that were interfering with Dale’s breathing were also sedating her. Dale could not even call for help as she suffocated. At 7 a.m. on April 10, a Waterbury Hospital nurse finally checked on Dale. It was far too late. Her heart had stopped beating.”

Lindsay Martin said he remembers the dreadful phone call from the hospital when she died.

“I hung up the phone, and I was in shock,” the dad said.

The family had been unaware of the issues with the hospital, which was long owned by California-based Prospect Medical Holdings, a company that filed for bankruptcy in January 2025.

Earlier this year, Hartford HealthCare bought the struggling facility and two others.

“What we expect to find is that this was a hospital that was largely operating on fumes as a result of Prospect dismantling infrastructure within the hospital, reducing staff, training, and finding every way possible to extract value out of the hospital in a way that jeopardized care,” Mattei said.

A rep for the hospital declined to comment because Dale’s death predated its ownership.

The former CEOs of Prospect, David Topper and Von Crockett, did not respond to calls and emails from WNBC-TV News seeking comment on the lawsuit.

While today's freezers are packed with ice cream flavors such as cookies and cream, salted caramel and mint chocolate chip, some old-time favorites seem to have melted away.

Flavors including Butter Brickle, rum raisin and maple walnut were once familiar options at ice cream counters and grocery stores, but many have become harder to find as tastes have changed.

The food site Tasting Table recently looked back at a variety of nostalgic flavors that defined childhoods for many Americans. Here are five that might bring back some sweet memories.

NATIONAL ROOT BEER FLOAT DAY CELEBRATES AMERICAN CLASSIC THAT YOUNGER GENERATIONS ARE LEAVING BEHIND

Once-familiar ice cream flavors from the 1970s have become harder to find in today's freezer aisles. (H. Armstrong Roberts/ClassicStock/Getty Images)

Butter Brickle ice cream was inspired by a butterscotch-flavored candy created in Omaha, Nebraska, in the 1920s, according to Tasting Table. Featuring a butterscotch flavor with crunchy toffee pieces, the ice cream had become a national favorite by the 1970s but is harder to find today.

In a Facebook group dedicated to memories of the 1970s, the flavor came up repeatedly as fans reminisced about its signature bits of crunchy toffee.

YOUR FAVORITE GROCERY AND SNACK ITEMS MAY HAVE DISAPPEARED FROM STORE SHELVES IN 2026

Rum raisin ice cream dates back to the 1930s but surged in popularity in the 1970s, when the rum-soaked raisins and vanilla ice cream combo became widely available in shops and grocery stores. The flavor even made it to the White House, where President Richard Nixon reportedly served it for dessert.

Rum raisin ice cream surged in popularity in the 1970s and was reportedly served at the Nixon White House. (iStock)

Though it can still be found today, rum raisin has become harder to spot in many parts of the country. "I miss it so much! It’s my favorite ice cream flavor," one Reddit user wrote in a subreddit dedicated to ice cream.

CENTURY-OLD ITALIAN ICE RECIPE IS CREATING CHILDHOOD MEMORIES FOR A WHOLE NEW GENERATION

Baskin-Robbins introduced its bright Pink Bubblegum ice cream in the 1970s, complete with small pieces of chewy bubblegum mixed into each scoop, Tasting Table reported. The unusual flavor became a childhood favorite for some and has occasionally been brought back by Baskin-Robbins for limited runs.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"It was my favorite. I would eat the ice cream and save the bubblegum for later," one Reddit user recalled.

Classic ice cream counters offered an array of flavors that may be harder to find today. (Lambert/Getty Images)

Bodycam footage of a Georgia police officer gunning down an 1-year-old donkey named HeeHaw shows the heartbreaking moment the beloved animal is killed.

Cedartown Police Department released the shocking footage of HeeHaw — who was barely waist-high on the officers — getting shot as it trotted inquisitively to the cops who were in a field searching for a missing 12-year-old girl.

“Firearm discharged at a donkey. It was trying to attack us on a pasture,” Officer Trenton Garner could be heard telling dispatch in the video.

Footage showed HeeHaw walking slowly with his ears up towards the officers, who were carrying flashlights as they passed through Elsberry Riding and Farm ranch in Rockmart, Ga., at around 12:45 a.m. on Oct. 4.

HeeHaw ambled towards one officer who quickly deployed a Taser, which failed, Garner said in an incident report.

Then, from roughly 10 yards away, Officer Garner shot HeeHaw with a Glock 17.

The poor pet donkey then ran away, collapsed, and was later found dead from the gunshot wound.

Garner said in the incident report that a CPD officer, a K-9 handler, and a bloodhound team searching for the missing girl were able to scare off horses on the farm and that the donkey was the only animal that allegedly charged.

Owner Hannah Israel mourned the loss of her tiny yearling and pushed back on Garner’s account.

“HeeHaw thought people were his family, and HeeHaw was family,” Israel told WSBTV.

The bodycam footage is finally out.And now the truth is there for everyone to see.HeeHaw wasn’t charging. He wasn’t attacking. He wasn’t some uncontrollable threat.He was doing what everyone who knew him said he always did: running up to greet someone in his friendly,… pic.twitter.com/9ivOmuMVll

“Cops entered my pasture searching for a missing person WITHOUT permission or warning  and shot and killed my bottle raised BABY donkey,” she wrote online Sunday, vowing to take legal action.

“We are heartbroken. He was my SON!!” she wrote.

Israel operates the Elsberry Riding and Farm ranch where HeeHaw was featured as part of the petting zoo.

Garner has been put on administrative leave.

The Georgia Department of Agriculture is investigating the incident.

Neither Israel nor the Cedartown Police Department could be reached for comment.

Zach Bates has qualified on pole for Sunday's Bathurst 1000, topping the time sheets during the Top 10 Shootout at Mount Panorama.

Qualifying king Brodie Kostecki failed to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions, finishing second.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.

Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.

Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.

But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.

Bates denied Kostecki with a scorching lap of Mt Panorama.  (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.

Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.

In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.

Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.

But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.

Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.

Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.

Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.

But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.

Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.

Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.

Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.

The Winnipeg Police Service said it is aware of a video circulating online that appears to show two children robbed while walking home from the library.

The mother of the siblings said the Sept. 26 incident, which happened in the area of Andrews Street and Magnus Avenue at around 7:30 p.m., has left her children afraid and her feeling guilty.

“I should have been there with them. I felt horrible,” said Brittany Beaudet. “I would have been out the door if I knew any sooner to help them out.”

In the 40-second video, the two children, 14-year-old Mason and nine-year-old Kenzie, are approached by a man wearing a black shirt, black pants and white shoes.

The man is seen speaking with Mason, who cooperates and puts up his hands and appears to comfort his little sister.

The man then pats down the boy and checks his pockets before moving over to his sister and taking a neon pink backpack off her. Beaudet said it was filled with toys, snacks and other trinkets.

The robbery was captured on camera by the Andrews Street Family Centre. A representative from the organization was not available for an interview.

“We are aware of the incident and the video and are in the process of reaching out to the victim,” WPS Const. Pat Saydak said Thursday.

The children were not hurt in the incident.

“My daughter is more shaken up to walk by people under the influence now after this has happened,” Beaudet said. “She thinks it’s going to happen again.”

The mother said she doesn’t know for sure if the man in the video is under the influence, but said his behaviour indicated he may have been.

The video, which was posted by a friend of Beaudet’s, has been viewed thousands of times. Dozens have reached out to the family to offer support.

“I’m really shocked at how big it blew up and how many people are reaching out to check on the kids,” she said. “It’s really amazing how much people really care about other peoples’ kids.”

SUPPLIED

Mason Beaudet, 14, and his sister, Kenzie, nine, can be seen enjoying a carnival ride.

Beaudet said while the incident left her reeling, she was incredibly proud of her son, who she said kept calm in a dangerous situation.

“If he did react, and tried to push the guy away, or try running or something, it could have been a different outcome and that could have been a lot worse,” she said.

The mother said she hopes the man captured on video turns himself into police, as she feels it’s only a matter of time until he is arrested.

“It doesn’t matter what you’ve gone through in life,” she said. “You shouldn’t be touching other kids. You should be looking out for them.”

Jalud and the West Bank’s epidemic of settler violence, explained.

In the weeks and months following Hamas’s brutal October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and Israel’s devastating campaign in Gaza that followed, the world’s attention turned away from the West Bank.

Over the past three years, however, the situation in the Israel-occupied territory has worsened as Israeli settlers have carried out more violent attacks on Palestinians.

The attacks can range from acts of daily harassment and trespassing to a major mob assault in the West Bank village of Jalud that overwhelmed Israeli security forces and blocked a displaced Palestinian family from returning home. Last week, Israeli settlers shot and killed a Palestinian man.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has largely dismissed violent West Bank settlers as an issue, blaming the Jalud attack on a “handful of rioters” and referring to settlers as “juvenile delinquents” in a speech to the UN last month, in which he argued that the world should focus on violence committed by Palestinians instead.

But even as he downplays the problem, human rights organizations have documented a record level of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. The International Committee of the Red Cross has said that such attacks have made everyday life “untenable” for the more than 3 million Palestinians living in the West Bank.

The Israeli settlements are also clearly illegal, as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp explained in September — but that hasn’t stopped them from expanding.

Ahead of Israel’s elections later this month, settlers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing with the explicit backing of some Israeli cabinet ministers, led by young militant Jewish settlers that are part of a loose network known as the Hilltop Youth.

The Wall Street Journal’s Feliz Solomon reported on the Jalud attack and has written about the role of Hilltop Youth in worsening settler violence. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the reality on the ground in the West Bank, the settler groups behind it, and how Israeli officials are responding.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

Tell me about the last three years in the West Bank. What’s been happening?

The October 7 attack really hardened a lot of people’s views in Israel, and that’s played out in the West Bank in a number of ways.

One is that the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, which has some powerful members who are settlers themselves, became much more overtly supportive of expanding the Jewish settlements.

The second thing that changed was basically a total breakdown of trust, both between Jews and Arabs, and also between Jews and the state, because a lot of people felt that they were really on their own in terms of security.

All of this created a really combustible environment. There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.

What does that total impunity look like? We often hear the term “settler violence.” What does that mean?

There’s really a whole spectrum of violent actions. It’s mostly by younger male settlers. There are some acts of daily harassment, like trespassing on Palestinian property, vandalism, stalking people, blocking roads, and preventing access to resources like water wells. And then on the other end of the spectrum, there are also acts of extreme violence.

There have been some very serious physical assaults. Settlers throwing rocks with slingshots. Last year, there was a viral video of an elderly woman who was beaten with a stick. She was hospitalized for days. And lately, we’ve been seeing more mob violence where a large group of settlers will raid a Palestinian village. They’ve set mosques and other property on fire.

Just to be clear, there’s violence by Palestinians too, but we’re really seeing an alarming surge of violence by settlers that’s often unpunished, and increasingly it’s happening when settlers go into Palestinian areas where they’re not supposed to be.

You reported on an attack that happened last week in the West Bank near the Palestinian village of Jalud. Tell me what happened.

Over the summer, some young settlers who are associated with a group called the Hilltop Youth set up an encampment around three houses on the outskirts of the Palestinian village, Jalud, and essentially besieged the houses. They blocked their access to essential goods and harassed the residents until, in late July, they felt so unsafe that they fled.

Two of those houses belonged to the Tubasi family. In early September, Israel’s high court ordered the state to ensure their safe return, and in late September, they tried to go back. We spoke with Wael, who’s one member of the family, and also with their lawyer about what happened when they tried to go back.

A few dozen [Israeli] security forces were deployed to escort them home in the middle of the night, and when they got there, they found that the house was totally ransacked. They showed us before and after pictures, and the windows were smashed, the doors were broken, electrical wires were cut, and there was just debris all over the place.

When they came inside for the first time in about two months, they were walking through the property looking at the damage with flashlights, and they’d only been there for a few minutes when suddenly they were surrounded by a mob of settlers. They said at first that there were about 50 settlers around the house, and the military later said that there were more than a hundred people that took part in what they called a riot.

The authorities told the family to take cover deeper inside the house, and they hid inside a stairwell as the soldiers tried to force these settlers to retreat, but they were shouting and throwing rocks at the house, and then, according to Wael, they even started climbing in through the windows. At that point, the authorities told the family to go upstairs, all the way up to the roof and to hide in a corner of the rooftop.

Wael explained what he saw up there. He was looking down and he saw the soldiers battling it out with this large group of settlers and this thick cloud of tear gas and loud bangs from stun grenades.

“There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.”

Eventually, the security forces realized that they weren’t getting the situation under control. They had to get this family out of there. They took them back downstairs and outside and put them in a military vehicle, but then the settlers surrounded the vehicle and they were rocking the car. They slashed the tires so that [the family] couldn’t leave. Then the soldiers had to move them into an armored military vehicle and eventually they got them out.

A short while later, not long after they had escaped, they started receiving video messages from some of their neighbors that showed what happened after they left, which was that their car and their house had been set on fire.

All right, so the Israeli authorities in the form of soldiers were trying to help this Palestinian family legally return and settlers violently blocked them. This is settlers versus the authorities. What do we know about who these settlers are and what is motivating them?

This was a very large group. We know of three people who were detained in this incident. All of them were teenagers. The youngest one I believe was 15 years old.

A lot of the harassment in this area comes out of a nearby settlement called Esh Kodesh and smaller, more informal settlements around it that are called outposts. And these outposts are usually pretty crude encampments. They often start with just tents or a camper van or a trailer with no electricity and no water. And the people who choose to live in these places tend to be very young, very extreme ideological settlers.

You mentioned something called the Hilltop Youth. Who are they?

The Hilltop Youth is a loose network of settlers that live outside the mainstream, and they often have much more extremist views than the mainstream settler movement. It’s an offshoot of religious Zionism, which is one of the main ideologies of the settler movement, and it sort of fuses the ideas of Orthodox Judaism with ultranationalism.

The Hilltop Youth take these ideas to the extreme, and I’ve spoken with a bunch of them myself. They believe that they’re on a divine mission to reclaim the Holy Land for Jews, and they’ll cite parts of the Torah and other religious texts that they interpret as empowering them to take the land back and even to use violence. They see it as a preventive type of self-defense, and they see themselves as protecting all other Jews.

These are young people, some of them teenagers. Where are they coming from? Why are their parents not grounding them? How has this been allowed to unfold the way it has?

It’s a good question, and I should say also that not all Hilltop Youth are violent, but a lot of the violence that’s committed by Jews in the West Bank does come from this group, and they come from all over the place. Some of them grew up in the settlements, and then as teenagers, they kind of wandered and they struck out on their own. And then there are others who come from all over Israel.

A lot of the Hilltop Youth, we’re finding, are kind of troubled kids. Sometimes they’re dropouts from strict religious schools, sometimes they have behavioral issues or ADHD, and they just didn’t really fit in. We heard from some kids who said that they found out about the outposts by word of mouth, like someone at their school had invited them to come for the weekend and they’d come and they’d stay a few days and eventually they’d start spending more and more time there until at some point they’re just living there.

There are a number of NGOs that recruit young kids to come work as farm hands on agricultural outposts in the West Bank, and some of those are in these areas that are more prone to radicalization. These organizations present themselves as very innocent in that they’re identifying kids that need help and are bringing them to a place where they will learn some discipline and they will have a purpose and they’ll have something to do. But that often puts them into a more extreme environment.

In the case of the family you profiled in Jalud, it’s clear that the Israeli authorities, in the form of soldiers, attempted to help the family get back to their home. How does this typically play out, though? How do Israeli soldiers typically respond when settlers attack Palestinians?

There have been a number of high-profile examples of video footage circulating that appears to show Israeli soldiers either standing idly by or even, some would argue, siding with the settlers.

In one recent example, there was a video that showed some soldiers praying alongside settlers who had besieged the home of a Palestinian American man, and that was actually not very far from where the Tubasi house is. The military said that it was looking into it to determine whether disciplinary action needed to be taken.

In general, military officials acknowledge that this violence by settlers is a big problem, and the security establishment definitely does not support what’s happening here. They see it as getting in the way of counter-terrorism efforts and overall efforts to bring stability to this very volatile area.

I’ve heard this directly from military officers, but on the ground there does seem to be a breakdown of discipline in some cases and a lack of clear instruction in other cases. Some soldiers simply don’t know how to deal with threats from other Israelis, especially really young ones, as you pointed out. It’s just not what they’re trained to do.

Do you think the government could put a stop to these attacks by settlers if it wanted to, or has the government lost control?

This problem has gotten so big that it’s going to be very difficult to solve without significant backlash, but I have spoken with a number of former Israeli security officials who say yes, much more could be done — starting with a more frank acknowledgement of what’s happening, clearer law enforcement procedures, and more disciplinary actions.

Democrats have discovered a wonderful new word for the 2026 elections coming to primetime.

Affordability.

Healthcare needs to be more affordable.

SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

Housing needs to be more affordable.

Childcare needs to be more affordable.

Energy needs to be more affordable.

Groceries need to be more affordable.

Who could possibly disagree?

Certainly not me.

LET SOCIALISTS ROB FROM THE RICH 100% AND YOU STILL WON’T BE ABLE TO PAY THE BILLS

But as a financial advisor, I have one question whenever somebody tells me they're making something more affordable.

Did you actually lower the cost, or did you just find somebody else to pay the bill?

Because those are two very different things.

Democrats have made affordability a centerpiece of their 2026 economic message.

LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN

Among the ideas being discussed by progressive Democrats are $1 trillion toward new housing supply, government-produced prescription drugs, federal utility-rate standards and limits on what families pay for childcare.

Other Democrats are pushing expanded healthcare subsidies and additional government assistance for families.

Some proposals could attack legitimate underlying problems. Cutting zoning and permitting restrictions to build more housing, for example, could actually increase supply.

I'm all for finding ways to make America build again.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

But too much of the affordability conversation still follows an old formula.

Something costs too much. Have government pay more of it.

We've seen this movie before.

We used to call it tax and spend.

Now we call it affordability.

Imagine your health insurance costs $20,000 a year.

Government gives you an $8,000 subsidy.

Your personal bill falls to $12,000.

Fantastic.

But healthcare didn't suddenly cost $12,000.

It still cost $20,000.

We simply changed who wrote part of the check.

The same principle applies to childcare subsidies, housing assistance and countless tax credits.

Government money isn't created by a magical ATM underneath the Capitol.

It ultimately comes from taxes, borrowing or shifting resources from somewhere else.

This would bother me less if the federal government were swimming in excess cash.

It isn't.

The United States continues running enormous annual deficits while carrying a federal debt measured in the tens of trillions of dollars.

Imagine a family earning $100,000 annually but spending $130,000.

They're already buried in debt.

Then Dad walks into the kitchen and announces:

"Great news. I just made groceries more affordable."

How?

He put them on another credit card.

Nobody would call that an affordability plan.

They'd call Ted Jenkin for a financial reality check.

Yet Democrats, and frankly, Republicans, when it suits them, regularly embrace government benefits without spending nearly enough time discussing the ultimate bill.

Here's the affordability agenda I'd rather hear debated.

Why does America have a housing shortage?

Why does it take so long and cost so much to build?

Why are healthcare prices nearly impossible for consumers to understand?

Why aren't there enough doctors, nurses and childcare providers?

Why can't we produce and transmit more energy faster?

Those are cost questions.

And solving them means attacking supply, competition, regulation and productivity and not merely subsidizing demand.

If we have 100 families fighting over 80 houses, giving everybody a bigger government check doesn't magically create another 20 houses.

Democrats say their affordability agenda would lower costs for working families, and some of their proposals deserve a legitimate debate.

But Americans should apply one simple test to every promise:

Did you make it cheaper, or did you make somebody else pay for it?

Because I suspect we're entering another era when government spending will increasingly be sold as the solution to the cost of living.

The terminology has changed.

The sales pitch is better. The algorithms repeat the message.

But Americans have seen this movie before. At least I have.

Tax. Spend. Subsidize. Repeat.

Just don't call it that anymore. Call it affordability.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky has returned Poland’s highest state honor, after the Polish president stripped him of the award as a politically charged dispute over World War II history resurfaced.

Ukrainians believed the order “was meant for the Ukrainian People and our army,” Zelensky wrote in a social media post explaining the gesture. “Today, I sent the Order back to the President of Poland. I believe the future will confirm the respect Ukrainians deserve.”

The message published on X is accompanied by photos of the Polish order and a postal receipt that it was about to be mailed to the Polish presidential office.

President Karol Nawrocki decided to strip Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle over the Ukrainian leader’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during WWII.

Former Polish President Andrzej Duda bestowed the award on Zelensky in 2023 for services to security, resilience and the defense of human rights.

Zelensky issued a decree on May 26 naming a unit of Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA, which operated during the 1940s and 1950s and has been accused in Poland of mass killings.

“For the majority of Polish society, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army remains above all a formation responsible for cruel crimes against the citizens of the Polish Republic during World War II,” Nawrocki said in a 13-minute address on social media.

The Ukrainian decree was met with widespread criticism in Poland, which has hosted millions of Ukrainian refugees and is a key supporter of Kyiv as it battled Russia’s four-year invasion. However, Nawrocki is a nationalist politician who has exploited anti-Ukrainian sentiment for electoral gain. Ukrainians in Poland have been facing increasing prejudice despite their contribution to the economy.

The decision to revoke the honor did not mean Poland’s support for Ukraine in its defense against Russia would decrease, Nawrocki said.

Ukraine is grateful to Poland for its support, and would stay open to resolve historical differences with Poland, Zelensky wrote Saturday in his post. “I am proud of our people and of EVERY Ukrainian warrior.”

Ukrainian Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov wrote on Telegram that Nawrocki’s decision was “an unfriendly act toward our people” and “a gift to the Moscow aggressor, which will certainly use it against both of our countries.”

Four Ukrainian officials including Budanov said they would return state honors that Poland had issued them.

Some in Ukraine criticized the decision to return the Polish honors.

Arseniy Yatsenyuk, Ukraine’s former prime minister, wrote on X that one “harmful and incorrect decision by the current president of Poland cannot be corrected by other incorrect decisions of ours.”

Poland is scheduled to host a major event on Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction next week, which Zelensky was expected to attend.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a political rival of Nawrocki, urged the two leaders to “tone down emotions, not stoke tensions.”

“The front line runs elsewhere,” Tusk wrote on social media Friday night, adding that the row between Poland and Ukraine “delights Putin and shocks our allies.”

Zelensky’s May decree said the designation was meant to restore military traditions and recognize the unit’s performance in defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity and independence.

The UPA fought for Ukrainian independence against both Nazi Germany and Soviet forces. But it has been accused of killing tens of thousands of Poles, mostly in the Nazi-occupied regions of Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. In 2016, the Polish Parliament recognized the crimes committed by UPA as genocide.

Ukrainians say armed formations on both sides, including the UPA and Polish underground forces, were involved in attacks and reprisals that led to large-scale civilian casualties among Poles and Ukrainians.

Poland and Ukraine had recently made progress on the issue of exhumation of Polish victims. A December meeting between the two presidents in Warsaw had signaled progress on historical reconciliation.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said five members of the Voronov family were killed in a Russian attack last month. (X: Volodymyr Zelenskyy)

Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in a Russian attack that killed a Ukrainian family.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said based on "preliminary data", the missile that killed the family was the result of the alliance between "Moscow scumbags" and Pyongyang's "deranged regime”.

"Of course, more examinations will follow, and everything will be verified, but as of now — it is a North Korean ballistic missile," he said.

North Korea has previously supplied missiles used in the war, but this suggests Russia may have received fresh stocks at a time when Ukraine's air defences are under strain.

Earlier today, Mr Zelenskyy hit out at the growing alliance, claiming Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements" from North Korea.

It came just a day after he said "a decision has been made" for up to 50,000 North Korean troops to be sent to fight for Russia.

"Everyone around the world must understand what this means," Mr Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed to fight for Russia. (Reuters: Marko Djurica)

In late 2024, North Korea sent an estimated 14,000 soldiers to fight for Russia.

But if Mr Zelenskyy is correct, more troops may be on the way in what would represent a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Last week mourners gathered in the village of Radushne in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region to farewell the Voronov family, who were killed in the Russian attack at the end of July.

Five coffins were carried into the church – for the father, mother and three of their children. Soft toys were placed on two of the lids.

Mr Zelenskyy shared a photo of the family in a post on X on July 30, and wrote the Russian missile strike was so powerful that "almost nothing remained of the family's house.

"This was the Voronov family: mom Olena, dad Artem, seven children — Mark, Dominika, Zakhar, Azariah Ilay, Federica, Emilia, Viorika — and their one-and-a-half-year-old grandson Artem, the child of their eldest son, who is currently defending Ukraine," Mr Zelenskyy wrote.

The fate of the five of other family members, including Artem, who were in the house at the time of the strike, remained unknown, he said.

At the funeral, Artem's mother, Iryna Bolhar, told Reuters news agency: "I got a phone call and was simply told that he was no longer with us."

"We still held out hope that they would find him wounded, but they had already said for certain that he was gone."

Ukraine's military intelligence agency has said a specialist missile unit from North Korea had begun deploying to Russia.

It said the unit could be equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles, six launchers and 90 personnel.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un shares a laugh with soldiers during a visit to a base in November. (Supplied: KCNA via Reuters)

Anton Sokolin from Korea Risk Group said videos were circulating online in Russia and Ukraine "purporting to show" those North Korean soldiers.

He added there was speculation more details about the missile unit may be revealed next month during some sort of engagement between the two leaders, but confirmed detail is scant.

Mr Zelenskyy said in July that Russia had requested 30,000 additional troops from North Korea, in a later social media post he said it is "30,000 to 50,000".

He paired the information about the potential troop deployment with a call for South Korea to provide support for Ukraine's air defences.

The potential deployment is yet to be confirmed by a secondary source, like South Korea's National Intelligence Service.

"The movement of soldiers is not that difficult to observe," Dr Go Myong-Hyun from the Institute for National Security Strategy told the ABC.

"North Korea is under surveillance pretty much 24/7, that is the combined surveillance of America and South Korea."

He said that does not mean the deployment is not happening — it could be in early preparation stages — but he warns it should be treated with "caution" until there is confirmation, given it represents such a significant escalation.

Mr Sokolin was similarly circumspect. He said as the information had come from a "credible source like Zelenskyy" it should be treated as "legitimate", but it was necessary to watch for actual signs of the deployment.

"It is really hard to rule it out completely, at the same time I do believe we have to treat this information with a grain of salt."

Russia and North Korea have been significantly deepening their ties in recent years.

The Ukrainian leader has said Pyongyang is supplying weapons to Russia, with Kyiv finding some North Korean missiles in Ukraine's territory.

In May last year North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-Un, justified sending soldiers to Russia as being part of the defence of a "brother nation".

North Korea and Russia signed a treaty, which included security assistance obligations, when Vladamir Putin visited Pyongyang in 2024.

Russian President Vladimir Putin turned to North Korea when he needed soldiers to bolster his invasion of Ukraine. (Pool: Alexander Nemenov via Reuters)

Work on the first road bridge to connect the countries is also nearing completion.

The bridge across the Tumen River will allow for easier transport of goods — including military equipment, to pass between them and will make it more difficult to surveil.

"If that link is fully functional there will be even more exchanges and something that is very hard to track, because there will just be trucks going in and out of the country — you can put pretty much any exchange on the table, it all could be hidden," Mr Sokolin said.

Analysts say North Korea would be rewarded for sending more soldiers to fight in Ukraine, with economic support and access to military technology.

Ukraine's military intelligence agency has said a specialist missile unit from North Korea had begun deploying to Russia.


  (Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP)

"There would be high suspicion that North Korea is only doing this because they got the right price for their soldiers' lives," Dr Go Myong-Hyun from the Institute for National Security Strategy explained.

"Last time North Korea deployed soldiers to Russia, we believe that led to the transfer of some critical technologies from Russia to North Korea."

The "price" this time could include Russia giving Pyongyang sophisticated weapons components or military technology, potentially for things like nuclear propulsion for submarines or drone development.

Kim Jong Un called North Korea’s involvement in the Russia-Ukraine an exercise of sovereign rights in defence of a "brother nation".

"If there is to be a repeat of the process (seen in 2024), the chances are that North Korea is only sending soldiers to Russia because they received the right reward for the troubles," Dr Go said.

"The reward would be proportional to the size of the troop deployment. So, if they are sending that many soldiers to Russia then chances are they're getting back something commensurate."

He said that would have "huge implications" for the security of countries like South Korea and Japan, "especially if Russia is transferring technology or components that are related to the production and deployment of weapons of mass destruction."

If North Korea deploys such a significant number of troops, it would "merit a response" from its neighbours, which he said have so far been "relatively restrained" in the face of Pyongyang's tightening ties with Moscow.

Mr Sorkin agreed that "troop movements of this size are of note" and would "raise a lot of alarms across the world."

A further deployment would also build on the experience North Korea's soldiers have been gaining in Ukraine.

"Troops would get a rare chance to learn modern combat techniques and modern warfare," Mr Sorkin said.

Mr Zelenskkyy has pointed to the threat against countries in Asia, while arguing they should provide support to Ukraine, particularly with its air defences.

"The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots, the greater the danger will later be for Japan, the Republic of Korea, the Philippines, and other countries in the region."

Late last week North Korea fired a short-range missile into the sea toward Japan, the first in more than a month, since a series of weapons tests earlier in the year.

It came shortly after Pyongyang criticised Tokyo's defence build-up, and ahead of planned military drills between South Korea and the United States.

The drills will start next week and will have a focus on responding to North Korea's evolving capabilities — an acknowledgement its forces are bringing lessons from the war Ukraine home to the peninsula.

Mark Zuckerberg has staked out his position in the industry’s growing argument over how fast AI should advance, aligning himself with President Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang against Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, and Elon Musk.

CNBC reports that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out his views in a post on X and other social media platforms Tuesday, weighing in on a debate that has split the industry’s most prominent leaders over the past week. “There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up,” Zuckerberg wrote. His own take: “My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models.” He added a warning for companies tempted to move fast and skip safety work: a “focus on alignment will fall behind.”

Zuckerberg argued that market pressure, not government mandates, will keep AI developers in line. Labs face “significant liability if their models cause harm,” he said, which creates an incentive to catch problems before they occur. He pointed to Meta’s own choices as an example, saying the company “delayed shipping” its Muse AI technologies for reasons of “safety and security.” He described the move as voluntary rather than the product of outside pressure: “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

The comments follow an essay Amodei published over the weekend arguing the industry should “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk endorsed the idea afterward, while President Donald Trump harshly criticized it.

Breitbart News reported Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang publicly supported Trump during a phone call in front of a live audience:

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, sitting for an interview with the All-In Podcast, turned to the phone and told the President, “I’m onstage with the besties,” referring to hosts Chamath Palihapitiya and Jason Calacanis, along with White House advisers David Sacks and David Friedberg. Trump needled Huang about the setup: “The great thing about life is Jensen can develop the most complex computer chip in the world … but he can’t figure out how to put you on speaker.”

The call landed in the middle of a live industry debate over how fast AI development should move. Onstage, the hosts had been discussing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI.” Elon Musk and Sam Altman have both said publicly that they agree with Amodei. Huang does not agree with this approach, and Trump used the call to back him up.

Huang then pushed back against Amodei’s slowdown in a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, arguing that AI model makers should hold themselves accountable rather than push for government regulation. He went further in a separate interview on CNBC’s Mad Money, calling many proposed AI-specific laws and regulations “just completely unnecessary.” Existing rules, he said, already cover the ground: “We have plenty of laws. We have plenty of regulations that govern the reliability and the functionality of products.”

Dario Amodei has launched a full spectrum PR campaign to push political and industry controls that would build an unbeatable moat around Anthropic’s business.
