Just name an important issue. Whether standing up to the Trump administration, tackling homelessness, boosting Portland Public Schools, or funding the Oregon Health Plan, Governor Tina Kotek has been a skillful advocate for our city and state.

Kotek has been a more effective governor than her predecessor Kate Brown, and, if re-elected, could become one of the best Oregon governors in decades.

Her values also fit Portland like a hand in a glove, more so than her opponent, state Sen. Christine Drazan, R-Canby. The sunniness of Drazan’s beautifully produced television commercials belies the harshness of her campaign positions.

Drazan’s focus is gutting the Corporate Activity and Estate taxes for high incomes and vetoing any other increase on high-income- bracket businesses and individuals. Those actions would reduce state revenues, thus harming public schools and universities, hollowing out state health coverage for many,  and under-cutting Portland Mayor Keith Wilson’s efforts to reduce homelessness.

Drazan is also a Climate Change denier and vows as governor to reverse decades of state environmental, land-use and consumer protections.

And Drazan is a President Donald Trump ally. The Clackamas County Republican has supported or been complicit in Trump’s authoritarian assaults on Oregon, including inflation-creating tariffs, federal climate and health care cuts, forcing utility rate increases by sabotaging the Bonneville Power Administration, and trying to place Army National Guardsmen on the he streets of Portland with e contrived excuse of law and order.

Kotek and Attorney General Dan Rayfield have battled Trump blow-to-blow with legal challenges to his every attack on our state. Drazan almost certainly won’t even try.

Kotek isn’t perfect. She stumbled early in term involving her wife, Aimee Wilson, in state policy matters that were inappropriate. Her management of the state transportation budget deficit could have been much better. Kotek also has a serious, tech-minded personality that hurts her with some voters impressed with Drazan’s extroversion and cosmetic qualities. But on substance, Tina Kotek is a champ.  Many N/NE Portlanders remember well her long service as state legislator and Speaker of the House before becoming governor. She’s had a strong first term. Portland needs her for another.

[The writer ran against Kotek in a three-person race for the Oregon House of Representative’s District 44 seat in the May 2006 election.]

The Trajectory

A recent study suggests GLP-1 drugs may weaken links between impulsivity, alcohol use, and violence.

Share

About a year ago, Rutgers University researcher Daniel Semenza was listening to a podcast about an expansive study of GLP-1 medications when a question occurred to him.

The 2025 study, published in Nature Medicine, had examined millions of Department of Veterans Affairs records to map the potential benefits and risks of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, a class of drugs better known by brand names like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

In addition to treating diabetes and obesity, the medications appeared to affect substance use, impulse control, and other behaviors associated with the brain’s reward system. Researchers and patients had also begun reporting possible reductions in compulsive shopping, gambling, skin picking, and other repetitive behaviors.

“The lightbulb kind of went off,” Semenza told us. “What about aggression? Or what about violence?”

Semenza, who is research director at the New Jersey Gun Violence Research Center, knew that impulsivity and substance use — particularly alcohol use — are two established risk factors for violent behavior, including gun violence. His question became the basis of a new study he conducted with Christopher Thomas, a Rutgers University professor of sociology, anthropology, and criminal justice.

Published in June in the journal Criminology, their resulting study suggests that GLP-1s may somehow blunt the links between impulsivity, alcohol, and violence. It found that associations between impulsivity and violence, and alcohol and violence, were weaker among people currently taking GLP-1 medications than among those who had stopped taking them.

The association between impulsivity and violence was about 62 percent weaker among current users of the medications than among former users, according to the study. The association between alcohol use and violence was about 52 percent weaker.

The findings are a preliminary look at GLP-1s and violence and do not necessarily suggest that GLP-1 drugs make people less impulsive, Semenza said. Instead, the medications may affect whether an impulsive tendency turns into an aggressive or violent reaction.

“Their impulsivity isn’t necessarily going away, but that impulsivity isn’t turning into such a reaction that they are then reporting they’re engaging in violence,” Semenza said.

GLP-1 receptor agonists include medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus, and Trulicity. Since initially being prescribed for Type 2 diabetes, their use has expanded rapidly as they became FDA-approved for weight loss beginning in 2021. Similar drugs like Mounjaro and Zepbound also act on GLP-1 receptors.

Emerging research suggests the medications may also affect dopamine signaling, cravings, reward-seeking, and stress regulation. Those possible effects have led researchers to study GLP-1 drugs in connection with alcohol use disorder, other substance use, and compulsive behaviors.

For their study, Semenza and Thomas examined data collected in 2025 through a nationally representative survey of 7,521 U.S. adults, 821 of whom reported having used a GLP-1 medication at some point. Of those, 597 were current users, and 224 were former users.

Respondents answered questions measuring impulsivity, alcohol consumption, and self-reported violent behavior during the previous 12 months. The measure of violence included questions about whether respondents had hit someone who insulted them, participated in a physical fight, threatened someone with a weapon, or committed robbery.

As expected, greater impulsivity and alcohol use were both strongly associated with more reported violence. But those associations were weaker for respondents who were currently taking a GLP-1 drug.

The researchers adjusted for a range of characteristics, including age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, income, employment, health insurance, diabetes, perceived weight, and neighborhood safety. As a result, the impulsivity result proved more consistent. The alcohol finding, which relied on only two questions, was less stable, becoming statistically insignificant under some alternative analyses. The authors said that finding should be interpreted cautiously until it can be replicated with larger samples and more detailed measures.

“There is much more work to do, but the robustness and sturdiness of the impulsivity finding were striking to us,” Semenza said.

Other recent studies suggest GLP-1 medications may reduce alcohol consumption and craving. And research has long connected alcohol to gun violence. A 2024 study, for example, found that shortening late-night alcohol-sale hours around bars and taverns in one Baltimore neighborhood was followed by a 23 percent annual decline in violent crime.

“Two of the most well-established risk factors for violence are impulsivity and alcohol use,” said Rose Kagawa, a researcher at the University of California, Davis School of Medicine. “If there’s something that can sort of dampen the effects of those risk factors, that’s a really powerful tool potentially.”

But neither line of research establishes that GLP-1 use reduces gun violence, and drawing that connection will require much stronger evidence, Kagawa said. “Right now, we’re not looking at individuals over time under different conditions.” Future research could use more robust methodologies, such as case-control or cohort studies, or, if possible, a randomized controlled trial.

Semenza was also clear that the study has limitations. It captured respondents’ medication use and behavior at one point in time, meaning it cannot determine whether GLP-1 use caused the weaker associations. And the survey did not identify why former users stopped taking the medication — cost, side effects, insurance coverage, or health differences. Violence was also relatively uncommon in the sample, making it more difficult to identify statistically significant associations.

Semenza and Thomas’s study also didn’t address another major player in U.S. gun deaths: suicide.

As injuries and deaths from community violence and interpersonal gun violence have plummeted since 2022, firearm suicides — which account for the vast majority of U.S. gun deaths — have continued to tick up.

Earlier research has shown that suicide attempts often occur during brief periods of acute distress, impaired judgment, or impulsive action — the same broad behavioral processes Semenza’s study suggests GLP-1 medications might affect — while firearms make those attempts more likely to result in death compared to other means.

Other studies have identified more direct links between alcohol abuse and firearm suicide, Kagawa said. A 2021 study she coauthored found that people who purchased a firearm after a prior conviction for driving under the influence of alcohol were at elevated risk of subsequent suicide when compared to gun buyers who had no previous alcohol-related convictions. Another 2023 study found that as the amount of alcohol consumed increases, the probability of using a firearm as the method of suicide also increases.

Taken together, the research suggests scalable interventions targeting alcohol use may potentially reduce the suicide mortality rate.

Despite some concerns that GLP-1s might be associated with depression, an early but promising body of research has instead found associations between GLP-1 use and lower risk of suicidal ideation, attempts, or self-harm among some groups. The possibility that GLP-1s could interrupt the progression from suicidal impulse to action remains an open research question.

Regardless, Semenza cautioned against treating medication as the solution to violence. Poverty, unemployment, inequality, and neighborhood disadvantage remain central drivers of violence, he said. “I would never advocate for medicalizing violence as a social problem,” he said.

Instead, he sees pharmacological research as one possible component of a broader violence-prevention strategy. If more intensive studies confirm the results, GLP-1 medications could help researchers better understand how biological, behavioral, and environmental factors interact.

Semenza said researchers are now exploring ways to link administrative data, including Medicaid and arrest records, to examine the question more closely. That could better establish when people were taking the medication and whether their behavior changed over time.

“Violence is preventable,” Semenza said. “If we can find different ways and different opportunities to make that so, then I think it’s worth pushing in every direction that we can.”

The blast on Saturday evening at the Balzi Rossi, an upscale Italian establishment in central Moscow, killed three people, including the female bomber, Russian state media said, citing local officials.

At least 21 people were wounded when the explosive device detonated at the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square, Russia's National Anti-Terrorism Committee (NAK) said late on Saturday, according to Russian state news agency Ria Novosti.

The Town of Mosman Park has introduced a new planning policy aimed at protecting some of the suburb’s most prized views, including sweeping Swan River vistas, Indian Ocean sunsets and the Perth city skyline.

The council unanimously adopted its new local planning policy covering views of significant at its May 26 meeting, following two rounds of community consultation and nearly a year of policy development.

The policy establishes a formal framework for assessing how future developments could affect significant views when developers seek approval to exceed standard building height limits.

Under the new rules, applicants proposing taller developments will be required to provide detailed visual assessments, including 3D modelling and geospatial analysis, to demonstrate how their projects may affect important views from neighbouring properties and public areas.

Town officials say the policy fills a gap in the current planning framework, which provides limited guidance on how views should be assessed when developments depart from standard height requirements.

The policy was prompted in part by a 2024 legal review of State Administrative Tribunal decisions involving disputes over significant views, which highlighted the challenges local governments face when making discretionary planning decisions without detailed assessment criteria.

As part of the initiative, the town will also investigate purchasing specialist 3D aerial mapping and modelling software to help simulate the visual impact of a proposal from specific locations.

The technology is expected to cost about $20,000 upfront, plus annual software subscription fees of about $3500.

The town argues the investment could ultimately save money by reducing legal disputes over contentious development applications.

Council documents reveal Mosman Park has recently faced three judicial reviews relating to proposed developments and their impacts on significant views, with legal costs reaching as much as $30,000 per case.

Community feedback broadly supported the policy, with 70 per cent of respondents backing the town’s proposal to fund 3D aerial mapping technology.

The policy and accompanying guidelines are now in effect and available on the town’s website.

Emma Lewell, Labour MP for South Shields will lead a debate calling for tougher legislation on houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs)

A town's MP has said she believes growing numbers of shared houses are causing overcrowding, parking problems and anti-social behaviour.

Emma Lewell, Labour MP for South Shields, will lead a debate in Parliament later calling for tougher government legislation on houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs).

Speaking to Radio Newcastle, Lewell said: "We don't even know how many HMOs there are in South Shields. This is like the wild west."

In a statement the Department for Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Councils already have powers to prevent too many HMOs being allowed in their area but we're looking at tougher rules that would give local leaders even more control over HMOs."

A local petition supported by Lewell and presented to Parliament in 2025 said too many HMOs were leading to problems.

She also said that HMOs were letting down the people living in them.

"People who are vulnerable deserve better, they deserve supported living, they don't deserve to be dumped in a property and told 'there's your room, there's your shared bathroom, crack on'.

"I am not trying to stigmatise people here - they deserve better and my community deserves better," Lewell said.

Local resident Eddie Arfaoui said he was concerned about crime and HMOs.

He said: "The type of people put in shared houses are not really responsible people.

"They'll commit crimes and every so often you'll have police knocking on your door asking if you've seen this person."

Nic and Scott said they were concerned about drug culture in some HMOs

Nic said she was concerned about drug use in HMOs and wanted her son Scott to avoid this type of accommodation when he leaves home.

She said: "I dread the day when he's got to fly his wings, it's crime and all sorts, you could get lured into something, followed home at night, we talk about girls' (safety) but what about young men?

"I know there are a few areas around here that have shared accommodation where someone who's got off drugs has gone in and ended up back on them - it's sad."

Scott, 20, said he would rather wait longer to afford to live in his own accommodation.

He said: "It has crossed my mind but it's more hassle than it's worth. I'd rather get my own place and stay with my mum in the meantime.

"One of my friends had got clean but went into supported accommodation and ended up in a worse state."

Joe Mason lives in a HMO which allows him to live close to his daughter

Joe Mason lives in a HMO in the area, and said people living in shared accommodation were being unfairly blamed.

The 42-year-old told Radio Newcastle: "I can understand where people are coming from, but people are getting paranoid about illegal immigrants.

"They need to do more research on it, I live in one just down the road and there's not a single illegal immigrant near it.

"I think the current rules are strict enough, there's rules you've got to abide by, there's CCTV on every property I've been in, it's not like they're unsafe.

"Crime happens everywhere, you can't just blame it on HMOs."

Jason said housing was needed but he worries that HMOs can attract troublemakers

Jason, 53, said he does not mind HMOs existing, but has concerns over the behaviour of some occupiers.

"They're building flats at the bottom of my street, and I'm worried that it'll potentially cause trouble.

"If there's people who need housing, that's fair enough, but if it's people that are going to cause trouble, no.

"They just seem to be coming up all over the place."

South Tyneside Council said it used additional powers to prevent any HMOs from being converted without planning permission.

Council leader Paul Mackings, said: "South Tyneside Council already uses all the powers available to us to regulate HMOs and manage their impact on our communities.

"In addition, all HMOs that require a licence must meet clear legal standards and management conditions.

"We carry out enforcement activity where these standards are not met."

What those opposing multiculturalism fail to grasp is that it is a natural adjutant of, and to, the human condition (“Hanson gives voice to Howard’s view”, July 3). My late mother spent her formative years during the 1930s in Iran, then Persia. Her parents worked there under the Shah and she witnessed Christians, Muslims, Jews and others living in a multicultural harmony, celebrating the weekly Sabbath day of each of the major religions. That period ended with World War II. But the human objective to socialise and mix has never ended and it never will, notwithstanding the blind prejudices of one Pauline Hanson and her ilk. We live in a world of many cultures on a planet celebrating multiculturalism. Frederick Jansohn, Rose Bay

As the Coalition digs around in ancient mounds of conservative values, it has alighted happily on Hanson’s diatribes over mono/multiculturalism. I expect our Indigenous people would be the first to agree. Foreigners flooding the land, imposing their values, speaking in foreign languages and not just at home, destroying an ancient and homogeneous culture – see what happens. Nola Tucker, Kiama

To add to Waleed Aly’s comments on cultural identity, one of the most devastating attempts to engineer a national monoculture occurred in Nazi Germany. Before 1933, Germany enjoyed a vibrant, progressive, and inclusive cultural life. Giants of the interwar era — dramatist Bertolt Brecht, filmmaker Fritz Lang, composers Kurt Weill and Felix Mendelssohn, painter Otto Dix, and Nobel-winning author Thomas Mann — shaped a dynamic intellectual landscape. Yet, following the Nazi rise to power, these figures were declared non-Aryan or “decadent”, their works were banned, and an ugly, austere, anti-intellectual monoculture was forced upon society. History shows that enforcing a single cultural mould inevitably requires the erasure of diversity, dissent, and free expression. When Hanson’s One Nation advocates for an idealised Australian monoculture, one must ask: how does it propose to achieve it without walking the same dark, exclusionary path as those in 1930s Germany? John Bailey, Canterbury

Waleed Aly expertly chronicles the anti-multicultural sentiment of the Coalition, especially under the social re-engineering period of John Howard and his attack dog Tony Abbott. Across 25 years, the Coalition (initially through Howard) raised doubts about multiculturalism in Australia; then it proceeded to “white-ant” (excuse the pun) a concept that previous generations of Australians had generously embraced; then it moved more boldly to express dislike and distrust of multicultural Australians; and finally it seized the opportunities through immigration and terrorism debates to demonise people from other cultures. Aly identifies that the Coalition’s “winks and nudges” — releasing and directing antagonism towards multiculturalism — had in effect “set the hounds loose”. Along then comes a rejuvenated Hanson and the Coalition, with its continual shift to the right, now “grasps in vain to find a leash” to control the opening which it has created for Hanson. Warren Marks, Long Beach

What is this sudden panic about mono versus multiculturalism? In retirement, I travel around seeing hordes of schoolchildren with obvious backgrounds from all corners of the globe, conversing mostly in English or, just as often, not conversing at all while glued to their devices. We all know it is easier to travel overseas with English as your first or second language than any other single language. The most universal language of all, internet connectivity, is unifying the world, and all those youngsters are English-speaking Aussies, who just pay lip service to the backgrounds of their parents. The mono/multi problem is a political beat-up that doesn’t exist. Let’s not go back to the monocultural diet of the 1950s that I saw at the Bonegilla Migrant Camp museum near Albury, where the daily Aussie menu was mutton prepared three ways – with veggies boiled to near extinction. Having visited the countries of my ancestors, I can say they are never as good as I was told by my parents, who were essentially reminiscing about their childhood rather than the country itself. I am a proud second-generation Aussie. Peter Kamenyitzky, Copacabana

I was struck by Sarah Yassien’s thoughtful insight, “Patriotism can be complex as well. You can love something deeply and equally care about another culture deeply, and so I think you find joy in all of it” (“Win-win will be ‘pure joy’ for Egyptian Australians”, July 3). How much better is her view than the strident jingoistic statements about patriotism made by some blinkered politicians, media commentators, and self-described “real” Aussies? Do we really want to adopt the American mindset of ‘My country right or wrong’? How blatantly self-righteous, ignorant and wrong, would that be? Thank you, Ms Yassien, for your clarification – and for making my day. Jennifer Fergus, Croydon

Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy is right (“Fury over minister labelling Menzies a ‘Nazi appeaser‴⁣⁣ , July 3). Robert Menzies was a Nazi appeaser. Menzies suggested, after the invasion of Poland by Hitler’s forces, that Britain should let Hitler have Poland and France and make peace with Germany. At a public meeting in July 1939, Menzies said: “History will label Hitler as one of the really great men of the century.” Menzies also wrote to his sister extolling the virtues of Hitler’s harsh dealing with trade unions. He also praised the way Hitler had the whole citizenry committed to the common goal of the state. Menzies joined the war effort only because Britain did. If I were the Coalition, I would be using a very long pole to come anywhere near Menzies’ pre-World War II engagement with Nazi Germany. Barry Welch, Bridgeman Downs (Qld)

Perhaps Conroy should have also explained the epithet of “Pig Iron Bob”, given to Menzies for encouraging exports of scrap metal to Japan just before World War II, and perhaps he could have noted the appeasement policies of the Lyons’ government.Perhaps, too, he could have said organised labour such as the Wollongong wharfies were well ahead of the conservatives in being aware of Japan’s threats after its invasions of China. He was too generous. As for Gerard Henderson, a former chief of staff to Howard, claiming that “Menzies put on the khaki” – he was never a soldier in either war. Tony Sullivan, Islington

Whether you should label Menzies an appeaser can be argued about. That he thought in July 1939 that Hitler was a great man defies understanding, given that Hitler by then had occupied Czechoslovakia, had introduced the Nuremberg racial laws and launched the violent persecution of German Jews with the “night of broken glass”. To follow Great Britain into the war was more likely loyalty to the Empire then deep conviction about Nazi Germany. Dierk Mohr, South Turramurra

In September 1940, during the Battle of Britain, Hitler (motivated by a vengeful pique) made a serious strategic blunder and switched the Luftwaffe’s bombing targets from RAF airfields and infrastructure to English cities (“Russian blitz hits Kyiv apartment buildings”, July 3). It allowed the RAF to regroup and rebuild. He believed it would break morale but instead it strengthened English resolve. It altered the course of World War II and many historians rank it as the major cause of Germany’s defeat. Vladimir Putin appears to be making the same mistake. Gary Stowe, Springwood

High-rise apartments are not the solution to the housing crisis (“NSW housing promise falls well short of the target”, July 3). They are expensive to build, expensive to maintain, their floor plans are inflexible and their security arrangements, such as needing a pass to operate the lift, mean kids need constant supervision, even if they’re just going to the playground. We need more gentle density, more dual occupancies, duplexes, small two-storey apartment blocks, townhouses that can slot into the existing fabric of a suburb without smashing it to smithereens. We need the large housing companies to design family houses that could be easily split into two apartments so that people have flexibility at all life stages, and we need governments to support this through the ability to subdivide and sell these as needed. We need so much more than what we are being given. Gina Hay, Bayview

We are well short of the 75,000 new homes that need to be built each year in NSW, but something else should be remembered. In the inner west, we see lots of duplexes. They are counted as two new homes when, in fact, it is only one additional dwelling. The situation outlined in the article is understated. Neville Turbit, Russell Lea

Here we go again (“Global search for architects of new Bays West precinct”, July 3). Yet more publicly owned harbourside land to be handed over to the rich, with a mere 10 per cent allocated to “affordable” housing. The government’s definition of such housing involves a 20 per cent discount on rents, with such properties reverting to private ownership after just 15 years. I suppose it’s a slight improvement on the total absence of affordable housing in perpetuity at the nearby Blackwattle Bay redevelopment, with Building 1 on this publicly owned site being allocated to a private company to build yet more housing for 601 students. Shame. Elizabeth Elenius, Pyrmont

I am sick and tired of the privacy lobby, which I suspect was formed to help rich men hide assets from their departing wife and kids (“Privacy fears over new digital laws”, July 3). We’re kidding ourselves if we think social media companies don’t already have intimate and sensitive information about us. Whenever you log in to another platform using your social media account, personal data is being shared. Anonymity in social media contributes to bad behaviour. Content creators should own their words or shut up because we need to protect kids from harmful social media content. Anne Matheson, Gordon

It seems to me that privacy advocates take too broad an approach to online privacy; wanting guarantees of free speech and anonymity where there should be no guarantees. The anonymity/privacy situation was so aptly described by the great philosopher Mike Tyson, ″⁣Social media made y’all way too comfortable with disrespecting people and not getting punched in the face for it.″⁣ Peter Butler, Wyongah

Sometimes some things just don’t make sense (“X ’fought to keep Bondi shooting content online‴⁣⁣, July 3). When I hear that the world’s only trillionaire and owner of social media platform X likens footage of the Bondi massacre to being no more graphic than a “gore movie”, I wonder how an obviously well-educated, privileged person could ever use such a boneheaded analogy to defend the right of his platform to keep such graphic and upsetting content online. This has nothing to do with freedom of speech. Real people died. Bill Young, Killcare Heights

With billionaires proliferating like mushrooms and making all kinds of questionable deals in an attempt to amass even more wealth, how refreshing to read of the philanthropic work of Isaac Wakil (“Reclusive philanthropist dies aged 104”, July 3), who lived to an extraordinary age. He spent his money without undue noise in making his adopted part of the world a better place both culturally and in the field of healthcare and education, the joy of giving accurately portrayed in his Art Gallery photo. Well done, good and faithful servant. Bernard Moylan, Bronte

Most of our elected representatives have fled the chill of Canberra for the comforts of home during the winter recess. If parliament were still sitting, there could have been plenty of heat being applied to government members on the issue of a gas tax. The widespread support across the nation earlier this year for a fair levy on gas exports has just been further justified by the news that Australia’s gas industry giants will reap a windfall profit of $18 billion as a result of the Iran war (“Gas giants to reap $18b from Iran war fallout”, July 3). This is over and above the handsome cut they make in the normal course of events. The war-fuelled boost to their profits makes headlines but is not the real issue. Its importance lies in drawing attention again to the status quo by virtue of which the gas industry plunders a national resource at little cost to itself and fattens its coffers at the expense of the taxpayer. Sadly, this will be forgotten by the time the Canberra circus resumes. Tom Knowles, Parkville (Vic)

There has never been a better example of shortsighted political gain than the way we treat our gas exports. Australia started exporting LNG in 1989, following the completion of the North West Shelf project in WA. Since this time, our top four gas exporters have profited, and been assisted by every federal government, to the tune of billions of dollars. If we had taxed the net profits of gas exports at the rate of 78 per cent, as Norway has done from the beginning, we would not now be arguing about a mere 25 per cent tax. This finite, precious resource is the gift that keeps on giving, with our government’s approval. When will we learn? Daniela Catalano, Haberfield

After much research into the “free” three hours of electricity (Letters, July 3), one recoils with confusion, caution, reluctance and annoyance. A fellow traveller and good friend found listening to The Beatles for half an hour a small mercy while waiting for his provider to take his phone inquiry. Tempted to “let it be”, he continues to seek solar sanity and reason. Brian Jones, Leura

I read with interest this week’s letters relating to correspondents’ electricity charge experiences. mushrooms-clean-rivers:
An awesome study that could help clean up rivers world-wide at negligible cost leveraged fungi as a pollution control filter.

The mushrooms in question were the very delicious and very helpful turkey tail, and the pollution in question was sewage: notably E. coli bacteria.

The river was in the English county of Devon and the results were so great that water industry regulator OFWAT gave local utility Anglican Water almost $2 million to implement the idea at scale.

Similar success was had in Lincolnshire, where the mushrooms were instead used to clean up agricultural runoff of phosphorous and nitrogen which can cause abnormal blooms of algae that choke waterbodies of oxygen.

The application was ever so simple: a bag of woodchips impregnated with turkey tail spores left at the bottom of the river. The mycelia, or filament system of the mushroom, filtered out 80% of the E. coli, 83% of the phosphorous, and 35% of the nitrogen.

Joshua Mercer, at Anglian Water said the fungi would act as a “second line of defense” to normal sewage treatment.

“If [this work] can have a positive impact on water quality, then it’s benefiting everyone,” Joshua told the BBC.

In December 2025, about a month before the U.S. invaded Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, President Trump had a secret meeting with Elon Musk, Time magazine reports. This was roughly seven months after Musk left his role in the Trump administration at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

During this meeting, Trump “spent hours” talking to Musk’s Grok chatbot, including asking how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of their president, a source told Time. Just a few months earlier, in September, Trump began ordering U.S. military strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump alleged were involved in drug trafficking.

People had apparently been turning to Grok asking about the boat strikes and political climate in Venezuela, as The Atlantic reported at the time. So Grok told Trump that Maduro was a “deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall,” Time reported.

When such celebrations indeed happened after the U.S. invaded on January 3, Trump apparently “came away thinking Grok was ingenious,” that source told Time.

So perhaps it should come as no surprise that in June of this year, the Pentagon’s head of AI said that the military used Gov Grok to deploy and strike targets during the Iran War.

While Grok isn’t the only AI model serving the DoD (OpenAI also has an agreement and Anthropic has been in a back-and-forth over how its models can be used for military intelligence and in modern warfare), Grok may become an even bigger favorite under this administration. This article is also available in: French

PARIS — France’s biggest far-right party isn’t that jazzed about an endorsement from the world’s first trillionaire.

After Elon Musk called presidential candidate Marine Le Pen “France’s last hope” in a post on X on Wednesday, her allies from her National Rally party were quick to downplay his backing as a matter that’s out of their hands.

Laurent Jacobelli, a spokesperson for and lawmaker from the National Rally, said on public radio Thursday that while he agrees with Musk’s statement, the party does not seek out overseas endorsements. The National Rally has taken a similar approach with Trump, keeping him at a distance and rebuffing support from Washington despite an ideological kinship.

“What matters isn't the opinion of people abroad,” Jacobelli said. “It’s the opinion of the French people.”

The X, SpaceX and Tesla owner has in recent years regularly weighed in on European politics and offered support to anti-immigration right-wing and far-right groups, including the AfD in Germany and far-right provocateur Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson, in the United Kingdom.

Musk’s politics and vision of free speech made him something of a hero among parts of the European right. National Rally MEP Thierry Mariani in 2023 even nominated Musk for the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, the EU's top human rights award.

But Musk’s association with U.S. President Donald Trump, who is highly unpopular in France even among the far right, and controversies like his stiff-armed gesture that critics say resembled a Nazi salute have turned him into a black sheep in the country.

“These marks of support matter more to reporters than they do to voters,” Mariani told POLITICO. “We haven’t asked for anything.”

Added fellow National Rally MEP Fabrice Leggeri: “There is no reason to seek partnerships with foreign business leaders, particularly those outside Europe.”

Musk’s post also immediately sparked accusations of foreign interference in French politics and concerns over how he might use his social media platform to influence the campaign.

“Musk has every right to express himself. That's not the issue. However, we need to ensure that the tools at his disposal do not skew the debate in France in favor of one candidate or another," said Pascal Confavreux, spokesperson for the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Former European Commissioner Thierry Breton, who repeatedly feuded with Musk over the EU’s attempts to enforce social media regulations, echoed the point on X: “Elon Musk is backing Marine Le Pen. That’s his right. It’s now up to the authorities to ensure X’s algorithm in Europe doesn’t favor any candidate."

A spokesperson for X did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

Leggeri told POLITICO he was concerned that Musk’s comments would lead his party’s critics to “wave the bogeyman of alleged algorithm manipulation” to undermine Le Pen’s campaign.

Leggeri was a fierce critic of the Romanian Constitutional Court’s decision to annul the results of the 2024 presidential election there after declassified intelligence documents showed that an ultranationalist candidate benefited from a TikTok campaign that was similar to influence operations run by the Kremlin in Ukraine and Moldova.

The French president spent years pushing a ban on minors using social media.

French tech leaders and politicians don’t want the country’s strategic supply of electricity to end up lining the pockets of American AI giants.

The information appears to have come from an attorney representing the family.

The records also noted that Matthew was retired while his wife was on leave from work, indicating the family may not have had the funds to cover Thomas Crooks’ funeral expenses.

In other portions of the records reviewed by the NYP, Matthew said he was unemployed at the time of the shooting.

The cremation was first disclosed by Republican Louisiana Rep. Clay Higgins, who questioned why the FBI released Crooks’ body to his family just 10 days after the July 13, 2024, assassination attempt.

President Trump’s would-be assassin was born without making a sound on Sept. 20, 2003, according to a separate NYP report.

“When Thomas was born, he did not scream, and he was always quiet from that point on,” his father, Matthew Crooks, told federal investigators.

That quiet demeanor followed Thomas Crooks throughout his life. He was killed at age 20 by Secret Service gunfire moments after firing at Trump and grazing his ear.

In interviews with the FBI, Matthew Crooks said he “never really had a father/son bond” with Crooks and described him as emotionally reserved. He rarely showed strong emotions, hardly laughed, and was difficult to read.

Matthew Crooks told investigators that his son never appeared to pursue romantic relationships and “never showed interest in girls,” according to the NYP.

His father also said his son “repeatedly denied” being gay when the subject came up over the years.

Thomas Crooks became increasingly interested in guns and shooting as a teenager, though he had little interest in hunting or fishing.

Matthew Crooks said their conversations were often brief and centered on firearms, including Thomas Crooks asking whether he would need a background check to buy his father’s Glock — a question Matthew considered “odd.” He also asked about inheriting his grandfather’s guns.

Thomas Crooks began going to a gun club around the start of the pandemic, initially as a “terrible” shot. Matthew said “he could not hit the paper [target],” and estimated it took four to five years of practice before his son became proficient.

Eventually, the would-be assassin began using targets set up more than 100 yards away. When Crooks’ father asked why he was “going out so far,” Thomas Crooks said, “he wanted to see how far he could shoot with rudimentary sights.”

After buying a prism sight, Thomas became “very knowledgeable” about measuring and zeroing his weapon and calculating the precise number of clicks needed to adjust the sight.

As his interest in guns grew, the would-be assassin also began ordering large numbers of Amazon packages, including “parts, tools and items to increase the capacity of his rifle.” (RELATED: Widow Of Butler Rally Victim Says Trump Assassination Attempt Was ‘An Inside Job’)

He sometimes used the pseudonym “Bob Dole” as a delivery name, a practice Matthew said began after his Citizens Bank account was hacked and fraudulent BetMGM charges appeared.

Thomas Crooks also believed using an assumed name would help protect his accounts from being compromised.

Matthew Crooks explained that the purchases were still linked to his bank account regardless of the delivery name, but his son dismissed the explanation and continued using pseudonyms for online orders.

Crooks also introduced his father to privacy tools, which he said made them “less likely to be compromised by outside actors.”

He also used encrypted email services such as GMX and Mailfence.

Around that time, he began experimenting with 3D printing and attempted to build a Glock 19. Matthew told investigators his son used “carbon fiber plastic, a dryer and a toaster oven” to make the gun. After firing a single round, Matthew worried the frame could explode and refused to allow him to use it again.

His other projects included building a gaming PC and a security camera using a Raspberry Pi. Matthew said his son’s likely role model was Marvel’s Iron Man. (RELATED: Secret Service Agent Shot At WHCD Was Only One To Return Fire: Affidavit)

Federal investigators also interviewed an unnamed person who described Crooks as a “big history buff” who was “interested in politics,” though he generally discussed politics casually.

According to the NYP’s review of the records, Crooks frequently talked about Trump, Biden and Marco Rubio, including what he liked and disliked about each politician.

Despite his interests and political discussions, Matthew Crooks said the family saw no obvious warning signs. As they struggled to understand why their son attempted to kill Trump, his father told investigators that he “never showed any signs indicating something was wrong.”

mystery_bidder_buys_t_rex:
By

Joseph Kim

This undated photo provided by Sotheby's on Tuesday, July 14, 2026, shows "Gus," one of the largest and most complete Tyrannosaurus rex specimens ever discovered.
                
                    
                    Matthew Sherman/Sotheby's via AP
                    
                
                hide caption

An imposing, 38-foot long Tyrannosaurus rex fossil sold for a record $50.1 million at auction on Tuesday. But its purchase — likely by a private buyer — is being criticized by paleontologists and other scientists.

The fossil nicknamed Gus is considered one of the largest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever discovered. Many hoped a museum would buy the impressive specimen but the Smithsonian and three other large natural history museums that NPR contacted said they did not bid on it. Because the fossil may not be available for public viewing or research, the sale has upset many in the scientific community.

The president of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, an advocacy group of scientists, openly criticized Sotheby's, which handled the sale.

"The auction houses like Sotheby's and Christie's are complicit in removing data from the scientific process," Stuart Sumida told NPR. "And [they are] complicit [in] placing scientifically valuable specimens into the cabinets of curiosity of a few wealthy individuals and away from the eyes of children and adults alike for years to come."

Treasures auctioned off to private buyers do sometimes disappear from public view. In recent years, paintings considered masterpieces have been purchased by billionaires and have ended up on their superyachts. A privately owned Archaeopteryx fossil — one of just 14 ever found — was lost. Because of their size, T. rexes are more difficult to keep under wraps. But another auctioned giant dinosaur, known as Stan, disappeared for nearly two years, until a National Geographic reporter tracked it down.

Who profits and who loses?

Proceeds from the $50.1 million sale will go to Sotheby's, Theropoda Expeditions, which excavated the fossil, and the owners of the land where Gus was discovered. The fossil was found by the late Gary "Gus" Licking, a cattle rancher in Harding County, South Dakota. He had been coming across teeth and bones on his land for years and eventually called in paleontologists to dig in the area.

The Society of Vertebrate Paleontology issued a strongly worded statement condemning the sale. "[S]cientifically significant vertebrate fossils should be permanently curated in accredited museums, universities, and other public research institutions where they remain available for scientific investigation, education, and public exhibition."

Sotheby's has previously defended these auctions. NPR did not hear back in time for this story, but when asked by NPR about the controversial sale of another dinosaur two years ago, Cassandra Hatton, the Global Head of Science & Natural History at Sotheby's said, "we find that clients overwhelmingly purchase specimens either for museums or donate them."

Sotheby's says Gus sold after a ten-minute bidding war
                
                    
                    Sotheby's
                    
                
                hide caption

To date, no scientific work has been formally conducted or published on Gus. Sumida says this is because no reputable journal would accept a study based on a privately owned specimen as it may be unavailable for future review. "Proper science cannot be done with purchased private specimens," he says.

The Society of Vertebrate Paleontology has written letters of protest to auction houses in the past, but Sumida says it no longer plans to. He says the letters have not only been largely ignored, but also the information in them have been "cherry-picked" to prop up a fossil's valuation. Sumida says his organization has "never ascribed value to fossils" and considers them "invaluable parts of our planet's natural heritage."

Not everyone in the dinosaur world is a critic

Walter Stein, former collections manager for the Wyoming Dinosaur Center and the current owner of PaleoAdventures in western South Dakota, says finding and digging up fossils takes a lot of work, and corporations have an important role in making that possible. He says fossils like Gus require thousands of hours of "careful, patient, hard labor under rugged conditions" to dig up. Stein argues that $50.1 million is not as high as it might seem.

Stein credits more than half of excavated T. rex fossils to "commercial interests with a profit motive." Companies, he says, play an important role in finding and preserving these fossils, because public institutions don't have the resources to save all of them. Stein himself previously dug up a Teratophoneus — a cousin of the T. rex — that he found in 2002, and he says he's currently working on a T. rex named Leonard. He says he doesn't mind if some of these fossils go into private hands if the alternative is that they "weather away to dust."

As for research on privately held specimens, he says it's up to the field whether to study fossils such as Gus.

"If academics choose not to study specimens like this, then they are intentionally ignoring over half of the available data," he says, referencing the field's reservations about studying Gus and other privately held fossils.

If only it were that simple, says David Hone, a paleontologist at Queen Mary University of London. "I'll be amazed if this is ever donated to a museum and research happens on it." Academia just can't compete with wealthy individuals who want a trophy, he says.

Gus is the latest dinosaur fossil to fetch increasingly stratospheric prices. Tuesday's sale broke the previous record of $44.6 million set by a Stegosaurus fossil in 2024, which in turn broke another T. rex record of $31.8 million in 2020.

Paying this kind of money is basically out of reach of nearly anyone, says Hone. "You could probably pay the full salary and research costs of every dinosaur paleontologist in a museum or university around the world for a few years on that money," he adds.

But if he had to choose between $50 million to spend on research or a single dinosaur specimen, Hone says he'd much rather take the money.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un on Thursday reaffirms his commitment to lifting bilateral relations with China to a "new strategic level" in a letter to Chinese President Xi Jinping marking China's National Day, Pyongyang's state media reported.

A three-armed spacecraft has rocketed into orbit to rescue a NASA telescope that's in danger of crashing back to Earth.

Northrop Grumman launched Katalyst Space Technologies' Link spacecraft on Friday from the Marshall Islands in the Pacific.

The Pegasus rocket blasted off from the belly of a modified aeroplane, putting Link on course to reach and capture NASA's Swift Observatory in about a month.

Launched in 2004, Swift is sinking faster than ever because of recent solar storms.

NASA is paying $US30 million ($A43 million) for Katalyst to capture the telescope and boost its orbit so it can continue tracking some of the biggest explosions in the universe, such as gamma ray bursts and exploding stars.

If all goes well, Swift could be back scanning the cosmos by September.

Observations are on hold to preserve the telescope's orbit as long as possible.

NASA's Hubble Space Telescope could be a candidate for a similar salvage operation in a few years.

It's also slipping in altitude because of increased atmospheric drag caused by the sun's outbursts.

The 1.4 tonne Swift is circling 360km above Earth.

Katalyst aims to raise the telescope's altitude by 240km, back to where it all began.

Link's thrusters will fire to boost Swift slowly, so there's no heavy jostling.

Katalyst threw the mission together in just nine months.

NASA insisted on a rush job because the telescope will be too low to recover by the fall.

Without a boost, it's predicted to plunge to its demise in October.

Bad weather and technical issues caused a series of last-minute launch delays.

"This is a high-risk, high-reward mission," Katalyst Space CEO Ghonhee Lee said before lift-off.

"The biggest danger was always we don't launch anything and we let Swift burn up in the atmosphere. So we were always trying to avoid that risk, and our team has done that."

The National Trust of South Australia, the state's premier heritage preservation group, will be the subject of a parliamentary inquiry over the coming months.

The Environment, Resources and Development Committee will probe "a range of challenges over an extended period of time", concerning the charity's strained relationship with volunteers and the consequences for dozens of historic properties.

The trust has previously opposed calls for an inquiry and said it was actively working to address the issues.

The National Trust of South Australia (NTSA) has been referred to a parliamentary inquiry following a months-long campaign by discontented volunteers.

On Wednesday night, the Legislative Council voted to probe the state's largest heritage conservation group, which has been beset by numerous internal conflicts.

Shadow Environment Minister Nicola Centofanti brought the motion, which passed with rare unanimous support from the government and crossbench.

In February, the charity stood down the local leadership of its Moonta branch, which manages hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of historic assets, due to ongoing management disagreements and alleged compliance breaches.

The affected volunteers claimed their dismissal was unfair and are now seeking to overturn it in the Supreme Court, but the move prompted other branches across the state to speak publicly about their grievances.

A protest at the Moonta Cornish Mines in February after the local governing committee was suspended. (Supplied: Moonta National Trust branch)

Meanwhile, most attractions at the historic Moonta Mines remain shut after volunteers walked away in solidarity, costing tourism dollars for the Yorke Peninsula's economy.

Ms Centofanti told parliament the inquiry was about "ensuring the National Trust … remains a strong, sustainable and respected custodian of our state's heritage".

"This inquiry is about reviewing the legislation to ensure it is still fit for purpose. It is about understanding the challenges facing the organisation … hearing directly from those affected and identifying opportunities to strengthen the National Trust".

Nicola Centofanti says she met with volunteers about recent events within the National Trust. (ABC News)

Through volunteers, NTSA manages dozens of historic properties, including landmarks like Ayers House and the Cornish Mines at Moonta and Burra.

However, tensions have bubbled between volunteers and the charity's head office, over matters ranging from property disputes to the trust's financial sustainability.

Labor's Hilton Gumbys told the Upper House the government requested NTSA "make a public register of their assets and details of property transactions".

This comes after the trust signalled it would sell about five "non-core" properties to plug a $300,000 deficit, and confirmed it had done so in the past.

One of those is the 150-plus-year-old National Australia Bank in Burra, purchased by the local council earlier this year to be used as a visitor centre.

The heritage-listed former NAB bank building at Burra, with staff from the Goyder Visitor Information Centre standing in front. (Supplied: Goyder Regional Council)

Mr Gumbys claimed volunteers "had raised concerns about being asked to fund their own operations … through their own fundraising efforts while having very little oversight or accountability from the central organisation".

"When people give their time and their fundraising energy in good faith and find themselves without a voice in decisions that affect them, that erodes the goodwill that keeps these organisations functioning."

NTSA chief executive Nicolette Di Lernia previously acknowledged the organisation faced challenges, but argued a parliamentary inquiry would be a "wasteful" use of taxpayer dollars.

She also said any properties sold by the trust would be "below-market value" and preference given to community-minded groups.

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with George Yankovich at george.yankovich@proton.me

Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide Mornings on Wednesday, Ms Di Lernia said NTSA was trying to mediate with the ousted Moonta leadership.

"We are absolutely committed as an organisation to working with our volunteers, and to do that, we need the volunteers to work with us," she said.

"In Queensland a few years ago, [the National Trust] decided they couldn't have any branches moving forward. It had become so poorly suited to our current … environment, that they had to remove all their branches.

"We're hoping that's not where we need to come to, but we need to make sure that this organisation, which has an enormous part to play in communities across our state, has a viable future."

In a statement, the trust said it was "committed to good governance and accountability" and would "cooperate fully with the inquiry".

Plant Putin den Angriff? Großbritannien, die USA und Norwegen verfolgten Spionage-U-Boote, die in arktischen Gewässern eine Geheimwaffe testeten.

Spitzbergen – Großbritannien hat russische U-Boote beim Testen einer neuen Geheimwaffe erwischt, die darauf ausgelegt ist, kritische Unterseekabel außer Gefecht zu setzen, wie nun bekannt wurde. Das Vereinigte Königreich deckte gemeinsam mit US-amerikanischen und norwegischen Streitkräften im Frühjahr den Einsatz in den arktischen Gewässern vor dem Spitzbergen-Archipel auf. Die Unterwasserkriegsführungseinheit Gugi des Kremls soll den Tiefseetest durchgeführt haben, als NATO‑Streitkräfte die Operation durchkreuzten.

Dieser Artikel von Tom Cotterill entstand in Kooperation mit telegraph.co.uk.

Zwei westliche Beamte sagten der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters, dass Großbritannien, die USA und Norwegen die russischen Spionageboote verfolgten, bevor sie diese stellten. Den Geheimdienstquellen zufolge wurden die russischen Schiffe daran gehindert, ihre Tests abzuschließen, und schließlich vertrieben. Das Verteidigungsministerium hat sich zu der Operation nicht geäußert.

John Healey, der frühere Verteidigungsminister, erklärte im April, die Royal Navy habe eine verdeckte russische Operation in der Nähe britischer Gewässer aufgedeckt, an der zwei Gugi-U-Boote und ein Jagd-U-Boot der Akula-Klasse beteiligt gewesen seien. Die geheimen Aktivitäten des Kreml hätten fast einen Monat lang angedauert, seien jedoch von Seefernaufklärungsflugzeugen der RAF, der Fregatte HMS St Albans vom Typ 23 und norwegischen Streitkräften beobachtet worden, fügte Healey damals hinzu.

Bis heute waren jedoch weder die Entdeckung der mutmaßlich neuen Waffe, noch der genaue Ort der Operation oder die Beteiligung der USA bekannt geworden. Die Konfrontation in der Tiefsee ereignet sich zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem einige westliche Geheimdienstvertreter befürchten, der Kreml fahre Sabotageaktionen in Europa hoch und bereite sich auf einen Konflikt mit der NATO vor. Führende NATO‑Vertreter haben wiederholt vor Provokationen Wladimir Putins gewarnt. Dem Kreml wird vorgeworfen, Sabotageangriffe in ganz Europa zu planen.

Einige US-Geheimdienstanalysten sind zunehmend besorgt, Russland könnte zudem das gegenseitige Verteidigungsversprechen der NATO, den sogenannten Artikel 5, testen, möglicherweise durch einen begrenzten Einmarsch. Westliche Beamte deuteten gegenüber dem Telegraph an, dass Putin keine direkte Konfrontation mit der NATO wolle, was darauf hindeute, dass Russland nicht über die Mittel verfüge, das Bündnis militärisch zu schlagen. Zugleich warnten sie jedoch, seine Sabotagekampagne könne ungewollt zu einer „Fehlkalkulation“ führen, die einen offenen Konflikt auslösen könnte.

Stattdessen gilt es als wahrscheinlich, dass Moskau versuchen würde, auf dem Meeresboden liegende Unterseekabel zu zerstören, über die 99 Prozent der in das Vereinigte Königreich übertragenen Daten laufen. Die Sabotage solcher Systeme könnte Chaos verursachen und die britische Wirtschaft vorübergehend schwer beeinträchtigen. Das russische Verteidigungsministerium reagierte nicht auf eine Anfrage zu dem Vorfall. Der Kreml bestreitet konsequent, Sabotageaktionen in NATO‑Staaten durchzuführen oder eine Konfrontation zu planen.

Die Regierung von Andy Burnham steht derweil weiterhin wegen ihrer Verteidigungsausgabenpläne unter starkem Druck, nachdem er sich geweigert hat, Sozialleistungen zu kürzen, um eine Erhöhung des Militärbudgets zu finanzieren. Der Premierminister nutzte seinen zweiten Auftritt bei der Fragestunde des Premierministers am Mittwoch (9. September), um die Forderung von Kemi Badenoch zurückzuweisen, Großbritanniens explodierende Sozialausgaben zu senken. Auf die Frage, wie er die Mittel für das Erreichen der Verteidigungsziele aufbringen wolle, sagte er: „Wir tun alles, um unsere nationale Sicherheit zu unterstützen. Aber das darf nicht auf Kosten der sozialen Sicherheit gehen.“

Burnham ergänzte: „Ich glaube nicht, dass es den richtigen Konsens zu diesem Thema bringen würde, 4 Milliarden Pfund aus den Wohngeldleistungen zu streichen, denn das würde eine Obdachlosigkeit in diesem Land verursachen, wie wir sie noch nicht gesehen haben – Hunderttausende Kinder in Notunterkünften.“ Badenoch erwiderte: „Wo Großbritannien Führung braucht, haben wir im Moment nur Vibes. Er sagt, er habe einen Kanzler ernannt, weil ihm die Verteidigung wichtig ist, aber er finanziert sie nicht … Bei den wirklich wichtigen Fragen ist er doch nur Kontinuitäts-Keir, oder nicht?“

Die Labour-Partei hat sich wiederholt geweigert, zuzusagen, bis zum Ende des Jahrzehnts 3 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts für Verteidigung auszugeben, und stattdessen versprochen, ein langfristiges NATO‑Ziel zu erreichen: den Kernverteidigungsetat bis 2035 auf 3,5 Prozent des BIP zu erhöhen. Laut dem Haushaltsverantwortungsbüro wird erwartet, dass die Sozialausgaben von 333 Milliarden Pfund auf 407 Milliarden Pfund im Haushaltsjahr 2030/31 ansteigen.

Einige westliche Beamte argumentieren, dass Moskaus Angriffe auf europäische Staaten in den vergangenen Monaten zugenommen haben und eine neue Bedrohung für die NATO darstellen. Staaten wie Polen, Litauen und Rumänien haben verschiedene Verletzungen ihrer Sicherheit bestätigt.

Zuletzt löste ein versuchter Drohnenangriff auf den Flughafen Leipzig/Halle im August eine Reihe von Reaktionen Deutschlands aus, darunter die Schließung eines russischen Konsulats in Bonn und eines Kulturzentrums in Berlin. Im August reiste John Ratcliffe, der Direktor des Geheimdienstes Central Intelligence Agency, zu Gesprächen mit Geheimdienstkollegen nach Moskau, um Russland unter anderem davor zu warnen, Sabotageoperationen in Europa zu verstärken, wie zwei mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Personen berichteten.

The end of a footy season isn't just for finals; it's also prime territory for end-of-season awards.

Every team has them: the best and fairest for the star, the most improved for the biggest riser and the coach's award for the battler who came good.

Other than the top prize, there's nothing better than winning best forward or best back, and if you were giving out a trophy for the former for the entire NRL in 2026 it would have to end up in the mighty hands of Naufahu Whyte.

The iron Rooster enters Sunday's grand final after a season in which he's confirmed his place as one of rugby league's top players and certainly its premier front-rower of the year.

Whyte will lead the Roosters from the front in Sunday's grand final.  (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Given Whyte leads all forwards in metres gained and post-contact metres averages over 16 runs per game, it's hard to find a better battering ram through the middle of the field.

He's also fifth among all forwards for tackle busts and just outside the top 10 for offloads, proving he's far from an empty calories stat-chaser.

Simply put, in all aspects of play, he's had the best year of any forward in the NRL and if he doesn't make the Dally M team of the year on Wednesday night we may as well call the whole thing off.

Other forwards might be his equal, but this year none of them have been better.

After two weeks on the leash, Whyte's performance in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins was his latest blunt-force masterpiece as he finished with 18 runs for 207 metres, more than all three opposition starting middles combined.

"All I remember is the start. I was getting ready to take the kick-off carry to start the game and the crowd was just roaring, the trumpets were playing and everything was just going off," Whyte said.

"I remember taking about the first carry and starting the game off and then I remember us winning it at the end and that is all I need. That's all that matters to me."

More than once Whyte took more than one run per set, something that has become his trademark this season as he's established himself as one of the NRL's apex predators.

If history is any guide, the 24-year-old will repeat the dose against Newcastle in Sunday's grand final, where he will once again be tasked with being the lead horse of the Roosters pack.

A sensational work rate in attack has driven Whyte to new heights in 2026.  (Getty Images: Matt Roberts )

"It's just what I want to do for my brothers and that's a superpower of mine, to carry that ball and I can create opportunities off the back of that for Sammy [Walker], Teddy [James Tedesco], Chez [Daly Cherry-Evans], all of those boys to really express themselves," he said.

"I just feel like every time I can get my hands on that ball I can create something special for them.

"I've got to make sure that's there for my teammates and brothers on that field every time I'm doing something, whether it's running the ball, tackling or whatever.

Whyte was one of the Roosters' best against the Dolphins on Friday night.  (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Nauiyu's community leaders and Indigenous organisations are appealing to the NT and federal governments to provide extra assistance. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Nauiyu / Daly River's Aboriginal organisations say they will not be able to reinstate key services without the support of the NT and federal governments to help repair buildings and replace equipment.

The community's Merrepen Arts Centre says residents will miss out on one of the few opportunities they have to generate private income.

The NT government says it is continuing its talks with Nauiyu's Aboriginal organisations.

When her whole town of Naiuyu / Daly River was swamped up to its roofs by the rain-swollen Daly River earlier this year, community leader Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann believed government assurances they would help the community to recover once the water receded.

Ms Ungunmerr-Baumann has been happy to see the NT Government make progress cleaning out Nauiyu's houses, but she is worried the town's 400 residents are coming home to a community with no services.

Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann says the community is worried they may not get enough money to run their services again. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"It's great to see the contractors cleaning and tidying up the houses," she said.

"But I don't know if there's going to be funding from the government to be able to replace what we've lost so we can get our services working again.

Dr Ungunmerr-Baumann, who was named Senior Australian of the Year in 2021, chairs the Green River Aboriginal Corporation which owns most of the non-government buildings in Nauiyu.

This includes the community's aged care home, women's refuge and staff housing for most of the people employed by the community's service providers.

The Green River Aboriginal Corporation says it can't afford to repair its aged care building. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

The corporation's chief executive Wayne Buckley said Nauiyu's four Aboriginal corporations had sent a joint plea to the NT and federal governments for funds to repair flood-damaged buildings and replace equipment the organisations do not have the money to pay for.

They have estimated essential rebuilding costs would be about $9 million in total.

Mr Buckley has teamed up with the Miriam Rose Foundation, which runs youth, culture and after school programs, the Merrepen Arts Centre and the Nauiyu Nambiyu Aboriginal Corporation which owns the Daly River Store and Daly River Inn.

He said the organisations started their entreaties after the NT government made an emergency declaration for Nauiyu in February, meaning it would start qualifying for federal and territory Disaster Recovery Funds.

Wayne Buckley says the organisations are not asking for a huge amount of money. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"We've written to both levels of government three times as a collective, starting from the beginning of March, and we haven't had a response thus far," Mr Buckley said.

The organisations have emphasised to the two governments that they haven't been able to try to protect their buildings with insurance in the flood prone community.

"The costs of adequate insurance would financially cripple our organisations. For example, last financial year, Green River Aboriginal Corporation was able to obtain a quote for a minimal level of flood insurance, but the cost of this would have been close to 20 per cent of our annual revenue," their funding request sent to the governments said.

Mr Buckey said while assistance with the cleaning has been "amazing", they still need more help.

Flooding of the Daly River earlier this year inundated buildings throughout Nauiyu up to their roofs. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"We're frustrated at the lack of support and information about other funding that might be available, that we thought was available, as victims of the flood emergency," he said.

Miriam Rose Foundation executive officer Julie Calvert said if it the foundation could not get buildings and equipment to restart its youth programs there was a risk returning young people would get bored and get into trouble.

She estimated the organisation would need about $70,000.

Julie Calvert is worried children may get into trouble in the community if there are no programs running. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"We provide art, culture, education and after-school programs for children, youth and their families, and if we cannot provide those activities to help them while they adjust and settle back in, they've got nothing" she said.

"We're ready to go, we have the will, and the staff, but we don't have the assets.

"For example, we had BMX bikes that the children could use to go on activities, they're all gone."

Nauiyu's Merrepen Art Centre, whose fabrics can be found on runways and museums from Los Angeles to New Delhi, has also been hit hard by the floods.

Chief executive Felicity Wright said Merrepen would not be able to resume generating what is one of the few private income sources for community members without government funding to help repair its building and equipment.

The Merrepen Arts Centre held a pop-up store in Darwin in March to help raise funds for the Nauiyu community. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"In our screen print workshop and printing area we've lost all our equipment, including the heat setting oven and the t-shirt carousel for printing t-shirts," she said.

"We have also had our screens impacted — we had about 25 different designs on about 50 different screens, so we've lost about $120,000 to $150,000 worth of equipment.

"The four organisations are saying 'This isn't a ridiculous amount of money, this is actually peanuts compared to all the expenses that a flood causes, but it will make a massive difference to the return'.

Felicity Wright says the community needs the private income their art generates from Merrepen Arts. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"If people return and services aren't available, that's setting us up for a whole lot of social problems.

"We've been doing pop-ups in Darwin generating some income but people want to be able to restart generating livelihoods for themselves."

A spokesperson for the NT government said it was "continuing to work closely with the Victoria Daly Regional Council, the Green River Aboriginal Corporation and other service providers to support long-term recovery".

The federal government told the ABC it was working to get services, including Naiuyu's aged care facility, restored "as soon as possible".

Many Nauiyu residents lost almost all of their possessions in the community's worst ever flooding. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Dr Ungunmerr-Baumann said she also wanted both governments to start planning to build an evacuation centre on nearby higher ground because she and other residents returning are facing the prospect of being flooded again in future.

"There's another wet season coming and we'll probably get another flood," she said.

When the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Bill 2026 (“The NDIS Bill”) was referred to the Community Affairs Legislation Committee on 14 May 2026, I felt an intense sense of urgency to make sure the Committee heard from as many people as possible on the impacts of the proposed legislation.

The community had been given mere weeks to read, absorb and respond to 400 pages of material that tried to justify billions of dollars in cuts to participant support with reference to fraud, misuse and a lack of “financial sustainability”—whatever that means.

At one point, I remarked to a friend that I wouldn’t be surprised if the Inquiry received close to 1,000 submissions, but over that would be just amazing. That night, while I was stuck on a packed V/Line on the way home from work, Jordon Steele-John posted on Instagram that his initial report of “over 300” submissions had been incorrect; in fact there had been over 4500 submissions made.

To put this into perspective, Working together to deliver the NDIS: Independent Review into the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS Review) received 3,976 submissions. The NDIS Review took just over 12 months in total from inception to produce its report. The Senate’s Community Affairs Legislation Committee has until the 16th of June, constituting just over one month, to seek submissions, hold hearings, and report its findings.

At time of writing, just over ten per cent (474) of the 4500+ submissions to the Inquiry have been published. It’s little wonder that many of the submissions contain deeply personal—often plainly traumatic—stories from participants, families, friends, supporters and carers.

This should not be necessary. The Disability Royal Commission, other Senate Inquiries, the NDIS Review, all compelled similar stories from the community. Stories that still hurt to tell, to read, and to remember. The community has been repeatedly forced to reopen unhealed wounds just to have its pain acknowledged.

If you read no other submission, I urge you to pay attention to Submission #7 (Claire-Louise McCrackan) in particular:

I am writing this submission because the men and women I have named, and the many I have not, cannot. Because most of them are dead. Because the ones still alive cannot reach a Senate committee. Because we have not prepared society. We have not educated society. We are expecting manifestation instead of carefully planned and constructed infrastructure. This is the fault of a poorly designed system.

I have spent more money than I can sensibly account for turning up at every event I could afford, so that a Minister might allow me five minutes. I have knocked on door after door after door, and I have been patronised and dismissed by politician after politician along the way. I am beyond shame. I am beyond embarrassment. There is nothing like disability to get a Minister moving pretty fast in the other direction.

I have done all of this with moral injury, for my own sheer survival, to atone for what I have seen and what I have not been able to stop. I have fought on. I resent the discourse from the fragmented disability community. I resent the exclusion from those who preach inclusion. I resent the dismissal and the patronisation from successive offices. And still I am here, because there is no one else, and because the work is not finished.

That is who I am writing for. That is why I am writing. The Committee should know it before reading anything else.

These words, or words like them, echo throughout the submissions to this Inquiry. The submissions I have seen thus far are almost unanimous on the dangers of passing the Bill, including those from institutions such as the Australian Human Rights Commission and the Commonwealth Ombudsman.

On the second day of public hearings in the NDIS Inquiry, the Senate Community Affairs Legislation Committee heard from Hannah Diviney:

[note: I transcribed Hannah’s words myself. Any errors or inaccuracies are mine]

You may cast me as a frightened little girl, but hear this: when Disabled people die, as a direct result of this bill—and they will—their blood will be on your hands. How do I know people will die? Because you will have made it impossible for them to live in so many ways. and you will have to live with that every single day for the rest of your life, haunted by their ghosts—and me, every time I have a platform. Because I’ll be damned if I ever let a single politician in this government forget what you did, if you dare position your own political power over our humanity. This Bill must be withdrawn, otherwise you are sentencing me, and everyone in my community—including Senator Jordon Steele-John—to the dark. And we’ve worked so damn hard to come into the light. Please don’t let that happen.

Hannah’s words may seem drastic, but to my ears they contain not a syllable of hyperbole. In many ways, they echo the final paragraphs of my own submission to the Inquiry (as yet unpublished):

We have not counted how many Participants, family members, loved ones and supporters who have [already] died due to a system that reaches beyond passive neglect and into the horrific realm described by Hannah Arendt as the ‘banality of evil’.

It is that same kind of evil that describes the NDIS as “unsustainable” and points to fraud with one hand, while cutting support for living, breathing people with the other, knowing that death is an inevitable result, and still actively choosing to plunge the knife into the hearts of our communities.

Please do not allow yourself to become complicit in that evil.

We should not have to slit our wrists in front of you to prove that we bleed. And yet, as I continue to read submissions to the Senate Inquiry into the NDIS Bill, I wonder what else the razor gang expected.
