As parents become increasingly concerned about the potential dangers of unrestricted smartphone access for children, a growing number of companies are developing devices specifically designed for kids.

Today’s kid-friendly phones typically feature touchscreens, cameras, and communication capabilities similar to regular smartphones. However, the software on these devices is heavily modified to remove or restrict access to web browsers, social media, app stores, and other distractions.

Parents can usually manage these devices through a companion app, allowing them to approve contacts, monitor locations, set screen time limits, select available apps, and, in some cases, receive alerts regarding cyberbullying, explicit content, or online predators.

In addition to these modified devices, some companies offer a more minimalist approach, creating devices that focus solely on calling and texting.

There are also home phones designed specifically for children, like Tin Can and the recently launched Pinwheel Home.

Here’s a look at the major players shaping the kid-phone market.

The Bark Phone is probably one of the most popular kid-specific smartphones on the market.

Built on Samsung Galaxy hardware and powered by Bark’s monitoring software, it only allows calls and texts with approved contacts. Bark continuously scans texts, emails, photos, and supported apps for signs of cyberbullying, grooming, suicidal ideation, sexual content, and other potential concerns, then sends alerts to parents.

A big standout feature is that parents can gradually unlock web browsing, apps, and other features as their child matures. The phone also includes GPS tracking and screen-time management.

Current pricing for the standard model is $240, plus a required wireless plan beginning at $29/month. Higher-tier plans add internet access and unlimited texting.

Gabb is a well-known name in the kid-friendly phone category. Unlike Bark, however, Gabb focuses less on monitoring content and more on eliminating online risks altogether.

Its phones don’t include social media, a browser, or an app store. Instead, children get calling, texting, and a carefully curated selection of preloaded apps, including a camera, calendar, and calculator. The company also touts its “worry-free” music streaming library with millions of songs.

Additionally, parents can view location and manage certain device settings, while optional services such as “Gabb Guard” help block spam calls and unwanted texts.

Current phone pricing starts around $159.99, with cellular service starting around $24.99 per month.

With Pinwheel, parents approve every app, control contacts, schedule screen time, create custom routines, and monitor location history.

One standout feature is the ability to create different “modes” throughout the day. For example, limiting the phone to calling and navigation during school hours before unlocking additional features after homework.

Pinwheel phones start around $119, while the Caregiver Portal subscription begins at $14.99 per month without cell service. (Cellular service can be purchased separately through participating carriers.)

The company recently launched two landline phones for $68 and $79. It also offers a smartwatch at $160.

Launched in 2022, Teracube offers a tailored version of Android known as Thrive OS. This enables parents to approve every app download, filter web browsing, set app-specific and overall screen-time limits, monitor location, and create customized routines for school or bedtime. However, because it has more traditional smartphone features, it’s often recommended for older children.

Thrive currently sells for $99, with plans starting at $35 per month.

Unlike the other products in this roundup, Ooma MyPhone isn’t a mobile phone at all. This kid-focused home phone is designed as a modern replacement for the traditional household landline.

The service allows calls only between approved contacts through its Trusted Circle feature, offers scheduled Quiet Hours, provides address-based 911 service, sends emergency alerts when 911 is dialed, and lets parents review call logs through an online portal. There are no apps, internet browsing, texting, or social media.

The phone costs $99.99, while service starts at $7.99 per month.

For $100, Tin Can resembles a landline phone with a distinctive tin can design, which is the inspiration behind its name.

This device does not require a traditional phone jack, but connects via Wi-Fi. Only approved contacts can make calls, effectively preventing spam or unauthorized communications. Parents can easily manage contacts through a user-friendly companion app.

Tin Can offers a free plan for calling other Tin Can users, as well as a $9.99 per month plan that allows calls to all approved contacts.

Kimi K3, the latest AI model made by Chinese company Moonshot, escaped an environment set up to test its cyber capabilities, researchers said in a blog post published on Friday.

The news shows once again that companies and independent organizations are struggling to contain their AI models designed for hacking.

In recent weeks, frontier LLMs at U.S. artificial intelligence labs at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, as well as the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, all escaped testing environments in different ways and ended up hacking real targets that were not part of the experiment. This is starting to happen so often there’s now a website tracking all these incidents called Felony Bench, a nod to the fact that these LLMs may be committing crimes — at least theoretically speaking.

In the case of this Kimi test, the sandbox designed to contain the experiment was not properly configured. While the sandbox disallowed the AI model from accessing certain web traffic, the model instead bypassed the sandbox by relying on command line tools, according to the researchers at AI-focused cybersecurity firm Frontier Security.

“This suggests that some of the evaluations on cybersecurity the community uses are susceptible to security vulnerabilities and allow models to cheat, and that there are models that intentionally seek loopholes and vulnerabilities which allows them to cheat on evaluations,” the researchers wrote.

If you are keeping score at home, according to Felony Bench’s tally, Moonshot now joins OpenAI and Anthropic, which have seven recorded incidents each, and Meta, which has one.

Jimmy Kimmel depicted Donald Trump in a diaper after the president stormed out of an interview last week, an episode the late-night host labeled a “hissy fit.”

During a wide-ranging on-camera interview with NBC News Friday in Wisconsin, host Kristen Welker pressed Trump on his claims that California elections are “crooked” and riddled with Democratic “cheating.”

When the journalist asked the president to provide evidence for his claims, the exchange quickly unraveled. Trump told Welker “you’re either crooked or you’re stupid,” before tearing off his microphone and walking off set.

Kimmel played a clip of the confrontation for his Jimmy Kimmel Live audience Monday and joked: “This is why he mostly dated women that don’t speak English.”

“I don’t know if he was worried about the cotton candy on his head getting wet or he just didn’t like the fact that he was being taken to task by a woman,” Kimmel continued. “Either way, their talk ended in a full blown Trumper tantrum.”

The comedian then proceeded to air another clip from the Meet the Press sit-down — this time, with a few modifications.

“You’re crooked, and the press is crooked, and so is ABC, and CBS and CNN. You’re one-sided, crooked networks…Right, let’s call it quits,” Trump says in the clip. The camera then cuts to a wider shot, depicting the 79-year-old president without trousers, wearing a seemingly soiled diaper as he stands up and traipses off camera.

“When that dinner bell rings, he’s gone,” Kimmel joked. “Can you imagine any other president in the history of any other place doing that? That was a hissy fit.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle dismissed the comedian’s commentary.

“Nobody in their right mind cares what seriously unfunny Jimmy Kimmel thinks,” Ingle told The Independent.

Shortly after the NBC interview, recorded in a Wisconsin barn, Trump told a crowd of supporters that he became upset on account of the weather.

“It was raining. And it was with NBC fake news,” the president said. “And because it was raining, I got a little bit angry at them. I was not happy with them. But we had a good time.”

Kimmel and Trump have traded barbs for years. Trump has repeatedly dismissed the late-night host as “seriously unfunny,” and called for him to be taken off the air.

In April, Trump complained about a segment of Kimmel’s monologue in which the host joked that First Lady Melania Trump had the glow of “an expectant widow.” Trump condemned the remark as a “despicable call to violence” and said it was “far beyond the pale.”

Tensions between Jimmy Kimmel Live and the administration boiled over in September, when ABC News suspended the show following criticism from conservatives and administration officials over Kimmel’s comments about the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was shot dead on a college campus.

Following widespread backlash, ABC News announced days later that the show would resume production.

King Charles hosted a private summit Thursday with some of the most prominent names in AI and the U.K. government, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic, the U.K.’s new AI minister Kanishka Narayan, and even the head of the U.K.’s foreign intelligence service. Paolo Benanti, who advises the pope on AI, was also there.

The king’s remarks at the summit —  held at Dumfries House, an 18th-century Ayrshire estate owned by King Charles’s charitable foundation —  were notable because the royal family is usually careful, for constitutional reasons, about veering too deep into political issues — and AI is one of the most hot-button issues in the world right now. The king urged the leaders in the room to find a way to control AI “before it’s too late,” adding that the fast development of this technology — and its “substance” — was “both intriguing and deeply concerning.”

“AI is already showing immense capacity to improve and save life,” he said, citing medicine and science as an example. “Yet those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities, perhaps even to take life.” This remark came just days after an Anthropic researcher quit, writing online that AI companies were “racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human” and that humanity “may not survive this.”

The king continued, saying it’s urgent to properly consider the “existential dangers” of what would happen if this technology fell into the wrong hands and was used in “potentially catastrophic ways.”

“Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it’s all too late?” he said. As King Charles wrapped up, he urged leaders to find a way to harness the good of AI and to build international cooperation and consensus to achieve that outcome. (This remark comes after Anthropic shut off access to its Fable and Mythos models to only U.S. customers, shocking the Euro tech scene and leaving many to think about the concept of AI sovereignty.)

“The task before you is not to merely advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community, and the natural world,” he said as he finished his speech. “As we embrace what is new, we must not lose what is timeless.”

Outlets report that he stayed for around 20 minutes, leaving the guests to discuss these matters among themselves. For the king’s summit, OpenAI sent its CFO Sarah Friar while Anthropic sent Tino Cuéllar, who leads global affairs. When reached for comment, Cuéllar said the company was honored to have taken part in the discussion and that it was grateful to the king for “convening industry leaders and voices from across society to discuss the role of AI in serving the public good.”

This is not the first time King Charles has spoken about the challenges and benefits of AI, having done so in 2023 and 2024. This summit, however, is especially timely as AI continues to dominate every industry, topic, and form of conversation. This month, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei called for a deceleration in AI development, but Nvidia’s Huang and President Donald Trump quickly rejected those calls. “We’re leading China in AI,” the president said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”

It shows how complex the matter has become, as the interests of Big Tech, politics, and society collide. For the past year, OpenAI and Anthropic have teased blockbuster IPOs, though OpenAI recently said its IPO plans were stalled this year as concerns over AI safety persist.

âJustifiedâ or 'no business being thereâ? Tennessee munitions town loyal to Trump but divided on Iran

As one local puts it, there's a "church on every street" of the Appalachian community of Kingsport, in the US state of Tennessee.

Christianity reigns supreme in this working-class area. Above downtown's historic Lamplight Theatre, a sign proclaims "Jesus first in all things".

And while more than 300 area churches may be providing spiritual sustenance to this town of 58,000 people, there's another institution that supplies it with economic nourishment.

The Holston Army Ammunition Plant churns out explosives used in Patriot missiles, warheads and other heavy weaponry in the midst of the country's costly and prolonged war with Iran.

The war, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Recent polling has placed his approval at an historic low of 32% - down 14% from when he first took office in January 2025 - with many Republican respondents citing disillusionment with the president's policies.

Veteran David Carter, 66, is an outspoken Christian who supports US action in Iran

The two big drags on the president's popularity are the cost of living and the Iran War, with one bleeding into the other. The conflict has caused gas prices in the US to spike to above $4 a gallon, a painful hike to any US business that relies on transport.

But in Kingsport, support for the president approaches an almost-religious fervour. The city voted overwhelmingly for Trump in all three of his elections. So did wider Tennessee, a Republican state for more than 25 years.

When it comes to the Iran conflict, most residents either outright support the military action or rationalise the war's necessity - despite Trump's repeated campaign promise of "no more wars".

"If he can stop anyone from having a nuclear bomb, then I'm for it," says Pam Robinson, 65, who spent 20 years working at the local chemical plant.

David Carter, a bearded veteran who plays Santa Claus at Christmastime, says "the whole reason we go over there, and we keep everything under control there, is [so that] we don't have it on our doorstep."

Others are more blunt.

"Honestly, I think we should turn them into a parking lot and don't worry about it anymore," says veteran James Camper, 63, wearing a Trump lanyard around his neck as he exits a discount grocery.

Veterans account for around 10% of the region's population, and many other households have active duty family members.

Robinson, a staunch Christian and independent voter who says her faith informs her candidate choices, believes the remote nature of the war may be preventing local people from being more upset with Trump.

"Let me say this: If it was hand-to-hand and more people were getting killed, people would be banging the doors down," she says.

Daniel Overstreet, 53, believes Trump's 'hands are tied' by Congress

Kingsport's position as a main munitions manufacturer - with Holston standing as the only domestic supplier of some essential explosive and propellant components -  gives its residents a unique perspective when it comes to the war in Iran.

The plant employs around 1,000 people and is just one of many sprawling industrial complexes standing out starkly from the lush Appalachian Mountain landscape.

"The plant's going to be open regardless of whether we're at war or whether we're not," says Daniel Overstreet, 53, standing next to his Harley Davidson in downtown Kingsport. "It is what it is."

He believes Trump and the administration are "doing a great job" but there are "too many people trying to fight him."

"[He said] he would get the gas prices under control, and they were for a while," says Overstreet. "He said he was gonna get food prices down, but he has no control over that. The president is basically a puppet for Congress and the Senate.

"His hands are tied, to a certain extent."

It's not that people here don't complain about high gas and food prices, inflation and other economic woes - it's just they don't blame Trump for any of it.

"He's done good on some things; I think he needs to check his advisers and see on some things," says Robinson. "I think he's advised wrong on some things."

It was Trump himself, however, who announced his decision to strike Iran in February 2026 following failed negotiations. In an eight-minute video posted to social media, he said "the objective is to defend the American people by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime" - and claimed Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon".

Evangelist William Bogle believes Trump is 'imperfect' but there is no 'alternative'

Evangelist William Bogle, 75, voted for Trump every time he ran and believes the president is "doing a good job" - even though his wife "has to stretch a grocery dollar until, you know, it's big as a bedsheet".

Trump is "just gonna have to do a little bit better in some things than he's doing right now," he says.

"I know he wants the country to prosper."

This stalwart support reflects a deeper truth sometimes hidden in the polling headlines. Although Trump has lost favour among more traditional Republicans and independent voters, his base - who self-identify with his "Make America Great Again" mantra - remains much more steadfast in backing him.

So while much of the US watches to see how much Trump's sliding popularity may damage Republicans in November's midterm elections, here in the Bible Belt, sometimes red is the only option.

As voters turned out last week for local elections, the ballot included a single Democratic candidate. Of the county commission's 11 districts, seven featured only Republicans running, with some unopposed.

Many say they can't and won't cross party lines for moral reasons, citing abortion as the single biggest deciding factor, with opposition to socialism and "woke" issues too hard for them to ignore.

Those fears outweigh any personal criticisms they may have, says David Carter, 66, a grandfather and Christian as well as a veteran.

Trump needs to humble himself more, he concedes, but Carter would only consider a candidate who "supports the morals" of the population. That means opposing  abortion, for example.

Democrat Adam Teague points out 'there's a church on every street' in Kingsport

Those who hold more liberal views exist in Kingsport, but they're vastly in the minority and less vocal.

Piercing artist Adam Teague, 44, is a gay, heavily-tattooed Democrat working in downtown Kingsport.

"Before Trump took office, I was wearing, like, rainbow shirts and everything," says Teague, who was raised Baptist. "I kind of toned it down, just to feel safer."

Trump was triumphant in the 2024 election in part because of his ability to attract a diverse coalition including people of all ages and races. But while his Maga supporters are sticking by him, polling suggests that many young people who helped get him over the line against Kamala Harris are now disillusioned.

Mary Herron, 21, who is leaving a boutique cupcake shop with two friends, has noticed a difference in attitudes amongst her contemporaries.

"I am seeing a shift in the support â¦ that's kind of rare around here," says Herron, a student who works part-time. "But I've seen a handful of people who have been like, 'Oh yeah, well, I voted for him, and now I'm not with him anymore'."

Caden Bayless, Mary Herron and Emily Villalpando are 21-year-old liberals

Trump first entered politics when the women were in middle school, says her friend Emily Villalpando, 21. "So a lot of the people that we grew up with kind of just adopted their parents' views.

"And so now that we're growing up, we're having more responsibilities," says Villalpando, who's studying biomedical science and wants to be a doctor. "The economy affects us a lot more."

The three college students - their friend Caden Bayless makes up the trio - cite women's rights and heavy-handed immigration agents as major concerns, but they are sceptical of major attitude or voting shifts in the region.

Bayless said she is hopeful the younger generation can make a change, but "given where we live â¦ it would be a very difficult change."

Bogle, summing up the Kingsport region, inadvertently speaks to their fears.

"We live in a great place, and if you're not conservative, don't come here," the preacher says. "Because you wouldn't be a good fit. But if you're conservative, come here, and we'll embrace you."

He'll be praying for Trump, he says, as will the more moderate Robinson.

"All you can do is pray for your leaders, and God will give you what you want in the end," she says.

King Charles urged MSPs to help build a "fair and prosperous society" as he opened the new session of the Scottish Parliament.

The ceremony, which featured pageantry, poetry, drama and music, marked the beginning of the seventh session of Holyrood since it was established in 1999.

The event started with the Crown of Scotland being escorted down the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle.

Following the arrival of the royal couple in the debating chamber, the celebration began with a fanfare performed by the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland brass ensemble.

The Crown of Scotland was carried in by the Duke of Hamilton and Brandon, escorted by the Lord Lyon King of Arms

The mace, Crown and Elizabeth sword were carried into the chamber in a procession featuring three Team Scotland athletes preparing to compete in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow next month.

The Officers of Arms were joined by young people from a range of organisations, including the Scottish Youth Parliament, RNIB Scotland, and the Young Women's Movement.

King and Queen to attend 'milestone' Scottish Parliament event

Presiding Officer Kenneth Gibson then delivered his opening remarks to the audience, which included 65 new MSPs who were elected last month.

Gibson used his speech to praise the Tartan Army for "showcasing the very best of our people on a global stage".

And he joked that they would be enjoying an extended stay in North America "but for a couple of dodgy penalty decisions in the Morocco game".

All the leaders of the main political parties attended the event

The King then addressed the chamber to formally open the parliamentary session.

He said: "From its proud history and its treasured customs to the remarkable beauty of its land, it is the warmth and spirit of the people of Scotland that leave the deepest impression upon us and continue to inspire admiration."

The King said that since his late mother opened Holyrood in 1999 it had stood as a "powerful expression of Scotland's democratic tradition".

He also urged MSPs to show that debate could be "carried out with respect and courtesy" and that "disagreement is possible while honouring one's dignity".

The King greeted First Minister John Swinney before the ceremony

The King added that everyone in public service should be "seeking the good of the people we serve".

King Charles told the audience: "People across Scotland look for leadership and for practical action to help build a fair and prosperous society."

The monarch also highlighted his concerns for the environment when he last spoke in the chamber in 2024 and he revisited the theme on Saturday.

He told MSPs the planet's climate was "changing dangerously" and warned its biodiveristy was being "seriously depleted".

In response, First Minister John Swinney told the chamber that Scotland had the capacity to absorb and overcome every passing storm.

He called for co-operation and renewal and added that new politics was the basis for a new hope.

Swinney then spoke in Gaelic and said: "Our people need us to work together, to improve their lives to bring them hope. That is what we must now do," he said.

The parliament's piper, MSP Stuart McMillan, brought the event to a close with a performance in the members' garden of Bonnie Dundee and a Hundred Pipers.

Following the ceremony, the King and Queen met local heroes nominated by MSPs for their "extraordinary contribution" to local communities.

They included four-year-old Gregor Corse from Orkney, who was born with a brain condition which affects his balance and motor skills.

NEW YORK — The New York Knicks made a record comeback from 29 points down and moved to the brink of their first championship since 1973 by beating the San Antonio Spurs 107-106 on Wednesday night.

OG Anunoby tipped in the miss of Jalen Brunson’s long 3-point attempt with 1.2 seconds remaining to complete the rally, giving the Knicks a 3-1 lead and three chances to win the title.

It looked impossible early, when the Spurs rolled to a 27-point halftime lead. But Brunson helped bring the Knicks back with 36 points and Anunoby finished with 33, swooping in as Brunson’s shot bounced softly off the front of the rim and stretching high with his right hand to tap it in.

“I told OG as big, as strong, as athletic as he is, he’s got to be a monster on the offensive glass tonight,” Knicks coach Mike Brown said. “I don’t know if there was a play bigger than any other play in the history of Knicks basketball.”

Game 5 is Saturday night in San Antonio.

No team had come from more than 24 points down in a Finals game, when the Boston Celtics did it against the Los Angeles Lakers in 2008, since the NBA began keeping detailed play-by-play for all four quarters in 1997. The Spurs led 81-52 in the third quarter.

The only bigger comeback on record in any playoff game was 31 points by the Los Angeles Clippers against Golden State in Game 2 of a first-round series in 2019.

The Knicks had their 13-game winning streak snapped in Game 3 and seemed headed for a second straight defeat throughout the first half, when Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs opened the biggest NBA Finals halftime lead by a visiting team.

But the young Spurs, who made 11 of their first 16 3-pointers, went cold in the second half, going 3-for-17 from behind the arc as the Knicks outscored them 58-30.

“We got on our heels — we missed some shots,” Spurs coach Mitch Johnson said. “It’s disappointing, to say the least.”

Delirious fans at Madison Square Garden sang along to Journey’s “Don’t Stop Believin’” a few minutes after watching something that seemed almost impossible.

Wembanyama had 24 points and 13 rebounds but shot just 9-for-25 from the field.

Road teams had won the first three games, only the second time that had happened in the Finals. The Spurs were well on their way to making it 4-for-4.

President Donald Trump wasn’t at this game — Taylor Swift was — but the same restrictions remained around Madison Square Garden as when he attended Game 3. That angered the Knicks, who decided not to go forward with plans to hold an outdoor watch party outside the arena.

Inside the building in the first half, there wasn’t much for the hosts to be happy about, either.

But the Knicks gave themselves a chance by limiting the Spurs to 14 points on 4-for-20 shooting in the third quarter, using a 13-0 run to get back in it and cutting it to 90-75 heading to the fourth.

These Knicks, who erased a 22-point deficit in the fourth quarter against the Cleveland Cavaliers in Game 1 of the Eastern Conference finals, just don’t quit. Even when the comeback seemed for naught when Stephon Castle was fouled after the Knicks had taken the lead and made two free throws to put the Spurs back ahead with 30 seconds left, the Knicks had one more rally in them.

Dylan Harper scored 21 points and De’Aaron Fox and Devin Vassell each had 18 for the Spurs, who will try to regroup and send the series back to New York for Game 6 on Tuesday.

“I think it began before (the fourth quarter),” Wembanyama said of the Spurs’ collapse. “I can’t really explain it right now. I don’t know. … We clearly weren’t the most hungry in the second half.”

Fans booed Wembanyama when he came on to the floor to warm up about an hour before the game, and the Knicks tried to get rough with him, with Mitchell Robinson called for a flagrant foul for hitting him above the shoulders and Jose Alvarado reviewed for one after going below the belt.

Wembanyama — who also was called for a flagrant — stood up OK against the Knicks but will regret the two free throws he missed with 1:47 left and the Spurs leading 104-103.

KPMG is facing international intervention as its chief executive resigns and legal loopholes limit ASIC’s access to documents and capacity to penalise the company.

Six years ago, Brendan Lyon blew the whistle on conflicts of interest and a potential multibillion-dollar hole in the New South Wales state budget while working at KPMG.

Five people directly involved in the case were later promoted at KPMG. One of them, Andrew Yates, was forced to step down immediately as chief executive on May 29 over a different scandal.

“You can’t say the circus is different when the clowns are the same,” Lyon, who is now a professor at the University of Wollongong, tells The Saturday Paper.

“The organisation, when I was there, was amoral. All of the people who refused to change that amorality became very senior leadership, partially off the back of all of the money they got in profit from those kind of exercises.”

KPMG is now facing intervention by its powerful international governing body after new allegations of conflicts of interest and corporate misconduct were made in parliament.

The scandal has put at risk strategically important work KPMG does auditing the books of some of Australia’s top companies. It raises further questions about the extraordinarily lucrative stream of government and university consulting work enjoyed by the accounting giants and the legal loophole it and the other big firms use to avoid scrutiny by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

A parliamentary inquiry has heard allegations KPMG used information that should have been kept confidential to win audit contracts at some of Australia’s biggest companies.

According to one allegation, confidential information about property giant Dexus was left open on a laptop where it could be seen by members of a separate team bidding to win the company’s audit contract.

A whistleblower has also made allegations that data from long-time audit client Lendlease was used to bid for the audit roles at Dexus and Westpac – and that their attempts to report misconduct to management were initially rebuffed.

KPMG’s turn in the spotlight comes amid increased scrutiny of the outsized role in corporate Australia and the public service of the big four accounting firms – KPMG, PwC, Deloitte and EY. It follows the long-running scandal in which PwC was caught providing advice on tax laws to the government at the same time as it coached companies on how to dodge them.

The claims against KPMG, revealed under parliamentary privilege by Labor’s Senator Deborah O’Neill and the Greens’ Senator Barbara Pocock over the past month, reached a climax last week when the firm admitted its initial internal investigations “lacked rigour”. Yates and the firm’s head of audit, Julian McPherson, both resigned.

On Wednesday, chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett stood down, although she remains a partner. Dexus refused to have her sign off its financial accounts.

KPMG promises to reinvestigate the whistleblower’s allegations and “rebuild trust” with the community.

KPMG International, the global network that allows the Australian group to trade under the prestigious name, has become involved in the local firm’s woes. A KPMG International spokesperson says all members were required to work to its standards and it took the situation in Australia seriously.

“KPMG International will continue to support the Australian firm as it rebuilds trust with its people and among its clients and communities,” the spokesperson says.

The latest scandal involves allegations of misconduct within the audit division, which is responsible for checking the financial probity of Australia’s biggest companies.

It has rocked confidence in KPMG among corporate Australia.

“The organisation, when I was there, was amoral. All of the people who refused to change that amorality became very senior leadership, partially off the back of all of the money they got in profit from those kind of exercises.”

A source with knowledge of the Dexus case says the main problem was not the information said to have been shared, thought to be relatively low-value data about KPMG’s billing for work done at the property group. Rather, it was KPMG’s failure to properly investigate the whistleblower’s allegations.

“If they’re not doing the right thing internally, how can they be doing the right thing externally?” the source tells The Saturday Paper.

Lyon says blowing the whistle at KPMG came at huge personal cost, leaving him feeling isolated and shunned by people he had thought were his colleagues. He suspects the new whistleblower is going through the same pain.

“It’s been nearly seven years of my life,” Lyon says. “It is incredibly life-changing to challenge the system. I’ve got so much respect for the current whistleblower and the way they’ve conducted themselves.”

At accounting firms, the flow of confidential and commercially sensitive client information between teams is supposed to be stopped by so-called “Chinese walls”.

Lyon says that in his time at KPMG he saw no sign they existed – and pointed to evidence he gave to the NSW parliament showing senior executives in KPMG tried to “override client confidentiality”.

“When they asked about the existence of Chinese walls, I said they must be Japanese, because they’re extremely porous and very papery,” he says.

Despite consulting’s well-known problems, governments and universities continue to rely on the sector for advice and financial oversight.

Last year, KPMG was tapped by the University of Technology Sydney for a $4.8 million review to help plan $100 million in staff cuts – a move that prompted an investigation into “psychosocial harms” by the NSW workplace safety regulator.

Tender data compiled by The Saturday Paper shows that over the past decade, KPMG has won federal government contracts worth almost $3 billion.

Lyon says a hollowed out and politicised public sector relies on the Big Four to do work it should be doing – and to dodge accountability for it.

“They talk about evidence-based decision-making, but in practice the Big Four provide decision-based evidence-making, where they will come back and evidence anything that government wants to do, whether it’s robodebt, Snowy Hydro or NBN Co,” he says. “What they do is serve a market for excuses.”

Lyon says that at the same time as the Big Four help politicians and bureaucrats avoid accountability, the firms also dodge any accountability for themselves by using partnership structures.

This means they don’t pay tax and aren’t subject to the same rules about corporate conduct and dealing properly with whistleblowers that govern their clients.

Most partnerships are limited to 20 people, with each individual partner liable for the wrongdoing of any other partner.

The big professional partnerships are exempt from the cap, however, and professional liability laws limit the amount that can be clawed back from individual partners for misconduct at the firm.

Lyon says the Big Four should be forced to become corporations.

“The reality is that we already have a mechanism to oversight large, profit driven associations of people, and they are called corporations,” he says. “They’re regulated via thousands of pages of corporations law that’s developed over the last couple of centuries.”

Barbara Pocock agrees.

“The partnership model is completely broken,” she tells The Saturday Paper.

“They have lost their social licence to say they are special and they should have special let-outs. How many of these massive scandals do we have to see before we take them at their word, which is that they’re not to be trusted?”

Last week ASIC deputy chair Sarah Court, who took control of the regulator on Monday, told federal parliament it is investigating KPMG and has already used its powers to demand documents from the audit partners at the centre of the scandal.

ASIC only has jurisdiction to investigate the auditors, however, and not the wider partnership. It cannot fine partnerships or use its sweeping investigatory powers on them and instead relies on engagement and what Court describes as “moral suasion to rein in their excesses”.

“We do think there is a gap in the regulatory oversight of large partnership models,” Court told the hearing.

ASIC faces a battle with KPMG when it comes to getting its hands on the paperwork it has been able to demand. The firm says many documents are protected from disclosure because they are correspondence with lawyers, which means they can be kept from the regulator under the principle of legal professional privilege.

Senator O’Neill tells The Saturday Paper that PwC abused legal professional privilege in its tax scandal and KPMG should not do the same.

“It would be outrageous for them to claim legal professional privilege,” she says.

“Do not cost the Australian taxpayer another cent. Give over the information immediately and do not redact one word.”

A KPMG spokesperson says the firm had proposed handing documents over in two tranches to deal with the privilege issue. The spokesperson declined to comment on Lyon’s allegations or KPMG International’s role.

Parliamentary hearings into KPMG resume on June 19.

Topic:Funerals and Memorial Services

A date and location has been set for Kumanjayi Little Baby's funeral. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The family of five-year-old girl Kumanjayi Little Baby, who was allegedly murdered in April, has set a date for her funeral.

Her grandfather has thanked the Alice Springs community for supporting the family and invited them to come together again at "our last farewell for our little granddaughter".

The funeral will take place on Saturday, August 15 at the Alice Springs Garden Cemetery.

Months on from the desperate search for five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby by hundreds of volunteers, her grandfather is inviting the community to come together once more for her funeral in Alice Springs later this month.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article includes the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from Old Timers/Ilyperenye town camp, just south of the Alice Springs township, in late April, sparking one of the largest searches in Northern Territory police history.

Hundreds of community volunteers worked alongside police and emergency services to scour dense, grassy bushland for the five-year-old.

The search for Kumanjayi Little Baby in April lasted five days and involved hundreds of police and volunteers. (ABC News: Will Green)

Five days after she went missing, her remains were found 5 kilometres from the town camp, in the dry Todd River bed.

Her death triggered an outpouring of grief not just in Alice Springs but across the country, with vigils held in each state and territory, where thousands gathered in her favourite colour, pink, to pay their respects.

Mourners dressed in pink gathered at vigils for Kumanjayi Little Baby, where they paid tribute to the young girl. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Jefferson Lewis, 47, has since been charged with her murder and two other offences that cannot be published for legal reasons.

Since her death in April, Kumanjayi Little Baby's family has been in cultural grieving, known as sorry business.

Her funeral has now been set down to take place on August 15, with her family inviting members of the wider community to attend, and to wear her favourite colour again.

Five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from an Alice Springs town camp earlier this year.  (Supplied: NT Police)

Robin Japanangka Granites, a Warlpiri elder and Kumanjayi Little Baby's grandfather, told the ABC he wanted to thank the community again for their efforts to search for her, and for their outpouring of grief and support for his family.

"It was so nice of everyone getting together … the community of Alice Springs, who got together, everyone, not even saying who they were," he said.

"They are all as one with us, supporting, being out with us, during the hot days.

Robin Japanangka Granites says Kumanjayi Little Baby's life will be commemorated at the Alice Springs funeral. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Granites said it had been a difficult time for the family, but they were rallying together for the funeral.

He used the Warlpiri word jintangka, meaning "all in one" or coming together.

"Thank you everyone who is coming to this get-together and this funeral to have our last farewell for our little granddaughter," he said.

"I thank you all for coming and it was really good of you, being all together, in one, jintangka … our little baby granddaughter of ours will be with Father in Heaven."

The news of Kumanjayi Little Baby's alleged murder rocked Australia. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

The funeral for Kumanjayi Little Baby will take place at the Alice Springs Garden Cemetery at 10am to 1pm on Saturday, August 15.

The ABC understands another memorial is being planned for the Friday before the funeral, with further details around timing and location to come.

Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

The teal independents are in a similar place on the political spectrum to the United Kingdom’s Liberal Democrats, who hold 72 seats in the House of Commons. In Australia’s changing scene, they have similarities to a reinvigorated Australian Democrats, founded by former Liberal minister Don Chipp.

A looming challenge for the teal independents is what to do when, inevitably, they win the balance of power. There is a high chance that the 2028 federal election will see Albanese Labor lose seats and One Nation, the Greens and teal independents gain seats. Labor may keep its majority, but at some point that balance of power outcome is inevitable. What then?

Independents without some form of cohesion are easy pickings. The first threat by Labor will be to ask the governor-general to have it seek a vote of confidence in the House of Representatives. Without others to give Labor a majority, this would effectively force the independent teals to back Labor – or Coalition/One Nation – or face another election. In the case of another election, Australia’s right-wing media would be in full-throttle condemnation of the independents and anyone else on the crossbench for not supporting a new government.

More likely, the independents would be picked off by inducements from Labor or the conservative blocs. Offers might include the speakership or ministries, or hospitals, school halls, convention centres, sports grounds and better roads in home electorates. Perhaps there would be an underwhelming promise of a “reduction” – not a total ending – of approvals for new or expanded coalmines, gas fracking or forest logging. Without cohesion, the teal independents may end up losers, not the powerhouse they could be.

There is rumour and speculation about whether they will form a party. Don’t expect the press gallery in Canberra to think much outside the conventional bubble of two-party politics. It will tend to vilify rather than simply cover such a transformation to consolidate the teal independents’ power.

A teals party could allow freedom of conscience for its members on all matters. It would not be burdened by the forced solidarity of a party such as Labor. Similar freedom was allowed within the Democrats, and the Australian Greens’ party constitution allows for freedom of conscience for its representatives, except those from New South Wales, which required an exclusion clause when the constitution was adopted.

A teals party, under a suitable new name, would set out its basic objectives, including more action to tackle climate change. Party status would avoid the restrictive clauses for independents in the recent Labor–Coalition legislation giving parties privileged fundraising and election spending options.

The teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

There are, however, other good alternatives to becoming a traditional party.

One fine option would be for the teal independents to agree to a set of guidelines for negotiating as a group, to use the best possible leverage when minority government comes. For example, they could adopt baseline requirements for tackling the climate emergency or corruption. They could have an established mandate for post-election negotiations.

This would not be new. Five independents, called “The Independents”, including myself, were elected to the balance of power in the Tasmanian House of Assembly in 1989. We had a set of agreed requirements to put to Labor and the Liberals in order for them to form government. We negotiated with both parties and, when the Liberals dropped out, signed a Labor–Green accord that achieved many of the requirements we had set out, including prohibiting the proposed Wesley Vale pulp mill, enlarging the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area, the introduction of freedom of information legislation and an end to public funding for ministerial liquor cabinets.

After the accord was signed, the independents and our supporters set up the Tasmanian Greens and helped, in 1992, to formulate the Australian Greens. At the next election Labor lost office but all five independents were re-elected as Greens. That’s a direction in which the teal independents are not likely to go.

A third alternative would be for the teal independents to simply agree to negotiate en bloc in any future post-election scenario. This minimalist position would obviate the risk of them being played off against each other or picked off one by one. They would be committed to working together and equally negotiating an outcome.

In democracies in recent centuries, parties began forming to pursue the special interests of various sections of society, especially financial self-interests. More recently still, green parties arose around the world, as if by spontaneous combustion, to tackle the looming ecological crises, including climate change, forest destruction and species extinctions. That inevitably led them to also promote social justice, peace and democracy.

Money rules, however. Democracies – just like autocracies – are overridden by the corporate rich who wield the financial power of advertising, media ownership, lobbying and political donations. You only have to look as far as the recent gift of a plane from Gina Rinehart to Pauline Hanson, or see the weapons manufacturers’ billboards around Canberra Airport, or count up the 800 lobbyists who work in our capital.

Two factors are leading to a national and global showdown in human affairs: the environmental crisis, including global heating threatening prosperity, and the growing gap between rich and poor, which is a potent flux for civil disruption.

In Australia – one of the richest per capita countries on Earth if its resource base is considered – these factors are stalking politics and are destroying the time-honoured two-party political system. They shaped the emergence of the Greens and the teal independents and the fierce big-end-of-town opposition to both, although a portion of those rich voters, alarmed by the global crises, is shearing off.

Recent elections have shown voter support for the old parties dropping consistently. The 2028 election will likely see the lowest vote for the Coalition and Labor in history. Labor, duchessed by corporate interests, has replaced the Coalition as Australia’s right of centre party, leaving the Coalition splintering even further right, to territory it’s now unsuccessfully fighting over with One Nation.

The teal independents have occupied the middle ground abandoned by both the Liberals and Labor. The Greens have taken over much of the Labor left’s traditional concern for the environment; the least well-off citizens; human rights, including First Nations’ rights; and opposition to overseas military involvement.

The above analysis is contestable but gives an insight into what is not contestable – the collapse of the once-entrenched two-party system.

Here’s the crunch question emerging from that collapse: given that a new polyglot right could form a future government, can a new polyglot left? That is, if or when the teals and Greens win more seats than Labor, how do the teal independents take due control of their situation? A question that precedes that question is whether the teal independents and Greens should swap preferences before directing votes to Labor or the Coalition.

The appearance of teal independents as a grouping is already there. Their coherence should not be missing when the crunch comes. Some form of publicly understood agreement needs to be embraced.

The global economy could face a 50 per cent loss in GDP between 2070 and 2090 unless immediate policy action is taken on risks posed by the climate crisis, warns a new report by the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries in the UK. Billions of people will die in this scenario.

As the Albanese government fails to measure up, and the Coalition and One Nation offer denial and inaction, here’s a possible outcome of an election down the line as the climate crisis worsens:

The House of Representatives has 150 seats, so a majority is 76. In the climate crisis with the economy collapsing, Labor wins 40. The Coalition/One Nation/right independents win 34. The Greens and teal independents each win 38, totalling 76.

It will require the independents as well as the Greens being prepared to act together to form a crisis-management government. Assuming the age-old enmity between Labor and the Coalition and other right parties, the teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

Regardless of prognostications about Australia’s political future, it is healthy to talk about the alternatives that may be coming for voters. The teals will, of course, choose for themselves between remaining isolated independents or achieving some form of togetherness in the face of the unprecedented forces and fortunes challenging national politics.

It is a classic case of doing nothing being a decision of very great consequence.

Marnus Labuschagne is in the 16-man Test squad to tour South Africa. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.

There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.

Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.

"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.

After spending years as one of the luckiest Test cricketers in the game, Marnus Labuschagne's fortunes appear to BE turning and, unfortunately for him, so has his form.

"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."

Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.

Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.

Both players have traditionally batted in the middle order in first-class cricket.

It leaves the team without a huge number of options for change if the batting line-up continues to struggle.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," he admitted.

"But we've continued to win a lot of Test matches over that period and that ultimately is the key, scoring more runs than the opposition."

Connolly, 23, is one of three players in the squad under 30, along with 29-year-old Kuhnemann and 27-year-old all-rounder Cameron Green, with the latter the only incumbent in the team.

It raises concerns about an impending transition as the majority of the team ages out with little Test experience in younger players behind them.

"Age is a big focus for some, performance I think is important," Bailey said.

"We're confident around where that group's at and also over the ensuing months years as the transitions occur, be that through performance or players dropping out of formats, there'll be good people that are well placed to come in and perform in whichever team that is."

Nduru is a village that once was. Today, silence greets anyone who visits what remains of it.

In western Kenya, the highlands gradually flatten into the vast expanse of Lake Victoria, the world’s second-largest freshwater lake. Along its shores lies Kisumu, one of Kenya’s major cities, surrounded by wetlands that support fishing communities and small farming villages. Nduru was one of them. Today, only a few traces remain to show that a village once stood here.

On either side of an elevated earthen road, slick with recent rains, the fields have become shallow lakes. A line of electricity poles rises above the reeds — silent reminders that they once supplied power to the people of Nduru. Perched atop one of them is a grey crowned crane.

As the elegant bird spreads its wings and disappears over the waterlogged fields, Bernard Aringi Odenyi, a 49-year-old director of a community school, arrives on his motorcycle. A former resident of Nduru, he points toward a cluster of ruins. “You see those walls? That used to be my house.”

Odenyi pulls out his phone and shows a photograph of himself standing inside the house, floodwater up to his knees. Today, only a few crumbling walls remain.

Every rainy season, Lake Victoria swells, a problem worsened by the loss and encroachment of the surrounding wetlands. Fishing and farming communities along its shores bear the brunt as their homes and livelihoods are repeatedly disrupted.

After severe flooding during the 2024 rainy season, Nduru became uninhabitable, forcing almost all its residents, including Odenyi, to relocate to nearby villages.

It was the third time Odenyi had been displaced by floods. The latest disaster meant more than losing his home, as he had to move back in with his parents.

“In our tradition, once you are married, you never go back to live with your parents. Only a grandchild may return to the grandparents’ compound and stay there,” he says. “Worst of all is that the floods have forced people to lose their traditions and ancestral lands. I think nature is reclaiming its lost glory.”

Odenyi now lives in Nyang’ande, where the community school he heads is struggling to cope with an influx of displaced children. Built for 500 pupils, it now serves nearly twice that number.

Scientists attribute much of Lake Victoria’s rising water levels to climate change and heavier rainfall across its vast catchment, much of which lies in the Kenyan Highlands. Water from inland rivers drains into the lake, raising levels along its shores.

The Lake Victoria Basin Commission, headquartered in Kisumu, advises the governments of Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda on managing the basin’s shared waters. Paul Kariuki, the commission’s regional ecosystems monitoring specialist, says the rising water level is not a new phenomenon. “In some seasons, the lake level has risen by more than half a metre,” he says. “That’s enough to submerge ports, roads, and entire communities along the shoreline.”

Like Nduru, many of the farming and fishing villages around Kisumu have been affected by flooding. One of them is Sango Rota, where the Sondu River empties into Lake Victoria after flowing from the highlands of Kericho County. During heavy rains, the river regularly breaches its banks. In recent years, however, residents have faced a double threat: flooding from upstream and backflow from the lake itself.

Despite the challenges, Sango Rota’s Chief Seth Oluoch Agwanda, who oversees the government’s flood mitigation efforts, remains optimistic as he leads the way along a network of dikes and stone-filled gabions built to hold back the lake. During the floods of April and May, he said that about 1,500 residents of Sango Rota were forced to seek shelter in displacement camps. “But two weeks ago, we were able to close the last displacement camp,” he says proudly, stepping around pools of water to keep his leather boots dry. “People have been able to return to their homes.”

Near the shoreline, Agwanda greets a group of fishermen sheltering beneath a tarp stretched between wooden poles. But when they begin sharing their views on the government’s flood prevention efforts, including the construction of dikes, he quietly slips away.

Kennedy Otieno, a 49-year-old fisherman, says, “Every time during elections, politicians come here and promise us [to construct] cemented dikes. But after the elections nothing happens.” The other fishermen nod. “All are false promises. And we have to witness how the lake takes everything from us.”

In Nyang’ande, there is little sign of rain. Under a clear blue sky, sunlight glints off corrugated iron roofs and white tarps covering narrow walkways. “These days it’s not just the rains we worry about,” displaced fisherman Joseph Ogola says. “The lake has risen so much that even on a sunny day, a strong wind can push the water over into our land.”

Back at the Lake Victoria Basin Commission office, Paul Kariuki says encroachment on wetlands and peatlands is worsening the floods, as factories and housing developments are being built in areas that should be protected.

Environmental activist Michael Otieno Nyanguti, who founded the Magnam Environmental Network, has taken several cases to court in an effort to stop development on reclaimed wetlands.

“People get authorisation from the government to build on wetlands, and often there is corruption behind it,” says Nyanguti over the phone.

Some of Kenya’s wetlands are peatlands — carbon-rich ecosystems that play a crucial role in regulating the global climate.

Peatlands cover only about 3% of the Earth’s land surface, yet they store nearly twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests combined. Their destruction not only releases vast amounts of stored carbon but also removes one of nature’s most effective buffers against flooding.

Francis Odhiambo Omungo of Ecofinder Kenya, co-organiser of the International Workshop of the Venice Agreement for Peatlands, held in Kisumu in June, says peatlands are invaluable for climate protection, biodiversity conservation and flood control. “Apart from being the world’s most efficient carbon storage, they act like a sponge and absorb and retain huge amounts of water.”

Close to Kisumu, extensive wetlands line the shores of Lake Victoria. Some are believed to be peatlands but remain unmapped, making conservation more difficult.

Yet identifying peatlands is not always straightforward. During the workshop, Colombian ecologist David Santiago Rocha Cardenas pointed to bubbles rising through the water. “Look at the gases coming up; and the smell, these are typical characteristics of peatlands,” he said.

Katharina Renate, a German hydrologic researcher from the University of Hamburg, disagreed. “I’m not convinced,” she said. “For peat to form, the ground needs to be waterlogged for long periods of time to be able to store carbon. There is too much inflow and outflow here.”

While the scientists debated, 70-year-old Margaret Akinyi relied on local knowledge shaped over generations. Returning from harvesting papyrus, she explained that the Luo language has long distinguished between two kinds of wetlands.

“Thidnia is the swamp where the water is moving,” she says. “Anete is where the water stays. It is soft and keeps wobbling; you can even walk over it.”

She has never heard the term “peatland,” but her description suggests that anete refers to one.

For decades, Akinyi has depended on these wetlands for her livelihood, harvesting papyrus that is woven into mats and baskets.

“When they dry up, some people burn what remains of the wetlands so they can farm there; the land is very fertile,” she says. She has watched parts of the wetland give way to agriculture and real estate, despite the protection they provide to surrounding communities.

During floods, fishermen clear papyrus to reach fishing grounds. When the water recedes, farmers remove the vegetation to cultivate the fertile soil.

Intended as a temporary refuge, the displacement camp in Nyang’ande has become a permanent home for some residents displaced from Nduru. One of them is 37-year-old Judith Awino Litunge, who describes herself as a hustler because life has forced her to be one.

“We understand that wetlands can protect us from flooding,” she says. “But as displaced farmers, we often have no choice but to destroy them for farming or fishing in order to survive.”

Litunge pauses before adding, “The government gives us rations from time to time, but they won’t allocate us new land. We have nowhere to go. There is nothing more shameful than being a farmer without a piece of land to work on.”

Samuel Oron, Kisumu County’s Director of Special Programmes and Disaster Management, disputes residents’ claims that they have not been offered alternative land. He says some families decline — or even sell — plots allocated on higher ground and choose to remain near the wetlands.

“These people prefer to stay close to the wetlands,” Oron says. “They benefit from fishing during the floods and farming in the fertile grounds when the wetlands dry up or even when they have destroyed them.”

As villagers criticise the government’s flood response, Oron says the county is doing what it can.

“At the county level, we do everything we can to protect our communities from floods by desilting riverbeds and building dikes and stone-filled gabions.”

He acknowledges that wetland encroachment is a growing problem but says final approval for developments rests with Kenya’s National Environment Management Authority (NEMA). The county, he says, has mapped flood-prone areas and wetlands to guide planning, dike construction and disaster preparedness, while promoting farming practices that protect rather than degrade wetlands.

As Lake Victoria continues to rise, the fate of its surrounding communities is increasingly tied to that of its wetlands. While many local communities exploit wetlands out of necessity, activists warn that government-approved developments continue to encroach on them for profit.

Meteorologists warn that an El Niño event expected later this year could push Lake Victoria even higher. Scientists say wetlands remain one of the region’s best natural defences against flooding. But for families who depend on them to survive, conservation without alternatives is no solution at all.

FILE - Freed Hong Kong bookseller Lam Wing-kee stands next to a placard with a picture of missing bookseller Gui Minhai, left, in front of his book store during a march in Hong Kong on June 18, 2016.
                
                    
                    Kin Cheung/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

TAIPEI, Taiwan — Lam Wing-kee, a former Hong Kong bookseller who became a symbol of resistance to Beijing's crackdown on speech freedom after he was seized by Chinese authorities in late 2015, has died in Taiwan, the island's official Central News Agency reported, citing an unnamed source.

The news agency didn't give a cause of death, but said the 70-year-old Lam had a cancer relapse last year and was admitted to MacKay Memorial Hospital in Taipei on Tuesday. He fell into a coma on Wednesday and died Thursday evening, according to the report.

Lam, who previously worked at Causeway Bay Books in Hong Kong, moved to Taipei in 2019 over fears of legal troubles and reopened the bookstore under the same name in the Taiwanese capital in 2020.

Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te offered his condolences in a Facebook post.

"The passing of Mr Lam Wing-kee is deeply saddening, but the courage he left behind would not fade," Lai wrote. "Taiwan will remember that a Hong Kong bookstore worker once told us in the most ordinary yet most steadfast way how precious freedom is and reminded us that democracy requires the efforts of generation after generation to defend it."

Lam was one of five people affiliated with Causeway Books who disappeared in late 2015. The store sold books and magazines purporting to reveal secrets about the inside lives of Chinese leaders and the scandals surrounding them.

One of the five, publisher Gui Minhai, went missing from his holiday home in Thailand and was later sentenced to 10 years in prison in China on a charge of illegally providing intelligence overseas.

In an act of defiance, Lam gave an explosive account of his experience in 2016 that contradicted official Chinese accounts of what happened to the five booksellers.

He said that he was seized by Chinese authorities in October 2015 after crossing the border from Hong Kong to the city of Shenzhen on China's mainland, and that he was blindfolded for a 13-hour train ride to the eastern city of Ningbo, where he was kept under 24-hour surveillance in a room for five months by rotating two-person teams.

Speaking to a packed news conference in Hong Kong, he said he was later forced to appear on Chinese television to confess to crimes.

In June, Lam told the Central News Agency that he had temporarily closed the bookstore in Taipei because of his health and that he couldn't say when it might reopen.

Chinese and Hong Kong authorities have further tightened controls over the territory following massive anti-government protests in 2019.

Hong Kong police arrested two people in June on suspicion of selling seditious publications and receiving funds from foreign political organizations, acting under a recent national security law.

CBS may have canceled “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert,” but its legacy will live on at the Museum of Broadcast Communications in Chicago.

“The Late Show” set – desk, chairs and all – made a day-and-a-half sojourn in the back of a truck from a New Jersey warehouse, arriving last week at the Randolph Street museum for permanent display in Chicago, the city where Colbert cut his comedy teeth.

“It’s a very big deal,“ said David Plier, a former retailing executive and current part-time radio host at WGN who serves as chairman, president and CEO of the museum.

Donated by the network, “The Late Show” set was delivered Thursday at noon, a large white truck dodging lunchtime pedestrians as it pulled into an alley east of the museum, swinging open its rear doors to reveal the seat of late-night TV humor.

Getting the complete set seemed unlikely after the May 14 episode, when former host David Letterman joined Colbert in gleefully dropping guest and desk chairs from the roof of the Ed Sullivan Theater.

“Even though there were chairs thrown off the Ed Sullivan Theater, those were extras,” Plier said.

Colbert’s actual desk, chairs, credenza, stage columns and other set pieces arrived an hour late but intact Thursday. They sat in the truck for another half hour as Plier paced the busy sidewalk like an expectant parent, waiting for a separate moving team.

The most challenging piece was an enormous crate containing Colbert’s desk. Two movers somehow maneuvered it out of the truck and down the busy sidewalk, wedging it through the front doors, waiting for reinforcements to help bring it down to the main floor.

Colbert helped steer “The Late Show” set to Chicago, Plier said, where it will be displayed in perpetuity at the Museum of Broadcast Communications, an eclectic and itinerant 40-year-old institution that itself seemed close to cancellation in recent years.

Column: Stephen Colbert’s signoff reminds us of the days the Chicago Cubs were a late-night punchline

Launched by the late Bruce Dumont in 1987 at River City on South Wells Street, the museum moved to the Chicago Cultural Center in 1992, where it became a major tourist attraction with exhibits from Chicago TV shows.

The museum temporarily closed in 2003 amid ambitious plans to move into a four-story building it bought at State and Kinzie streets. But it took nearly a decade to raise funds and remodel the $27 million River North space, which finally opened in 2012.

Struggling financially, the museum sold its third and fourth floors in 2019 to real estate firm Fern Hill. In 2023, the developer exercised an option to take over the entire building, kicking out the museum.

In October, after going dark for more than two years, the museum reopened in a pop-up space at 440 W. Randolph St. in the West Loop.

Plier is hoping to make it a permanent home with the help of a $2.5 million grant from the city of Chicago, and a new $12 million capital campaign. He is also planning to rename the museum “after a very famous Chicagoan” while broadening its mission going forward.

“We want to be a national museum, we want to attract visitors from all over,” Plier said. “We will always keep Chicago as part of it, but we see ourselves absolutely as a national institution.”

The late-night TV exhibit features everything from Johnny Carson’s “Tonight Show” set to the saxophone Bill Clinton played on “The Arsenio Hall Show” during his 1992 presidential campaign. There’s even an original “Triumph the Insult Comic Dog,” as first seen on “Late Night With Conan O’Brien.”

The museum still has exhibits devoted to Chicago broadcast history, such as “Bozo’s Circus” and “Svengoolie.” It also houses the National Radio Hall of Fame.

CBS relegated the top-rated “Late Show” to broadcast history last July, saying it was losing $40 million a year. Some analysts contend then-CBS owner Paramount was seeking to curry favor with the Trump administration for its pending acquisition by Skydance. The FCC approved the $8 billion merger one week after the Colbert cancellation announcement.

“The Late Show” exhibit will likely be the star attraction when it opens to the public later this summer. Plier is hoping to get Colbert himself to cut the ribbon on his old desk and chairs.

“Whether you’re a Democrat or Republican, whether you liked that show or not, it’s still television history, and now it’s here,” Plier said.

A class action lawsuit was filed Friday in Cook County Circuit Court against WGN-TV and owner Nexstar Media, as well as several Chicago-area radio stations, for platforming Brandon Ellington, who allegedly used the airwaves to swindle hundreds of Chicagoans out of $15 million through a Ponzi-like investment scheme.

WGN-Ch. 9 featured Ellington, a convicted mortgage-fraud felon who rebranded himself as “Mr. Finance,” on several broadcasts last year, including its daily lifestyle show “Spotlight Chicago,” which airs weekdays at 1 p.m. with hosts Sarah Jindra and Ji Suk Yi.

“WGN-TV’s own hosts endorsed him in the station’s voice,” the lawsuit states. “The hosts asked no probing question about Ellington’s background and disclosed nothing about it; they presented a convicted federal mortgage-fraud felon to their viewers as a model of financial success.”

Ellington’s on-air interviews are still posted on WGN’s YouTube page.

A spokesperson for Dallas-based Nexstar declined to comment on the lawsuit.

The alleged scheme was marketed by Ellington on various media as a passive income real estate investment program promising high returns through his south suburban company, Access Capital Today. Instead, it collapsed, failing to make payments and leaving hundreds of Chicagoans holding the bag, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by Chicago attorney Alexander Loftus on behalf of Milton Harris and Byron Crawford, who invested and lost money after tuning into Ellington’s on-air pitches. The station’s endorsement essentially closed the deal, Loftus told the Tribune.

“He’s Mr. Finance, and he’s on TV, so he must be legit,” Loftus said.

In May, Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias issued a temporary order prohibiting Ellington and Access Capital Today from acting as investment advisers, calling the promoted program a “Ponzi-like scheme” that ensnared more than 300 clients.

Ellington, who is not a registered investment adviser, pleaded guilty in 2009 for his role as a loan originator in a sweeping mortgage fraud case in Chicago federal court.

In addition to WGN-TV, the lawsuit names several Chicago-area radio stations as defendants for promoting and airing Ellington’s investment advice programs, including iHeartMedia-owned WGRB-AM and WVON-AM, and Crawford Broadcasting-owned WSRB-FM.

Chicago sports fans are mourning the passing of Stacey King, 59, a role player on the Bulls early ’90s championship teams who became a star in the broadcast booth.

After a coaching stint for the Rockford Lightning in the CBA, King started at Comcast SportsNet as a studio analyst in 2006, joining Bulls’ TV announcers Tom Dore and Johnny “Red” Kerr as a color commentator during the team’s playoff run that season. In 2008, King was paired with TV play-by-play announcer Neil Funk, becoming the team’s lead color announcer.

Kerr, the Bulls inaugural head coach and longtime broadcaster, died in 2009.

King made a name for himself with his colorful catchphrases, knowledge and enthusiasm during a long run at the regional sports network, which was rebranded as NBC Sports Chicago in 2017. He and play-by-play partner Adam Amin joined the successor Chicago Sports Network at its launch in 2024.

“He was such a huge presence,” said Chuck Swirsky, who has been the Bulls’ radio play-by-play announcer since 2008. “He was more than an analyst. He was a showman, he was an entertainer with basketball as his foundation.”

While Chicagoans might be hard-pressed to name players on the current Bulls roster, King’s exclamations, from “gimme the hot sauce” to “mouse in the house,” have become part of the local sports lexicon.

But it was King’s “basketball IQ” that set him apart, demonstrating a knowledge of the game that Swirsky said would have made him a successful coach, if he had followed that path. Instead, for many fans, King may have been the best reason to watch the Bulls over the past two decades.

“There will never be another Stacey King,” Swirsky said. “They talk about generational talents in basketball as players. Stacey was a generational talent as a basketball analyst.”

Veteran Chicago sports and news anchor Ryan Baker is hanging up his mic this month after nearly two decades at WBBM-Ch. 2 to become the president and CEO of First Tee-Greater Chicago, a nonprofit organization that mentors youth through golf.

A south suburban native and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign graduate, Baker joined CBS 2 in 2008 as lead sports anchor after five years at NBC 5 Chicago.

In 2019, Baker shifted to morning news anchor before returning to the sports desk in 2024. His last day on the air will be June 25.

“Having grown up in the south suburbs watching Channel 2 every night and idolizing the legendary Johnny Morris, it’s been an indescribable dream come true to sit in his sports anchor chair for the bulk of the last 18 years at WBBM-TV,” Baker said in a news release.
