Two Phoenix police officers were fired and arrested after an unreported traffic stop in which they assaulted a man and woman and shocked them with a Taser, the police chief said.

Officers Antonio Felix and Luis Vasquez were arrested on charges including aggravated assault and kidnapping, police chief Matt Giordano said at a news conference Saturday.

“Detectives have confirmed that the two former officers physically assaulted both the man and woman during the traffic stop,” Giordano said. “The investigation also shows that a Taser was used on the victims during the stop.”

The officers did not report the Aug. 5 traffic stop and did not activate their body-worn cameras, police said.

“There is no video evidence, but we established what we believe is probable cause that these crimes were committed,” Giordano said, adding there was no indication that the officers knew the victims.

Dave Evans, a spokesperson for the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office, said Sunday that Vasquez had been released from custody while Felix remained incarcerated at the Lower Buckeye Jail in Phoenix.

Attempts by The Associated Press to determine who their defense attorneys were to request comment were unsuccessful.

During the late-night traffic stop in Phoenix, the male driver and woman passenger reported that the officers smashed the car window, according to a statement from Phoenix police.

Vasquez punched the man and threatened to shoot him, while the woman was removed from the vehicle and handcuffed.

The man managed to drive away and abandoned the car in neighboring Tempe, while the woman was released at the scene, the statement said.

A police officer in neighboring Tempe who responded to the abandoned car asked over dispatch whether it had fled from any neighboring police agencies and was told it had not, according to a Tempe police report.

The Tempe officer called the car’s registered owner, the mother of the male driver, and through her was able to connect with the woman passenger and eventually the male driver.

The woman passenger told the officer that both of them had been shocked with a Taser, while the man later told the officer that he had been punched in the face multiple times and that they had repeatedly asked why they had been stopped.

The Tempe officer wrote in the report that he believed they were victims of an attempted carjacking by people impersonating police officers.

Giordano, the Phoenix police chief, said he had a similar reaction when he initially learned of the incident as it was “so far outside the bounds of our policies.” But when detectives started looking into it, they realized Phoenix officers might be involved and transitioned the case to a special investigations detail, he said.

“That’s when they started putting evidence together, including the automatic vehicle locator that did put a vehicle at that location about the time that the victims reported it occurred,” Giordano said, referring to the location technology in city vehicles.

Vasquez and Felix had served eight and nine years with Phoenix police, respectively. Giordano, without elaborating, said both had previously violated department policy but that it was “nothing of this nature.”

The Phoenix department’s investigation and audit are ongoing. The officers have a scheduled court date on Friday.

Topic:AI

There are concerns that AI could impair the development of critical thinking skills. (ABC News: Justin Hewitson)

There are early signs the use of artificial intelligence is impacting learning, with a study finding use of the technology lifted homework results, while exam scores fell by 20 per cent.Some young people are boycotting the technology, while neuroscientists are worried deep thinking being increasingly offloaded to AI could impact the development of neural connections in the brain.

As humans adapt to using the new tool, the rise of AI might prompt a rethink in how education is delivered and assessed.

With the widespread use of artificial intelligence in schools and universities, there are concerns about its impact on learning and ultimately young brains.

"[AI] can be a great tool; it can help stimulate critical thinking, for example, if used in the right way," neuroscientist Professor James Vickers said.

But he said a recent study of students in China highlighted problems with offloading hard mental work to AI.

Published this year, the study of more than 26,000 students in grades 7 to 12 looked at how generative AI affected homework productivity and learning.

It found AI use lifted homework scores by 18 per cent and improved completion times by 30 per cent.

But it lowered monthly exam scores by 20 per cent within six months.

Professor Vickers has concerns that using AI instead of developing deep-thinking skills could have long-term impacts. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

Learning and deep thinking physically alter the human brain, creating new connections between neurons.

It is known as brain plasticity.

"The brain almost quadruples in weight from birth to adulthood, without adding any new neurons — it's all physical change driven by learning," University of Tasmania senior neuroscience lecturer Dr Matt Kirkcaldie said.

Neuroscientists are looking into the impact of offloading deep thinking to AI. (Jon Olav Eikenes / FlickrCC)

Over time, critical thinking, learning, and other cognitive tasks help build robust nerve networks that underlie what is known as cognitive reserve.

"[Cognitive reserve] is your ability to resist things that negatively impact the brain, that might be stroke or brain injury, multiple sclerosis and even dementia," Professor Vickers said.

Cognitive reserve is built up from early life through schooling, then higher education.

There are concerns AI could impair the development of critical thinking skills.

"They might read the AI-generated text and understand what it says, but they never went through the struggle of working through the ideas and how they might fit in the overall picture," Dr Kirkcaldie said.

A recent report by the eSafety Commission found 78 per cent of Australian children had used an AI assistant.

Professor Vickers has concerns that using AI instead of developing deep-thinking skills could have long-term impacts.

Alexis Shegog and her friends refuse to use artificial intelligence. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Some young people are so worried about the impact artificial intelligence could have on their learning they have decided to boycott it.

"I wouldn't want to cheapen my experience at uni, especially with the fees we pay," said Alexis Shegog, who is planning to return to university.

Alexis is part of a group called circa Lutruwita, which has been protesting the development of AI data centres in northern Tasmania.

Alexis Shegog and fellow members of the group circa Lutruwita protest against proposals for data centres in Tasmania and the impact of AI in general. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The group has concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centres and its use in military settings.

They are also worried about AI deepfakes and their impact on personal privacy.

And while they refuse to use AI as part of their studies, they are aware that AI will be in their futures.

"I would want to make sure that I was getting the full value from my course and learning the material, especially if I'm going to have to compete with AI in the future for my job," Ms Shegog said.

Members of circa Lutruwita making posters. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

"My friends who are in uni at the moment, none of them use AI.

"And most of them are quite concerned about the impact that it has environmentally, socially, and the impact that it is having on their education."

A recent report by the eSafety Commission found 78 per cent of Australian children had used an AI assistant.

Ninety-one per cent used it for learning or translation, 70 per cent used it for writing or editing, and 68 per cent used it for entertainment.

Students at Guilford Young College in Hobart have mixed feelings about the technology.

Lacey Tilyard says she uses AI for some subjects but not others. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Some said they used it for creating practice tests or simplifying ideas.

But she said some of her classes, like psychology, have a strict ban on the use of AI.

Ella Willmott said AI was a good learning tool and had helped her research future employment opportunities.

Ella Willmott has mixed feelings about the technology. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

But she was worried about its impact on creativity.

"I think it's the worst thing for artists. Because it just gets rid of the authenticity and almost the rawness of everyone's art," she said.

Professor Vickers said AI may drive a transformation in how educators teach and how student learning is assessed.

Professor Kathy Mills, from the Institute for Learning Sciences and Teacher Education at the Australian Catholic University, said teachers want their students to use AI critically.

"Both students and teachers want AI tools that are designed to do more than tell the answers, but which guide student learning," she said.

She said how student learning was assessed would be more important than ever.

Kathy Mills says teachers want their students to use AI critically. (Supplied)

"If teachers want to know what students can do without AI, take-home assignments are going to be more difficult for teachers to monitor the level of AI support accessed by students in that context," she said.

Professor Vickers said rethinking education was not just about "trying to catch students out" through exams.

But he said it was about ensuring students could apply learning to different situations, in the same way medical students were presented with clinical scenarios to test their knowledge.

Officials in Tehran got the United States to sign a document that even Americans described as degrading, mortifying, a total capitulation.

The Iran deal has been described as a “humiliation” for the United States, since the upshot is that America gets little that it didn’t already have before the war, and Iran gets security guarantees and a big pile of money. Donald Trump’s agreement leaves Iran a theocratic state free to arm itself with ballistic missiles and drones and to murder its own citizens. Its terms suggest that this much-despised state will, after a 60-day period of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz, have the ability to regulate maritime traffic.

Normally one would have to pay a lot of money to a discreet professional to be humiliated this badly. Watching Trump and his aides sell the deal is in some ways as humiliating as the deal itself. “If other countries have” ballistic missiles, Trump said at the G7 conference yesterday, “it’s a little bit unfair” for Iran “not to have some.” Elimination of those missiles was one of the primary aims of the war, and thousands of Iranians, as well as more than a dozen Americans, died contesting it. Trump began his remarks today by stressing that the United States could have kept up the bombing if it wished “for another three weeks, two weeks, four weeks, two years. You would never have the Hormuz Strait open.” Keeping the strait open is one of the main purposes of the United States Navy, so these words sound a lot like an admission that the military of the United States cannot do its job, and might be equally vulnerable elsewhere, too.

Jonathan Chait: All the sad hawks

Humiliation, however, is distinct from defeat. Only the United States was humiliated; both countries have experienced a catastrophic loss. The defeat for the United States is the more obvious of the two: a loss of standing and the confirmation that even a rich country cannot force its will on a poor but determined one. For Iran, the defeat is subtler. Bordering countries once considered it a problem neighbor and now know it to be an outright threat. They are arming themselves accordingly and seeking ways to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s economy has been a disaster for about 15 years and is now a total wreck. Sanctions relief will help, but who exactly will want to invest in a country whose government is sustained by brutality and ruled according to the whims of a junta led by a mangled religious fanatic?

The best defense of this deal, from a U.S. perspective, is probably one that takes into account these economic and political headwinds facing Iran, and notices that they are more likely to change the regime than any further military action. You don’t need to huff and puff to blow down the house when the weatherman is predicting a typhoon tomorrow.

Another possible defense is that, like all deals made by Trump, and most deals made by the Islamic Republic of Iran, it is not much of a deal anyway, because both parties intended to break it before it was even signed. An anonymous U.S. official told CNN yesterday that “people shouldn’t read too much into the language” of the agreement, because the core of the agreement is “understandings we have with each other.” This statement goes against all legal advice ever given. (Read the contract; ignore what the other guy tells you while he watches you sign it.) Much of what’s in the agreement is so vague as to be meaningless. We know what a nuclear deal looks like, because Barack Obama got one, and it established detailed and invasive inspections that are most certainly not delineated in any document leaked or mentioned by Trump officials. The deal might have been reached only because both sides wanted to stop fighting, and both were willing to add vague terms because they didn’t want to be bound by precise ones.

The same U.S. official’s other comment to CNN was assurance that the “language” of the document—the same language the official encouraged his domestic audience to ignore—is calibrated to let Iranian officials “say what they need to say for their domestic politics.” This intriguing comment reflects a view of Iranian leadership I have heard from officials in previous administrations, including Democratic ones: that they are susceptible to flattery, and that they regard the exasperation and humiliation of the Americans as an end in itself.

Daniel B. Shapiro: What did you expect?

The humiliation is the point. Iran got the United States to sign a document that even Americans described as degrading, mortifying, a total capitulation. Who cares if the deal never really happens, or if each part turns out to be a little less sweet than it first appears? Iran has never before won a war, and even the blows it has struck against the United States, Israel, and its own citizens have up to now been pathetic and furtive, taking the form of terror attacks and indirect action through proxies. The existence of an understanding, with humiliating terms for America, is a heap of symbolic and emotional capital that no Iranian regime has enjoyed since the Islamic Revolution of 1979.

Now it is time to see how Iran will use the dividends from this humiliation. The $300 billion in investments is hardly the biggest opportunity for Iran to cash in. Far more valuable would be a pivot by the regime’s leadership away from some of the dogmas of its past, and toward reform. No previous leaders have had the ability to make such a pivot, and they probably did not want to make one anyway. The current leaders, however, have positioned themselves as saviors of the Islamic Republic, and with that credibility could institute certain changes that are widely known to be necessary and desirable, but that would have looked counterrevolutionary if proposed by anyone else.

Iran has won the war, or at least not lost it. The peace is up for grabs.

Queensland’s public-spending watchdog has fast-tracked its probe of a bungled $188 million child safety IT system, as pressure mounts on the government over kids sleeping on department floors.

The Queensland Audit Office’s updated forward work plan, released this week, reveals a planned report into the rollout of the long-awaited Unify system is now expected to be tabled by September.

The report was initially not due until the 2027-28 financial year.

“We brought forward this audit to ensure timely assessment of the system implementation following its go-live in April 2025 and challenges identified in the December 2025 review,” the audit office’s 2026-29 work plan states.

The development comes as Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm faces pressure over details of children in state care sleeping on child safety service centre floors – which she is yet to respond to – amid scrutiny of her relationship with a colleague.

Camm commissioned the earlier Deloitte review in September after announcing there had been a “critical IT failure” in the rollout of a system meant to manage the records for some 16,000 kids in state care or known to the department.

At the time, Camm said she was concerned the “former Labor government’s bungled IT program” could result in the death of a child if frontline staff could not access timely and accurate information.

The 11-month Child Safety Inquiry, initially planned to run until November but cut short to May, said in its June report it did not investigate Unify “to any extent” but the state’s ability to protect children was “compromised” by a dysfunctional record system.

Details of the in-progress audit office probe note implementation of large-scale IT projects carry significant risks and “need to be carefully and planned managed to ensure they meet intended objectives and avoid these common pitfalls”.

Both the Child Safety and Youth Justice departments are being audited as part of the work, which will assess “whether responsible entities have effectively governed the design and implementation of the Unify system”.

“This will consider the governance and decision-making to support design and implementation, and whether governance, risk management, and remediation plans effectively respond to identified Unify system issues to minimise impacts to those in the child protection and youth justice systems.”

The Child Safety Department began work on an overhaul of its IT system in 2015 to give other agencies and service providers access to relevant information and to enable them to contribute to it.

This came after an earlier audit office report found issues with the patchwork processes put in place after the 2012 Carmody report that had not balanced access with data security.

In 2019, then-minister Di Farmer announced funding for the Unify overhaul – slated for completion by 2023 – after a follow-up audit found many of the problems persisted.

In a statement to this masthead, Camm welcomed the fast-tracking of the audit office work into the design and descoping of a system she said was “bungled” by the former Labor government and that created the “broken child safety system we inherited”.

Labor’s child safety spokesperson Corrine McMillan said the audit office should fast-track the review as a result of failures under Camm, which “potentially put the lives of thousands of children at risk”.

“The audit must be carried out as quickly as possible to ensure the system has been fixed and children are not still slipping through the cracks,” McMillan said.

Top-tier accounting firms could face a historic, government-mandated break-up of their lucrative consulting and audit wings under proposed federal options designed to tackle the structural conflicts of interest plaguing the sector.

Login or signup to continue reading

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has set his sights on addressing the significant gaps in regulation after a string of high-profile ethical scandals once again plunged the industry's culture and independence into the spotlight.

On Wednesday, the government released a Treasury options paper on the regulation of these large industry players. The paper serves as a consultation blueprint that outlines potential pathways for changes without yet locking them into law.

The sweeping regulatory response followed scandals involving the sector's big four, which led to KPMG being barred from bidding federal contracts until September 30, 2026.

The allegations were first raised in Parliament that KPMG partners leaked confidential client information and mishandled an internal whistleblower who attempted to raise the alarm.

Those claims were first brought forward by a whistleblower in May 2024, only to be dismissed by KPMG before Labor senator Deborah O'Neill who ultimately exposed it under parliamentary privilege.

In the political firestorm that followed, a number of senior partners at the firm resigned, including its chief executive Andrew Yates and chairman Martin Sheppard.

Separately, two Ernst & Young staff members were sacked and faced court after allegedly using their positions to breach Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's personal bank account.

Speaking on Radio National Breakfast, Dr Mulino said the inquiries into PwC and KPMG exposed "behaviour by large firms that simply isn't good enough", where confidential information was being misused across different parts of the firm.

"The nature of the kinds of activities that have been alleged against PwC and KPMG mean that some of the options we need to look at include separation of functions," Dr Mulino said.

"There have been a number of instances of opportunistic behaviour, of breaches of trust, of confidential information being used in ways that is highly inappropriate. So it is clear to me that we need to look at strengthening arrangements now."

Dr Mulino questioned the current self-regulation model of the sector, saying there was now "a question over whether ASIC needs to step in more as the federal regulator".

When pressed on the three-year delay after the initial PwC crisis, he cited a heavy legislative pipeline, saying the government had been intentionally sequencing its attack through whistleblower expansions and the creation of External Reporting Australia.

Addressing the current fallout at KPMG, Dr Mulino said that a formal material incident had been declared across government.

As a result, all federal departments holding existing contracts with the embattled firm were now "obliged to reach out to the contractors that they work with and ensure that all arrangements are appropriate", before a sweeping Department of Finance review.

The Treasury paper revealed a cultural imbalance driven by revenue. It showed audit revenue made up, on average, about 20 per cent of total revenue across the big four in 2025.

Between 2013 and 2018, non-audit consulting revenue outpaced audit growth, swelling from 73 per cent to 82 per cent of total firm intakes.

The paper warned this reliance on large advisory margins threatened to contaminate independent verification.

It said an overarching consulting culture "may be at odds with an auditor's role in challenging management and client perspectives".

Risks were heightened by internal competition for resources and a broader concern that large firms "may not have effective controls on client information".

Under the framework in place at the time, unincorporated partnerships could not be meaningfully sanctioned for internal, firm-level decisions that affected audit quality. Only the individual lead auditor bore personal criminal liability and the risk of deregistration.

To eliminate structural conflicts where firms effectively "reviewed their own work", the paper canvassed separating audit lines from non-audit divisions.

The proposed models ranged from a total ban on providing non-audit services to audit clients, to strict operational ring-fencing with separate chief executives and independent financial reports or fully mandated structural separation into completely independent entities.

To prevent firms from treating breaches as a cost of doing business, the government proposed supercharging enforcement by introducing a robust civil penalty regime, with maximum fines for significant global entities skyrocketing to 10 per cent of their annual turnover, capped at $910 million.

The paper took aim at severe market concentration. It showed the top four firms audited a staggering 96 per cent of the top 200 entities in Australia.

To address this dominance, the paper floated options to reduce the historical 1000-member accounting partnership limit down to 400.

It canvassed mandating a public audit tender process every 10 years, or forcing firms to operate exclusively as authorised audit companies under strict corporate directors' duties.

Other interventions described included requiring mandatory firm licensing by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and implementing size-based surveillance frequencies to force immediate remediation of flawed corporate books.

The paper drew immediate criticism from the crossbench, with Greens finance spokesperson Barbara Pocock accusing the government of "kicking the can down the road" with further talks.

"Back in 2024, Labor issued a consultation paper and nothing came of it," Senator Pocock said. "Now we have another paper and the test for Labor is: will it act or will it tinker?"

Senator Pocock called on the government to subject the major partnerships to the same tax, transparency, and corporate rules as other large commercial business entities, while halting the flow of millions of dollars in ongoing public contracts to compromised operations.

"The Government needs to stop expressing 'deep concern' at corrupt practices of the Big Four while dishing out millions of dollars to them in contracts," Senator Pocock said.

"Labor needs to put an end to the Big Four's special treatment and regulate them like other Australian businesses."

Stakeholders and industry members have been given until August 12, 2026, to provide formal feedback on the proposed regulatory blueprint.

august-2026-hottest-month-record:
Wildfires in Spain, July 2026. Photo: Unidad Militar de Emergencias

August 2026 tied July 2023 as the hottest month ever recorded worldwide, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service said Thursday. The global average surface air temperature was 1.65 degrees Celsius above estimated preindustrial levels.

The exceptionally high temperatures were recorded even before the developing El Niño weather system had made much of an impact. El Niño is a naturally recurring phenomenon in which changes in winds over the Pacific Ocean cause ocean temperatures to rise and transfer huge amounts of heat into the atmosphere. Its effects are felt around the world, including through floods, droughts and heatwaves.

The current El Niño is expected to reach full strength toward the end of the year and could become one of the most intense events on record.

Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said that while El Niño was beginning to intensify the heat, the main driver of this year's high temperatures remained the continued burning of fossil fuels. "While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver behind this year's high temperatures remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels," Otto said. "Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming."

The effects are still being felt worldwide, including devastating wildfires, excess deaths, heatwaves and disruptions to transportation. Food price inflation is also expected to continue rising as damage to harvests affects domestic supplies and imports.

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of UN Climate Change, said the economic and social damage caused by the summer was still being calculated. "Extreme heat has been killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food," Stiell said. "The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling."

Temperatures in August exceeded 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, the lower of the two temperature limits governments agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement. However, temperatures at that level would have to persist over a period of years before the agreement's long-term threshold was considered to have been breached.

The UN Environment Programme acknowledged this month that an overshoot of 1.5 degrees is now widely considered unavoidable and said large-scale removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere would be required as part of pathways aimed at bringing temperatures back down.

Data from Copernicus also showed that western and central Europe, southern Scandinavia and southeastern Europe experienced much drier-than-normal conditions during the summer.

Outside Europe, drier-than-average conditions were recorded across large parts of the southern United States and northern Mexico, parts of Canada, the Maghreb, parts of the Horn of Africa, Siberia, large areas of Central Asia, China, South America, South Africa and northern Australia.

Further warming beyond the 1.5-degree threshold could increase the risk of reaching climate tipping points. Such thresholds could lead to substantial additional warming and irreversible damage to key stabilizing components of the climate system, including Arctic ice and the Amazon rainforest.

By

The Associated Press

                    Rick Rycroft/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

MELBOURNE, Australia — Australia plans to double potential fines for social media platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, who fail to prevent Australian children from holding accounts as critics argue the world-first ban on under-16s was failing.

Communications Minister Anika Wells on Monday blamed the platforms' resistance to the age restrictions for the need to toughen the laws that came into force on Dec. 10.

"We can all agree we would like the scheme to work better than it is currently, but that is on Big Tech taking the Mickey," Wells told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., using an Australian slang term for deceiving, teasing or mocking.

The government announced Sunday it would introduce draft legislation into Parliament this week that would double the maximum fine to 99 million Australian dollars ($68 million) for platforms that fail to take reasons steps to prevent Australian children from holding accounts.

The amendments would also increase the powers of eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant, Australia's online safety watchdog, to demand information and documents to ensure platforms were complying with Australian law, a government statement said.

The new powers would also include information from third parties, such as age assurance technology providers, to test claims made by the platforms about how those under 16 continued to circumvent the ban, the statement said.

Senior opposition lawmaker Jane Hume said her party would consider voting for the reforms, saying the "social media ban wasn't working" because of deficient laws.

"The legislation was clearly undercooked in the first place. The eSafety Commissioner wasn't given the powers to be able to pursue these Big Tech companies," Hume said.

Parliament passed the initial legislation with overwhelming support in 2024. The targeted platforms were given more than 12 months to plan to implement the ban.

Many countries who have implemented or are planning similar restrictions have been closely watching progress of Australia's ban.

The government initially reported more than 5 million children had accounts removed, deactivated or restricted after the ban became law.

But eSafety reported in March that seven in 10 children who held accounts on restricted platforms on Dec. 10 remained on Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok.

Inman Grant said in April she was considering court action against those platforms and YouTube, alleging they were not taking reasonable steps to exclude children.

She had been satisfied with progress made by the remaining restricted platforms: X, Kick, Reddit, Threads and Twitch.

Wells said she had received monthly updates from eSafety since March and "we are not seeing improvements."

"These (draft) changes ensure that the eSafety Commissioner has the tools and powers she needs to hold platforms to account and we're making sure that she can do just that," Wells said.

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures show migration growth is above pre-pandemic levels but tracking steadily down

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Net overseas migration added 301,000 people to Australia’s population last year, the lowest increase since mid-2022 but still above the pre-pandemic pace.

The new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics come amid an increasingly fraught political debate around immigration, after Pauline Hanson’s declaration that Australian society should be “monocultural”.

After collapsing below zero during the Covid lockdowns, annual migration growth sprang back to as high as 556,000 in late 2023.

Since then, net overseas migration (Nom) has tracked steadily down – a fact the government has been keen to emphasise amid repeated attacks from the Coalition that Labor has failed to bring the numbers of arrivals back to “sustainable” levels.

In a statement after the release of the data, the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said “the facts clearly show that net overseas migration is coming down under Labor”.

The May budget had forecast Nom – the difference between the number of migrants arriving and leaving – would drop to 295,000 people in this financial year; to 245,000 in the next; and 225,000 in 2027-28.

But Terry Rawnsley, a senior economist at KPMG, said “the nation looks to have settled into a new normal level of net overseas migration of around 300,000 people per year”.

That would be about 25%, or 50,000, above historical levels, with the increase explained by strong migration into Queensland and Western Australia.

“The sunshine state is bringing in 75% more people from overseas than before Covid, while on the west coast there has been a 250% increase,” Rawnsley said.

“These large increases are reflective of the two states’ strong economies. Both are having to tap overseas workers to fill the jobs their economies are creating.”

In contrast, net overseas migration into NSW and Victoria is back to pre-pandemic levels, he said.

Despite the bulge in net overseas migration over the past few years, Australia’s population in mid-2025 was still about 350,000 less than Treasury predicted in the December 2019 mid-year budget and before the global health crisis.

But Jonathon Duniam, the shadow immigration minister, said annual net overseas migration of 301,000 was “still far too high”.

“Particularly at a time when Australians are struggling to find a home, rents remain under extreme pressure and public infrastructure and services are badly stretched.”
baby-purchasing-commercial-surrogacy-202:
The consequences of our unregulated commercial surrogacy industry continue despite receiving government and media attention.

The rent-a-womb business is booming, and politicians and the media are finally noticing the wild, wild West of third-party reproduction. That attention alone, however, doesn’t rectify the moral, ethical, and even national security costs that come with a largely unregulated surrogacy industry. If you want proof that the problems with third-party reproduction persist, take one look at the surrogacy news cycle over the last two weeks.

On September 9, an Alaskan surrogate who moved to Texas to protect the baby she was carrying from the abortion his parents demanded due to a treatable heart condition asked the Supreme Court to intervene in her legally complicated custody battle. Questions about whether McKenna West should have any authority on the life and care of the baby she carried for nine months continue to swirl as courts in several states attempt to sort out who gets a say over the child’s treatment.

No judicial body so far has a great answer for the situation because the legal system isn’t equipped to adequately address the fact that every surrogacy arrangement, even those that seemingly end well, involves commodifying human lives and violating natural rights.

Mere days after West filed her emergency application, CBS published an article exposing that “Loopholes and shady practices taint U.S. surrogacy industry.” The report highlighted the stories of several women who were paid to gestate babies for elderly couples and foreigners who had covertly commissioned the creation and carrying of multiple children by multiple surrogates.

The Trump administration is enforcing its promises to protect the “meaning and value of American citizenship” by targeting birth tourism schemes exploited by foreigners — mostly people from China. Fox News’ Bill Melugin reported this week that the State Department “revoked more than 2,300 visas in connection with birth tourism since announcing their birth tourism task force last month.”

[RELATED: Chinese Social Media Chatter Indicates Trump’s Birth Tourism Crackdown Is Starting To Work]

NEW: The U.S. State Department tells @FoxNews they've revoked more than 2,300 visas in connection with birth tourism since announcing their birth tourism task force last month.

Yet, the consequences of America’s unmonitored and expansive commercial surrogacy enterprise continue.

One of the women CBS interviewed believed she was providing surrogacy services to “a single father looking to expand his family.” Her suspicions about the rent-a-womb contract mounted when she learned the same man had allegedly hired at least two dozen others to have his children.

“Judy” reportedly pushed to meet the intended parent paying her five times over the course of her pregnancy. It was documents obtained by CBS, however, that ultimately revealed the purchaser was none other than Chinese billionaire Xu Bo.

Bo might be known in China for his fantasy video game empire. In America, however, he’s known as the noncitizen who allegedly purchased more than 100 children (some reports say 300) — all of whom entitled to American citizenship after being born on U.S. soil — by exploiting our nation’s birth tourism weak spots.

The Wall Street Journal noted last year that Bo granted nannies in the U.S. care of his freshly born children because he was too busy in China to be at their births. That factoid is alarmingly reminiscent of the story of Kyla Simpson, who gestated three babies, raised them for months, and even navigated one of their deaths, after the Chinese man who commissioned their creation failed to pick them up at birth.

Bo disputes the exact number of babies he’s commissioned. Yet he’s repeatedly insisted that “having more children can solve all problems.”

In past social media posts, Bo publicly expressed a desire for “50 high-quality sons” and hoped his kids will marry Elon Musk’s offspring. In a recent statement, Bo confessed that his life’s goal, including his mass third-party reproduction strategy, is “to benefit the long-term development of the Chinese nation.”

Chinese billionaire Xu Bo has allegedly purchased 100+ children who are considered U.S. citizens simply because they were born to surrogates on American soil. Foreigners are exploiting our lax rent-a-womb industry to “benefit the long-term development of the Chinese nation.” pic.twitter.com/t7EgHAp3Gs

CBS’s curiosity about the ethical pitfalls that have dominated American commercial surrogacy and the Trump administration’s attempts to address them is a step in the right direction, but it’s simply not enough. Babies and the women who carry them deserve better.

By ASHLEY NICKEL, NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA and JOANNA HYNDS FOR DAILY MAIL

Published:  18:12 AEST, 9 September 2026   |  Updated:  18:28 AEST, 9 September 2026

An Australian man who was caught having sex on the driveway of a resident's home has been deported from Bali and told not to return for a decade.

Brisbane man Billy Aspinall, 27, was arrested at Denpasar Airport on Wednesday as he was preparing to board a flight home to Australia. He then spent two weeks in immigration detention.

It followed CCTV footage surfacing of a man and woman allegedly engaged in a sex act outside a home in Tibubeneng village, North Kuta, on August 22.

The footage later went viral, prompting police to place Aspinall on a watch list for public indecency.

Indonesian authorities on Wednesday confirmed the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office had deported Aspinall.

He was also banned from entering Indonesia for the next ten years.

Aspinall was loaded onto a Batik Air flight from Denpasar to Brisbane on Tuesday night.

Head of the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office, Muhamad Novyandri, said the deportation was essential to maintain public order.

Billy Aspinall (above), from Brisbane, spent two weeks in detention before being deported

Aspinall was allegedly caught having sex with a woman on the driveway (above) of a home in North Kuta on August 22

Billy Aspinall (above) was deported from Bali on Tuesday night

'We will continue to strengthen immigration oversight and coordinate closely with law enforcement authorities, while taking firm action if any violations of applicable immigration regulations are found in the future,' he said.

It's understood the owner of the home had caught Aspinall and an unknown woman having sex in her driveway while she was on her way to a prayer session.

She'd yelled at them to stop but they allegedly ignored her.

North Kuta police described the incident as an 'immoral act' and claimed it lasted 15 minutes.

Residents performed a 'purification ceremony' on the driveway in the days following.

Facial recognition technology helped officers identify and intercept Aspinall at the airport on August 26.

Aspinall could have been given up to one year in prison for allegedly committing an 'immoral act', but instead was handed over to immigration authorities for deportation.

Badung Police chief Joseph Edward Purba at the time noted the homeowner had chosen not to press charges.

Aspinall (left) was loaded onto a Batik Air flight from Denpasar to Brisbane on Tuesday night

The Australian (second-left) was banned from entering Indonesia for 10 years

Aspinall told police he had been in Bali for four days to attend his friend's wedding.

He said he did not know the name or nationality of the woman involved, as they had both been drinking.

'He said that he met the woman in a club on the beach near the house,' said police investigator Azarul Ahmad.

Police were searching for the woman, who they believe was a tourist.

Indonesia has overhauled its Criminal Code which now criminalises premarital sex, cohabitation and public drunkenness.

Under the new laws adopted in January, adultery, premarital sex and cohabitation, or unmarried couples living together, are now potential crimes with penalties ranging from between six months to a year in jail.

By Simon Smale

By Henry Hanson

Topic:Cricket

Australia endured another torrid day in Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack has been ground into the Darwin dirt, experiencing another torrid day against Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium.

Led by a sparkling maiden Test ton to rookie-opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh lost just five wickets on day two, reaching stumps on 6-351 and 153 first-innings runs ahead of their hosts.

After an opening day that saw Australia bowled out for a well below-par 198, Pat Cummins's men picked up where they left off on day two, struggling for ideas and inspiration against a disciplined Bangladeshi batting line-up.

Mitchell Starc took the only wicket in an energy-sapping morning session for Australia, while Steve Smith was uncharacteristically slow in reacting to a deflected Tanzid edge, that, if taken, would have seen the opener depart for 62.

Tanzid, playing just his second Test match, took 188 balls to reach his century, and brought it up with a push back past Nathan Lyon after a nervous period in the 90s.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, the 25-year-old threw his wicket away only a matter of balls later, caught in the deep after mistiming an ill-advised slog against Lyon for 101.

That was the only wicket to fall in the second session as captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, who had shared a 93-run partnership with Tanzid, continued to take the fight to the Australians alongside 39-year-old, 103-Test veteran Mushfiqur Rahim.

Bangladesh's lead by the time the new ball was taken stood at 91, with seven wickets remaining.

Starc instantly got the new ball talking, sending the first ball swinging past the bat and stumps of Shanto to the giant left hander's complete disbelief.

But it was Hazlewood who made the breakthrough in his first over, finding the edge of Shanto to have him caught at second slip by Steve Smith for 84.

Starc got in on the act three overs later, having Litton Das caught behind, also by Smith, for a 12-ball duck.

Then Pat Cummins joined the party to find the edge of Mushfiqur, and give Smith a third consecutive catch, Australia's three great pacemen striking with fearsome force to reduce Bangladesh from 3-297 to 6-308.

That third catch put Smith level with Joe Root on 218 catches, the most ever in Test cricket by a non wicketkeeper.

But Australia once again toiled as the lacquer faded from the new ball, with six-wicket hero from day one, Hasan Mahmud (13 not out), providing able support to all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who reached stumps on 32.

A man in Colorado who had been free on a $3 million bond in his wife’s alleged killing was arrested Friday after prosecutors said he got in a hit-and-run crash with two other vehicles in Denver.

Barry Morphew was booked into the Boulder County Jail.

Alamosa County District Judge Amanda Hopkins set a hearing to discuss Morphew’s bond Tuesday, online records show.

Under the terms of his bond set last year, Morphew was not supposed to travel away from home in southern Colorado except for work and other limited circumstances.

“To go to the airport for any purpose other than work constitutes a breach of his bond,” read the filing by District Attorney Anne Kelly.

Morphew’s attorneys didn’t immediately respond to phone and email messages seeking comment Friday.

Morphew has pleaded not guilty and faces trial next summer in the death of his wife, who disappeared in 2020.

Suzanne Morphew’s skeletal remains were found off a dirt road in southern Colorado in 2023.

By then, charges against Barry Morphew had been dropped, but he was charged again with first-degree murder in his wife’s death and arrested.

Investigators found no sign of trauma in Suzanne Morphew’s remains but allegedly found traces in her bone marrow of a drug cocktail used to tranquilize wildlife.

Barry Morphew was the only person in the area other than wildlife officials with authorization to use the chemicals, prosecutors allege.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass carried far more Latino-majority neighborhoods than her rivals in last week’s primary election, an analysis of precinct data shows, helping her finish first and qualify for the Nov. 3 runoff with City Councilmember Nithya Raman.

Bass carried 35 Latino-majority neighborhoods, including Boyle Heights, Pacoima and Historic South-Central. That was a 46% increase from 2022, when she won 24 Latino-majority neighborhoods in a primary race against Rick Caruso and Kevin de León, according to a Times analysis of election data.

Raman was a distant second, winning seven Latino-majority neighborhoods including Highland Park, El Sereno and Lincoln Heights.

Pratt won a single Latino-majority neighborhood, Harbor City, which is 51% Latino, the analysis found.

Bass’ strong showing among Latinos was credited in part to her forceful challenge of the Trump administration’s immigration raids and mass detentions last year.

“Latinos came out for her because she has done a really, really good job in trying to fight the Trump administration,” said Nilza Serrano, the president of Avance Democratic Club, a Latino Democratic organization, which endorsed Bass.

Politics

Los Angeles primary election map: See how your neighborhood voted for Karen Bass, Spencer Pratt and Nithya Raman in the 2026 L.A. mayoral race.

Avance endorsed Caruso in the runoff with Bass four years ago, leading Bass to suggest Caruso bought their support. She later apologized to the group. This time around, she worked behind the scenes to secure endorsements from Democratic clubs like Avance and from important Latino activists such as Dolores Huerta and politicians like U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.).

“She had a lot more established politicos and respected figures in the Latino community,” said Matt Barreto, a professor of political science and Chicana/o studies at UCLA. “It makes her seem like the more established choice.”

Bass was helped by the fact that Caruso wasn’t in the race this year. Four years ago, Caruso flooded airwaves and televisions with Spanish-language ads as he poured more than $100 million into his mayoral campaign.

Bass carried more Latino-majority neighborhoods than Caruso overall in 2022 — 24 to Caruso’s 16 — but Caruso actually performed better in the most heavily Latino neighborhoods, with 34% of the vote in neighborhoods with populations that are at least 80% Latino. Bass had 27% of that vote in 2022.

This year, Bass took 38% of that vote while Raman had 25%. Pratt had about 17% support in those areas.

Barreto noted that Pratt didn’t take a strong stand against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, hurting his appeal to Latinos.

During the sole mayoral debate between the three candidates May 6, Pratt said there wouldn’t be major ICE raids on his watch.

“If they’re legal or illegal, if they’re a danger — I want them off our streets, that’s what I said,” Pratt said. “ICE won’t be coming here because … everybody they’re supposedly looking for, they’re going to be in jail when I’m mayor.”

Pratt didn’t have a coherent message for Latino voters, and didn’t have prominent Latinos campaigning on his behalf, noted Fernando Guerra, the director of the Center for the Study of Los Angeles at Loyola Marymount University.

“Why would he get any votes when he didn’t have a message, didn’t have a messenger and didn’t have a vehicle for that message?” Guerra asked. “He didn’t fund to organize a ground game in any of the Latino neighborhoods.”

Pratt’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Latinos make up about 37% of the electorate in Los Angeles, but polls conducted before the election suggested no single candidate had a lock on their votes.

Bass was leading among Latinos in a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll, co-sponsored by The Times, in March with 29% support, followed by Pratt at 16%, with Raman at the bottom at 9%.

But in a May poll by Berkeley IGS, Raman shot up among Latinos to 24% with Pratt at 21% and Bass at 20%.

The precinct-level data released by the county doesn’t show how Latinos specifically voted, but how precincts voted. The Times compared those results with census data for its analysis.

Like Bass, Raman made a concerted effort to win the Latino vote. She came out with ads in Spanish and had numerous events in heavily Latino areas, including doing a happy hour in Boyle Heights, meeting with street vendors and customers in Pico-Union and speaking with business owners on Olvera Street.

Six of the Latino-majority neighborhoods Raman won — El Sereno, Lincoln Heights, Highland Park, Montecito Heights, Glassell Park and Cypress Park — were flipped from supporting Bass in 2022. The seventh she won, Westlake, was carried by Caruso in 2022.

Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. from India with her family as a child, said in a statement that she was “proud to have co-authored L.A.’s Sanctuary City Ordinance and I will enforce it without apology as mayor. I will expand deportation defense funding and make sure no city data is ever used for immigration enforcement.

“I’ll work every day to make Los Angeles more affordable and create more opportunity, so that Latino families — and all families — can afford to live here and thrive,” Raman said.

Marco Santana, 35, a longtime Van Nuys resident who ran for City Council in 2023, said he was considering supporting Bass until Raman got into the race.

“For me, it’s not just being Latino, it’s also the intersectionality of being relatively young, being first generation,” Santana said. “I feel this sense of urgency from her.”

Bass flipped Boyle Heights and Historic South-Central, two neighborhoods that were won by  De León in 2022. She also took Pacoima, Arleta and Sylmar — all areas in the San Fernando Valley that Caruso won in the 2022 primary.

Her campaign said it was organic support that drew Latinos to her.

“This wasn’t some campaign strategy. Karen Bass is the parent of Latino kids and grandchildren and has been in the trenches with these communities for decades,” said Alex Stack, a campaign spokesperson for Bass. “Karen Bass has always fought for the Latino community.”

Stephenie Lucio, a resident of Northridge, had been undecided up until about a week before the election. She said she thought Bass hadn’t done enough to address the issues that are top of mind for her, including homelessness and the impact immigration raids have had on Latinos in L.A.

But in the end she said she voted for Bass, albeit “a little bit reluctantly,” seeing the incumbent as “really speaking up about things that are important to me and the Latino community.”

Administrators for a major housing developer have met a crucial funding deadline, but negotiations to keep the group afloat remain ongoing.

Insolvency advisory Teneo has been scrambling to secure $20million in short-term funding for the embattled Bathla Group since it entered voluntary administration in late August.

As administrator, Teneo set a deadline of Thursday to secure the cash injection, which is when payroll for Bathla's staff fell due.

On Thursday afternoon, Teneo announced it was yet to secure the short-term funding it is seeking from lenders but enough cash had been found to pay wages accrued since August 25.

The partial payment covers the period since Teneo was appointed administrator, but will not meet all wages owed by Bathla, with some staff having not been paid for weeks.

Administrator Stephen Longley said Bathla's employees had engaged with Teneo constructively, but stressed the payroll target was only the first hurdle.

'The situation is complex,' he said in a statement, adding the short-term funding administrators are still attempting to secure would only afford a few weeks of breathing room.

A Bathla insider told the Daily Mail: 'Truth is they have no bad intentions. They want to survive.'

Bathla Group (above) has received enough funding to cover its costs since it appointed an administrator in late August

Teneo will now set its sights on the first formal creditors' meeting slated for Friday, where those owed money would engage with administrators, he said.

The news left countless homebuyers and creditors wondering what it meant for their investments, with staff uncertain whether they would lose their jobs.

A $20million one-month injection would allow administrators to pursue longer-term funding and progress the group's 45 projects under construction.

Should they fail to secure a lifeline from lenders, the home developer is expected to be wound up after the NSW government declined to bail it out.

According to Bathla's website, the group has 20,000 apartments and 7,000 dwellings in its delivery pipeline, added to the scores of projects under construction, centred mainly in Sydney's northwest.

The projects comprise a significant share of the NSW government's target of 75,400 new homes a year for five years until 2029.

The cash injection is not enough to meet all wages owed by Bathla, with some staff having not been paid for weeks

Founded in NSW in 1997, Bathla joins a long list of Australian home developers which have recently entered voluntary administration or liquidation.

How does a major property developer collapse during a housing shortage?

That's the question confronting thousands of would-be homeowners after Sydney-based Bathla Group entered voluntary administration with an estimated $3.6billion in liabilities, leaving up to 15,000 homes and 500 jobs hanging in the balance.

The developer, which built its reputation delivering budget-friendly housing across Sydney's booming north-west, blamed a combination of weakening sales, rising construction costs and tighter lending conditions for its downfall.

In an Instagram post, Bathla Group managing director Bhart Bhushan described the company's financial troubles as the result of a 'perfect storm' of softening sales, tax changes and escalating building costs.

'These changes in market conditions have had flow-on effects to lending markets, putting further pressure on the business,' he said.

The warning signs were already flashing

Days before the company collapsed, NSW regulators fined Bathla and imposed stricter licence conditions over insurance lapses following months of complaints from purchasers left waiting on delayed projects.

The action came amid growing concern about financial pressures across the construction sector as developers grapple with supply chain delays, higher costs, tighter margins and weaker demand from investors.

Bathla Group builds budget-friendly housing estates, townhouses and apartments across Sydney

Bathla Group managing director Bhart Bhushan (pictured) cited a 'perfect storm' of softening sales, tax change impacts, and higher construction costs

Up to 15,000 homes that were under construction are now under a cloud of uncertainty

Housing Industry Association NSW executive director Brad Armitage said the industry is experiencing difficult conditions that mean many projects, especially in Western Sydney, are not feasible.

'Margins are beginning to recover but recent federal budget tax changes on the back of multiple rate rises means that market confidence is at an all-time low,' he told the Daily Mail.

'This is leading to more uncertainty in builders' and developers' pipelines... this means investment starts to go elsewhere, with many builders looking to commercial building work or even other investments altogether.'

Mr Armitage said while finance and lending conditions are making it harder for developers to bring projects to market or complete existing developments, it was tax settings, including the Foreign Investor surcharge and recent capital gains and negative gearing changes, which were having a much bigger impact.

'The housing industry has been calling for more support to make projects 'stack up' for years, so everybody already knew all of the issues contributing to this before today,' he said.

'What hasn't been looked at seriously is the enormous cost of infrastructure being heaped on new home buyers, though the entire community benefits, and without a drastic change, entry-level housing first home buyers can afford, will continue to be difficult to deliver.'

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed Bathla's collapse was due to the mounting pressures facing the residential construction sector, with developers squeezed by rising interest rates, soaring construction costs, project delays and a slowdown in new-home sales.

Mr Oliver said insolvencies among developers had remained elevated since the pandemic, warning the industry was still grappling with many of the same challenges that triggered a wave of collapses several years ago.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver (pictured) said Bathla's collapse reflected the mounting pressures facing the residential construction sector

'Property developers and home builders are getting hit from all angles: higher interest rates, higher costs, delays in completing things, more regulation and, more recently, a decline in new home sales,' he said.

Bathla's downfall appears to have been fuelled in part by its reliance on private-credit lenders. Traditional banks grew increasingly cautious about funding residential developments amid rising costs and weaker market conditions.

Mr Oliver said banks became more reluctant to lend to the sector because projects were riskier, pushing some developers towards private-credit providers who were willing to take on greater risk in exchange for higher returns.

'If the banks won't lend them any more, often they've got to issue debt that is taken up by these private credit funds,' he said.

'Private credit funds tend to be a more risky investment than a corporate bond fund.'

Mr Oliver said large corporate collapses often appeared to come out of nowhere because publicly acknowledging financial distress could trigger an immediate loss of sales and funding.

'If they were out there saying, ''It looks like we may not make it'', that would make life even more difficult for them, because home sales would dry up and any new loans they need would be harder to get,' he said.

Far-reaching impacts

Despite Australia's housing shortage, Mr Oliver said many projects were no longer stacking up financially, with developers facing higher interest rates on top of the rising construction expenses and falling demand for newly built homes.

Bathla's website claims its broader development pipeline includes 22,000 apartment dwellings and a further 3,500 homes highlighting the enormous scale of the collapse

'The collapse highlights the uncomfortable reality that even during a housing shortage, developers can fail when construction costs, borrowing costs and weak sales make projects unviable,' he said.

The failure also highlights the growing difficulty of meeting the federal government's target of building 1.2 million new homes over five years.

'We're running way below target already,' Mr Oliver said, noting housing completions have been falling well short of the pace required to meet the goal.

Bathla formally entered voluntary administration on Tuesday, with restructuring firm Teneo appointed to assess the group's finances and attempt to stabilise operations.

While administrators have estimated up to 15,000 homes could be affected, Bathla's website claims its broader development pipeline includes 22,000 apartment dwellings and a further 3,500 homes, highlighting the enormous scale of the collapse and the potential impact on buyers, subcontractors and lenders.

Teneo's Stephen Longley said urgent discussions with lenders were underway.

'Our priority is to stabilise the business so that construction activity and property settlements can continue in the ordinary course,' he said.

'Our objective is to ensure project continuity wherever practicable and work with lenders to minimise disruption for employees, customers and contractors.'

Mr Bhushan said appointing administrators was the best way to protect stakeholders and maximise the chances of completing thousands of homes amid Australia's ongoing housing crisis.

The company's main entity, Universal Property Group, owes almost $3.2billion, while related building arm Raj & Jai Construction carried liabilities of about $304million at the end of the 2024-25 financial year.

President Donald Trump speaks to reporters at the White House about Iran, falling oil prices, and making daylight saving time permanent.

The battle over Americans’ clocks reemerged in an unlikely way over the weekend, with President Donald Trump picking a fight with one of his top allies over the issue.

There have been many fights in Congress over the nearly two years that Trump has been in office for his second term that either ended in partisan victory or gloriously fizzled out, but one has quietly gone onto the shelf despite his pressure on Republicans to do something about it.

And that fight is over allowing states to voluntarily observe Daylight Saving Time year-round to effectively do away with the twice-a-year ritual of changing clocks. It’s a popular issue with voters and the president, and there’s a bill that passed the House this summer to enact the change. But it’s a policy issue that has divided both sides of the aisle and ground to a halt in the upper chamber.

TRUMP URGES SENATE TO PASS BILL MAKING DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME PERMANENT AFTER OVERWHELMING HOUSE VOTE

President Donald Trump wants to make daylight saving permanent, but a geographic coalition of northern versus southern states are in a heated debate over the merits of the change, which spells doom for the bill. (Evan Vucci-Pool/Getty Images; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., has been one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, vowing to block any attempts to fast-track it on the floor. That resistance earned him a Truth Social post from Trump, who over the weekend shared his personal phone number in a bid to pressure the lawmaker to change his stance on Daylight Saving Time.

"Almost everybody wants "The Sunshine Protection Act" to pass, except for Tom Cotton," Trump said. "To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself."

Cotton responded, and noted that Congress has tackled Daylight Saving Time before, only to roll back the change shortly after.

"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first."

TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END

In the 1970s, lawmakers did enact year-round Daylight Saving Time. But Americans rapidly soured on the change, especially parents whose children had to wait in the dark for the school bus. It was repealed about a year later.

And Cotton recently answered an off-the-cuff question from a fellow Republican during their weekly closed-door policy lunches, a source told Fox News Digital, where he made a similar case as his response to Trump. No one pushed back during the meeting.

The issue of Daylight Saving Time, and supporting a permanent fix or sticking to the status quo is more geographical than political.

It’s, in part, mountainous and Western states versus coastal states. On one side of the spectrum are lawmakers like Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Patty Murray, D-Wash., who introduced a Senate version of the bill last year.

"Every year, more Americans grow more frustrated setting their clocks back and forth, and every winter folks in Washington state despair at the prospect of losing an hour of precious sunlight when we are forced off Daylight Saving Time," Murray said in a statement at the time.

Lawyers for the BBC said the Trump family members ‘without question have personal knowledge’ about his behaviour leading up to the attack.

The BBC has attempted to force Donald Trump's family to testify over his £7.4billion defamation lawsuit

A new Christmas special of Doctor Who has been cancelled while the BBC plans the next phase of the sci-fi show.

The corporation announced last year that there would be a festive special in 2026, but confirmed on Wednesday that it will no longer proceed.

Instead, the broadcaster is inviting production companies to put themselves forward to help co-produce the next series.

Showrunner Russell T Davies also confirmed he will leave the long-running programme, writing on Instagram that it is "goodbye from me but hello to a big new future for the show".

Referring to the announcement of the Christmas special, he explained: "We only cooked that up to guarantee a future when no one knew what would happen, but now we do know, there's no need for it.

"You'll have to wait a bit longer for new Doctor Who... but you'll be waiting for more Doctor Who than a one-off. So it's worth it!

"For the record: there was no script, I never wrote it, and no actor was ever approached to play the next Doctor."

In a statement, the corporation said the decision to cancel the Christmas episode was made "after careful consideration" and "had not been taken lightly".

The last series of Doctor Who aired in May 2025 and was the final one to star Ncuti Gatwa, who had announced he was leaving after two series.

The finale saw his Doctor regenerate, and the episode closed with the surprise reintroduction of Billie Piper, who previously played Rose Tyler in the show.

It was not clear whether that meant Piper would become the next Doctor, and the BBC only said at the time that "just how and why she is back remains to be seen".

Since 2023, Doctor Who had been co-produced by Cardiff-based production company Bad Wolf, while the BBC struck a deal with Disney+ to co-produce and distribute the show internationally.

But Disney's involvement came to an end in 2025 after 26 episodes, and it was confirmed the company would no longer be involved with the show.

On Wednesday, the BBC gave more details of Doctor Who's next era and said it had collectively decided, along with Davies and Bad Wolf, not to go ahead with the planned Christmas episode.

"This decision was not taken lightly, and we know it will be disappointing for fans," the corporation said.

"But in order to set the show up for future series, it was decided that, rather than bridge the gap with a one off special, we are choosing to push forward to invest in the long-term future of the show which ensures that when the Tardis lands once more, it does so in all its glory."

The BBC said the plan was "part of securing the next phase of the show for future generations".

A spokesman said the the programme "remains an important part of the BBC" and the decision to put the show out to competitive tender "underpins the BBC's continued commitment to Doctor Who".

The BBC noted that putting the series out to tender was in line with the corporation's Charter and Agreement requirements.

In his Instagram post, Davies said he was "as excited as anyone to see what comes next!"

He added: "Will they keep the theme tune? Will they lose the blue box? Will they bring back the Drahvin?! It's all up for grabs, which is so Doctor Who, exciting and unpredictable and new! Here comes the future."

A previously announced new Doctor Who animation series for CBeebies remains in production.

Doctor Who originally ran from 1963 to 1989, but was revived by Davies in 2005 with Christopher Eccleston in the lead role.

Since then, David Tennant, Matt Smith, Peter Capaldi and Jodie Whittaker have played the Doctor, under showrunners including Davies, Steven Moffat and Chris Chibnall.

Davies returned to the series as showrunner in 2022, and oversaw the show during the Ncuti Gatwa era.

The Luton-born actor appeared in the most watched episode of Doctor Who alongside Tom Baker.

Brendan Sheppard and friends spent two years recreating the console room at home in Lincolnshire.

The sci-fi series currently faces an uncertain future after its annual Christmas special was axed for the second year in a row.

California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton wants the FBI to re-interview rival Xavier Becerra in a federal corruption case linked to the alleged theft of $225,000 from Becerra’s campaign account.

In a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of California Eric Grant dated Aug. 30, Hilton demanded that Becerra be questioned again after three figures close to him were federally indicted in November 2025 and have since pleaded guilty.

The case centers on money allegedly funneled from Becerra’s dormant campaign account through a consulting firm run by Dana Williamson, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s former chief of staff, and ultimately to the wife of Sean McCluskie, Becerra’s longtime aide and former chief of staff.

McCluskie, Williamson and Sacramento lobbyist Greg Campbell have all pleaded guilty.

Hilton and California attorney general candidate Michael Gates argue that evidence developed since Becerra’s initial interview raises questions about what he knew.

Hilton told the California Post that Becerra needs to be pressed about his knowledge of the payments.

“He needs to be put under oath and asked very direct questions about every aspect of this,” Hilton said, adding that Becerra should not be allowed to “get away with vague answers.”

Hilton said he believes Becerra was not the focus when federal investigators previously interviewed him because the investigation had centered on other people.

“But since that, he is now a candidate for governor, and when you look at the things that he’s been saying, it’s completely inconsistent with the evidence,” Hilton said.

“He’s given two separate answers in television interviews. On one occasion, he said he knew about the money transfers, but he didn’t know what they were for. And on another occasion, he said he didn’t even know about them at all.”

Hilton and Gates argue that Becerra was interviewed before Williamson and McCluskie pleaded guilty and before investigators had developed all of the evidence now available to prosecutors.

“He was not pressed on the central question: What did he know about the scheme involving his own campaign account and his own chief of staff?” they wrote in the letter.

The candidates pointed to allegations in the federal indictment involving “Public Official 1,” whom Becerra has publicly identified as himself.

According to the letter, the indictment alleges that McCluskie spoke with Public Official 1 when the payments were established and again when the method used to route the money changed. It also alleges that McCluskie told Public Official 1 that $10,000 a month was a reasonable payment and that false campaign disclosures were reviewed by “McCluskie and/or Public Official 1.”

Hilton told the California Post that communications between McCluskie and Williamson are among the evidence he believes investigators should confront Becerra with.

“That suggests that he did know,” Hilton said. “I don’t know whether he knew, I don’t know whether he lied, but the public deserves to know the answers.”

Hilton claimed there’s a possibility Becerra knew about the alleged scheme because its purpose was to provide additional money that would allow McCluskie to accompany Becerra to Washington when Becerra became U.S. Health and Human Services secretary under the Biden administration.

“The whole point of it was for Becerra to have his guy with him,” Hilton said. “So the idea that he didn’t know about it, to me, is hard to believe.”

Becerra has consistently denied knowing that the payments were part of a criminal scheme, although his descriptions of what he knew have varied.

On Monday, Becerra’s spokesman, Jonathan Underland, completely dismissed Hilton’s claims.

“Reading comprehension is an important skill for the next governor, and Steve is clearly struggling,” he said.

”The Justice Department’s own filings are clear: Xavier Becerra was the victim. The people who stole from him pled guilty and now owe him $225,000 in restitution.”

After McCluskie and Williamson were charged, Becerra acknowledged knowing that payments were coming out of his campaign account.

“I knew what was being paid,” Becerra told FOX40, while adding, “What I didn’t know was all the underlying activity that was occurring that was against the law.”

Becerra has previously said he believed the payments were legitimate fees for managing his dormant campaign account and that he relied on McCluskie to handle the matter.

“I was told that’s the rate I would have to pay to get someone who could manage that and make sure that I don’t have to worry about [violating any federal rules],” Becerra told the Los Angeles Times.

The federal indictment says Becerra was told Williamson would receive $10,000 a month to manage the campaign account and that McCluskie’s wife would work for Williamson’s company. But prosecutors alleged that Becerra was not told that campaign money would ultimately be routed to McCluskie or that McCluskie’s wife would allegedly hold a no-work job.

Becerra has also disputed remembering some of the conversations described in court records. After McCluskie’s plea agreement stated that he told Becerra about his wife working for the consultants, Becerra told the Los Angeles Times that he did not recall McCluskie telling him that.

Following Williamson’s guilty plea, Becerra was more categorical.

“I did nothing wrong. Case closed,” he wrote on X.

Becerra spokesman, Jonathan Underland, has previously said he “had no idea what was going on” and that the scheme was designed to deceive him.

Federal prosecutors have characterized Becerra as a victim, and he has not been charged with a crime.

Hilton and Gates aren’t the only ones questioning Becerra’s statements about the case.

Billionaire Tom Steyer’s campaign pointed to an ABC10 report about comments from McGregor Scott, an attorney for Williamson, concerning evidence obtained during discovery.

ABC10 reporter Becca Haiger said Scott told her that McCluskie had represented to Williamson that he had cleared the arrangement with Becerra.

“I asked if there’s documentation of that reassurance, if McCluskie had texted it or something to Williamson, and he said in discovery, it’s not public record, but in discovery there are electronic records of McCluskie telling Williamson ‘Becerra okayed this,’” Haiger reported, according to Steyer’s campaign.

“Becerra can’t tweet his way out of tough questions,” Steyer campaign spokesperson Danni Wang said. “Voters deserve to know about his role: Is he incompetent, or is he corrupt?”

Asked how he responds to criticism that his demand for another FBI interview could itself be politically motivated, Hilton argued that voters should know the facts before deciding who should become governor.

“That’s in the interests of full information for the voters,” Hilton told the California Post.

The demand comes as the November election approaches, potentially complicating any federal investigation involving a candidate.

The U.S. Department of Justice, however, has longstanding policies often referred to as the “60-day rule”, which generally discourage federal prosecutors from taking overt investigative or prosecutorial steps close to an election if those actions could affect the outcome.

The California Post has contacted the FBI for comment.
